children.title: Bellman Sufficiency Principle
children.top_down_role: Optimal-substructure and information-sufficiency issues specific to finite integer-optimization state models.

children.title: Stagewise Optimal Substructure
children.top_down_role: Optimal-substructure organization over ordered integer decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Stagewise Optimal Substructure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bellman optimality for a finite, deterministic integer-decision process with an exact state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let stages be indexed by \(t=1,\ldots,T\), with state \(s_t\), feasible integer actions \(A_t(s_t)\), transition \(s_{t+1}=F_t(s_t,x_t)\), and additive cost \(c_t(s_t,x_t)\). Define \(V_{T+1}(s)=0\) and \[V_t(s)=\min_{x\in A_t(s)}\{c_t(s,x)+V_{t+1}(F_t(s,x))\}.\] If the state determines every feasible continuation and its future costs, then the restriction of any optimal policy to stages \(t+1,\ldots,T\) is optimal for the subproblem beginning at its reached state \(s_{t+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With an exact state and additive costs, every tail of an optimal integer-decision policy optimally solves the subproblem starting at the reached state.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\) and every \(A_t(s)\) is finite or has an attained minimum.
Future feasibility, transitions, and costs depend on the past only through \(s_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_t(s)=\min_{x\in A_t(s)}\{c_t(s,x)+V_{t+1}(F_t(s,x))\}\), and optimal-policy tails are optimal continuations.

notation.meaning: minimum cost from stage t onward when the current state is s
feasible integer actions at stage t and state s

children.title: Continuation-Equivalence State Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Criteria for retaining exactly the information needed to distinguish feasible continuations.

children.title: State Sufficiency Criteria
children.top_down_role: Information retained by finite integer-optimization states to support valid continuation comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: State Sufficiency Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for aggregating integer-decision histories into a valid dynamic-programming state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a stage \(t\), let \(H_t\) be the set of feasible partial histories and let \(\sigma_t:H_t\to S_t\) be a proposed state map. The map is sufficient for exact representation of the continuation problem if and only if, whenever \(\sigma_t(h)=\sigma_t(h')\) for \(h,h'\in H_t\), the two histories have the same feasible continuation set and every continuation \(y\) feasible after both histories has the same incremental objective value after either history.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state is sufficient for exact continuation representation exactly when equal-state histories have identical feasible continuations and identical incremental costs for every continuation.
assumptions_latex: \(H_t\) contains all feasible histories through stage \(t-1\).
Continuation cost excludes objective value already incurred by the history.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_t(h)=\sigma_t(h')\) implies continuation-feasibility and continuation-cost equivalence of \(h\) and \(h'\).

notation.meaning: set of feasible histories before stage t
proposed history-to-state map at stage t

children.title: Continuation-Equivalence Classes
children.top_down_role: State groupings based on indistinguishable feasible continuation sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuation-Equivalence Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical state classes induced by indistinguishable future integer decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a stage \(t\). For feasible histories \(h,h'\in H_t\), define \(h\sim_t h'\) when their feasible continuation sets coincide and, for every feasible continuation \(y\), their incremental continuation costs coincide. The relation \(\sim_t\) is an equivalence relation. Its quotient \(H_t/{\sim_t}\) is the continuation-equivalence state space, and the canonical state of \(h\) is its class \([h]_t\). Any sufficient state map must be constant only on subsets of these classes; merging histories from different classes loses information relevant to an exact Bellman recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two histories share a canonical state precisely when they admit the same continuations with the same future cost for every continuation.
assumptions_latex: All histories in \(H_t\) terminate immediately before the same decision stage.
Continuation cost excludes objective value already accumulated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_t/{\sim_t}=\{[h]_t:h\in H_t\}\) is the coarsest exact state partition at stage \(t\).

children.title: Insufficient-State Failure Modes
children.top_down_role: Loss of relevant history that causes invalid state aggregation.

knowledge_statements.title: Insufficient-State Failure Modes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnostic boundary for state aggregation that merges continuation-distinguishable histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\sigma_t:H_t\to S_t\) be a proposed state map. It is insufficient for exact representation of continuation problems whenever there exist \(h,h'\in H_t\) with \(\sigma_t(h)=\sigma_t(h')\) such that either their feasible continuation sets differ or some continuation \(y\), feasible after both, has different incremental cost. In the first case, a continuation-feasibility rule depending only on the state cannot reproduce both feasible sets. In the second, a continuation-cost function depending only on the state cannot reproduce both cost functions. Thus no exact Bellman model using only \(\sigma_t(h)\) can represent both continuation problems, although their scalar optimal values may coincide accidentally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Merging histories with different feasible futures or future-cost functions prevents exact state-based representation, even though the two optimal values might accidentally be equal.
assumptions_latex: The recursion uses no information about a history beyond \(\sigma_t(h)\).
Continuation cost excludes objective value already incurred by the history.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Continuation-distinguishable equal-state histories preclude an exact representation of both continuation problems on \(S_t\).

notation.meaning: set of feasible histories before stage t
proposed state space at stage t

children.title: Optimal-Substructure Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: History dependence and coupling that invalidate an incomplete state model.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Substructure Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary at which omitted history invalidates stagewise optimality over the modeled state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Bellman decomposition over a proposed state \(s_t\) is not exact if future feasibility or incremental cost depends on a past quantity not determined by \(s_t\). Concretely, suppose histories \(h,h'\) reach the same \(s_t\), but a remaining integer sequence \(y\) is feasible after exactly one history, or is feasible after both and satisfies \(C_t(h,y)\ne C_t(h',y)\). Then the histories induce different continuation problems despite sharing a modeled state. A model conditioned only on \(s_t\) cannot reproduce both continuation problems, and replacing a continuation after one history by one selected for the other is not guaranteed to preserve feasibility or global optimality. Their scalar optimal values may nevertheless coincide accidentally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimal substructure over the modeled state is not guaranteed when equal states conceal history that changes future feasibility or future-cost functions.
assumptions_latex: The proposed recursion conditions decisions solely on \(s_t\).
At least two feasible histories reach the same modeled state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(s_t\) does not determine the continuation problem, Bellman's state-based replacement argument is not valid in general.

notation.meaning: proposed modeled state at stage t
incremental cost of continuation y after history h

children.title: Integer-DP State Design
children.top_down_role: Canonical state coordinates used to summarize partial integer decisions.

children.title: Ordered-Decision Index States
children.top_down_role: States organized by item, variable, period, or another ordered decision index.

children.title: Stage-Indexed States
children.top_down_role: State organization by periods, layers, or other explicit stages.

knowledge_statements.title: Stage-Indexed States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States whose first coordinate identifies the next ordered decision stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an ordered integer program with decision blocks \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\), a stage-indexed state is a pair \((t,q)\), where \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T+1\}\) identifies the next block to be selected and \(q\in Q_t\) summarizes all continuation-relevant information produced by \(x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1}\). At \((t,q)\), only actions for block \(x_t\) are considered; a feasible action \(u\) produces \((t+1,F_t(q,u))\). The terminal stage \(T+1\) admits no decision. The state is exact only if \(q\) distinguishes all histories having different continuation feasibility or cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stage-indexed state records the next decision stage and a sufficient summary of earlier decisions.
assumptions_latex: Decision blocks have the fixed order \(1,\ldots,T\).
The summary domain \(Q_t\) is defined for every reachable history at stage \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transition has the form \((t,q)\mapsto(t+1,F_t(q,u))\).

notation.meaning: index of the next decision stage
updated summary after feasible action u at stage t

children.title: Variable-Index States
children.top_down_role: State organization by the next integer variable or item under consideration.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Index States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered-variable specialization of stage indexing for scalar integer decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) be integer variables processed in a fixed order. A variable-index state is \((i,q)\), where \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n+1\}\) identifies the next variable \(x_i\) and \(q\) summarizes the continuation-relevant effects of \(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1}\). For \(i\le n\), choosing \(z\in D_i(q)\subseteq\mathbb Z\) sets \(x_i=z\) and yields \((i+1,F_i(q,z))\). The state \((n+1,q)\) is terminal. Exactness requires the feasible domain, transition, and remaining objective to depend on prior assignments only through \((i,q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable-index state identifies the next integer variable and retains the sufficient effects of earlier assignments.
assumptions_latex: Each variable \(x_i\) has an integer domain.
Variables are assigned once in the fixed order \(1,\ldots,n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Assignment \(x_i=z\) induces \((i,q)\mapsto(i+1,F_i(q,z))\).

notation.meaning: index of the next variable assigned
feasible values of the next integer variable at summary q
updated summary after assigning z to variable i

children.title: Ordered-Decision Index Variants
children.top_down_role: Alternative index orders for finite sequential decision models.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordered-Decision Index Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent index conventions for forward and backward ordered-decision recursions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\) ordered decisions, the layer index may represent the next decision, the number already completed, or the number remaining. If \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n+1\}\) is the next-decision index, define \(k=i-1\) and \(r=n-i+1\). Then \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) counts completed decisions and \(r\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) counts remaining decisions. The transformations \(i=k+1=n-r+1\) are bijective. Consequently, recursions indexed by \(i\), \(k\), or \(r\) represent the same layered state graph when their boundary conditions and transition directions are transformed consistently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Next-decision, completed-decision, and remaining-decision indices are bijective conventions for the same layered dynamic program.
assumptions_latex: Exactly \(n\) decisions are processed in a fixed order.
Each transition processes one decision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(i=k+1=n-r+1\), so the three index conventions are equivalent after relabeling layers.

children.title: Resource-Activity State Coordinates
children.top_down_role: States tracking accumulated integer resources or partial constraint activities.

children.title: Accumulated-Resource States
children.top_down_role: Coordinates recording integer resources consumed or accumulated.

knowledge_statements.title: Accumulated-Resource States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward resource coordinates for additively separable integer constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider ordered integer decisions \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) with \(m\)-dimensional resource contributions \(a_i(x_i)\in\mathbb Z^m\). Before choosing \(x_i\), the accumulated-resource state is \((i,u)\), where \[u=\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}a_j(x_j).\] Choosing \(x_i=z\) updates the resource coordinate to \(u'=u+a_i(z)\). For an upper-capacity vector \(b\), a prefix may be pruned when no admissible continuation can make the final total satisfy \(u+\sum_{j=i}^n a_j(x_j)\le b\). The coordinate is sufficient when future feasibility and cost depend on prior decisions only through \((i,u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An accumulated-resource state stores the total resource contribution of decisions already made and updates it additively.
assumptions_latex: Resource contributions are integer-valued and additive across decisions.
Decisions are processed in the order \(1,\ldots,n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_i=\sum_{j<i}a_j(x_j)\) and \(u_{i+1}=u_i+a_i(x_i)\).

notation.meaning: vector of resources accumulated by the processed decisions
resource contribution of assigning value z to decision i

children.title: Constraint-Activity States
children.top_down_role: Coordinates recording partial left-hand-side activities.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Activity States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State coordinates recording current left-hand-side activity of integer constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraints with separable left-hand sides \(\sum_{j=1}^n a_{rj}(x_j)\), indexed by \(r=1,\ldots,m\), define the activity state before decision \(i\) by \[v_{ir}=\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}a_{rj}(x_j),\qquad r=1,\ldots,m.\] If \(x_i=z\), then \(v_{i+1,r}=v_{ir}+a_{ri}(z)\). Comparing \(v_i\), together with attainable contributions from unprocessed variables, against each constraint bound determines whether completion remains possible. The activity vector is an exact coordinate when histories with the same \((i,v_i)\) induce identical remaining domains, costs, and constraint tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint-activity state records each constraint's partial left-hand-side value after the processed decisions.
assumptions_latex: Every tracked constraint is additively separable over the ordered decisions.
All activity values belong to a discrete state domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{i+1}=v_i+a_i(x_i)\), componentwise across the tracked constraints.

notation.meaning: vector of partial constraint activities before decision i
contribution of decision value z to constraint r

children.title: Coupled Activity Coordinates
children.top_down_role: State spaces tracking several interacting resource or activity coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Activity Coordinates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint state representation for several coupled additive constraints or resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose decision \(x_i\) contributes the vector \(a_i(x_i)\in\mathbb Z^m\) to \(m\) coupled activities. The joint activity coordinate before decision \(i\) is \[q_i=\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}a_j(x_j)\in Q_i\subseteq\mathbb Z^m,\] and the transition is \(q_{i+1}=q_i+a_i(x_i)\). The Cartesian coordinate must retain every component whose value can alter a later feasible domain, terminal constraint, transition, or cost. Componentwise compression \(\phi(q_i)\) is exact only when equal compressed values imply continuation equivalence; otherwise independent one-dimensional recursions cannot represent coupling among activities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupled constraints require a joint activity vector unless a compression preserves every feasible continuation and its cost.
assumptions_latex: Activities are additive across ordered decisions.
At least one future feasibility or cost rule may depend jointly on multiple activity components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact joint transition is \(q_{i+1}=q_i+a_i(x_i)\); any compression must preserve continuation equivalence.

notation.meaning: reachable joint activity states before decision i
candidate compression of the activity vector

children.title: Residual-Resource State Coordinates
children.top_down_role: States expressed through remaining capacities, demands, or right-hand-side requirements.

children.title: Residual-Capacity States
children.top_down_role: Remaining upper-bound resources available to future decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Capacity States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backward-looking capacity coordinates obtained by subtracting accumulated usage from fixed capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\) be a fixed capacity vector and let decision \(x_j\) consume \(a_j(x_j)\in\mathbb Z_+^m\). Before choosing \(x_i\), the residual-capacity state is \[r_i=b-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}a_j(x_j).\] Choosing \(x_i=z\) is locally capacity-feasible when \(a_i(z)\le r_i\), componentwise, and yields \(r_{i+1}=r_i-a_i(z)\). With nonnegative consumption and only upper-capacity constraints, negative residual capacity is infeasible. This coordinate is sufficient when prior decisions affect all remaining feasibility and cost only through \((i,r_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual-capacity state stores unused capacity and subtracts each selected decision's resource consumption.
assumptions_latex: \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\) is fixed.
Every consumption vector satisfies \(a_j(x_j)\in\mathbb Z_+^m\).
Tracked resource constraints are upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_i=b-\sum_{j<i}a_j(x_j)\) and \(r_{i+1}=r_i-a_i(x_i)\).

notation.meaning: capacity consumed by assigning value z to decision i

children.title: Residual-Requirement States
children.top_down_role: Outstanding demand or lower-bound obligations left for future decisions.

assumptions_latex: Variables are processed in the fixed order \(1,\ldots,n\).
The covering constraints are \(Ax\ge b\), with \(A\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^m\), and bounded integer decisions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vector \(r^{(k)}\) is a sufficient residual-requirement coordinate whenever future feasibility and cost depend on the prefix only through \(k\) and \(r^{(k)}\).

notation.meaning: Residual requirement after the first k decisions

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard residual-demand state used in finite-horizon covering dynamic programs.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for nonnegative integer covering systems with a fixed variable order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a partial assignment \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\), the residual-requirement state is the vector
\[
r^{(k)}=\left[b-\sum_{j=1}^{k}A_{\cdot j}x_j\right]_+\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^m,
\]
where the positive part is taken componentwise. Its component \(r_i^{(k)}\) is the amount of covering requirement \(i\) not yet supplied by the processed decisions. Extending the prefix by \(x_{k+1}\) updates the state according to
\[
r^{(k+1)}=\left[r^{(k)}-A_{\cdot,k+1}x_{k+1}\right]_+.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual-requirement state records the unmet amount of every covering constraint after a decision prefix; subtracting the next contribution and truncating at zero gives the next state.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Requirement States

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-requirement definition and update are mathematically coherent and fit the leaf, but no source reference or inspectable locator supports the claim.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Layered shortest-path algorithm for standard-form ILP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes feasibility, unboundedness, optimality, and running-time boundaries for the constructed dynamic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n},\ b\in\mathbb Z^m,\ c\in\mathbb Z^n, and consider \max\{c^\top x:x\ge 0,\ Mx=b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}. If S bounds the absolute values of the entries of M and b, set U=(n+1)S(mS)^m. Construct the layered digraph with vertices \{0,\ldots,n\}\times(\{-U,\ldots,U\}^m) and arcs (i-1,b')\to(i,b'+k m_i) of length -kc_i for k\in\mathbb Z_+. A path from (0,0) to (n,b) encodes x_i=k and has length -c^\top x. No such path implies infeasibility. If a path exists and the LP relaxation is unbounded, the ILP is unbounded; if the LP relaxation is finite, a shortest such path yields an optimal integer solution. The running time is polynomially bounded by n,\ (2U+1)^m, and \operatorname{size}(c).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integral standard-form ILP, use layers indexed by variables and bounded integer right-hand-side states. Choosing a nonnegative value for a variable gives an arc whose length is the negative objective contribution. A source-to-target path encodes a feasible solution. Absence of a path certifies infeasibility; with a finite LP relaxation, a shortest path is optimal, while a feasible instance with an unbounded LP relaxation is unbounded. The running time is polynomial in n, (2U+1)^m, and the encoding size of c.
assumptions_latex: M\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n},\quad b\in\mathbb Z^m,\quad c\in\mathbb Z^n
S\ge \max\{|M_{ij}|,|b_i|:i,j\}
U=(n+1)S(mS)^m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The ILP is solved by the stated shortest-path construction in time }\operatorname{poly}\!\left(n,(2U+1)^m,\operatorname{size}(c)\right).

children.title: Mixed Residual Coordinates
children.top_down_role: State spaces combining remaining capacities with outstanding requirements.

assumptions_latex: Variables are processed in a fixed order.
The model contains packing constraints \(A^Cx\le b^C\) and covering constraints \(A^Rx\ge b^R\), with nonnegative integral data and bounded integer decisions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \(s^{(k)}=(c^{(k)},r^{(k)})\) simultaneously records remaining packing capacity and unmet covering demand.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Direct product of standard packing-capacity and covering-requirement coordinates.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed packing-and-covering residual state for bounded integer decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible prefix \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\), define
\[
c^{(k)}=b^C-\sum_{j=1}^{k}A^C_{\cdot j}x_j,
\qquad
r^{(k)}=\left[b^R-\sum_{j=1}^{k}A^R_{\cdot j}x_j\right]_+,
\qquad
s^{(k)}=(c^{(k)},r^{(k)}).
\]
A candidate value \(u\) for \(x_{k+1}\) is packing-admissible only if \(A^C_{\cdot,k+1}u\le c^{(k)}\). The transition is
\[
s^{(k+1)}=\left(c^{(k)}-A^C_{\cdot,k+1}u,\left[r^{(k)}-A^R_{\cdot,k+1}u\right]_+\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed residual coordinates pair remaining packing capacities with unmet covering requirements, so one transition updates both kinds of constraint information.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Residual Coordinates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mixed packing-and-covering residual representation is precise and locally appropriate, but it has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Decision-Memory State Family
children.top_down_role: State augmentations required by logical admissibility, ordering, or nonrepetition.

children.title: Logical-Admissibility Memory
children.top_down_role: State memory supporting logical eligibility restrictions.

assumptions_latex: A finite-horizon decision problem has finite action sets and prefix-dependent logical restrictions.
For every feasible prefix, the admissibility of future actions is determined by a finite logical summary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A map \(M\) is valid logical-admissibility memory exactly when equal memory values imply identical feasible continuation sets.

notation.meaning: Memory map applied to a decision prefix
Set of feasible continuation sequences after prefix p

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Sufficient-state condition obtained by continuation equivalence of decision prefixes.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite memory for prefix-dependent logical feasibility, excluding objective information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\) and \(q\) be feasible decision prefixes ending at the same stage, and let \(\mathcal C(p)\) denote all future action sequences that complete \(p\) feasibly. A finite-valued map \(M\) is logical-admissibility memory if
\[
M(p)=M(q)\;\Longrightarrow\;\mathcal C(p)=\mathcal C(q).
\]
Thus the admissible next actions and every later logical-feasibility test can be computed from the stage and \(M(p)\), without retaining the complete prefix. Under an action \(a\), the memory must admit an update \(M(pa)=U(M(p),a)\) whenever \(pa\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Logical-admissibility memory is a finite prefix summary: equal summaries must permit exactly the same feasible continuations and support deterministic action-by-action updates.
knowledge_statements.title: Logical-Admissibility Memory

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The continuation-equivalence condition fits logical-admissibility memory, but the asserted deterministic update property requires congruence justification or an authoritative source. No citation is supplied.

children.title: Sequencing Memory
children.top_down_role: State memory retaining order-dependent information.

assumptions_latex: Decisions form a finite sequence over an action alphabet \(\mathcal A\).
Sequencing restrictions are recognized by a finite-state transition system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The automaton state \(q_k\) is sufficient sequencing memory because it determines both next-action admissibility and the updated memory.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard finite-automaton representation of regular sequencing constraints.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state representation of order-dependent admissibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\) be finite, let \(q_0\in Q\), and let \(\delta:Q\times\mathcal A\rightharpoonup Q\) be a partial transition map. For a prefix \(a_1\cdots a_k\), sequencing memory is defined recursively by
\[
q_i=\delta(q_{i-1},a_i),\qquad i=1,\ldots,k.
\]
The next action \(a\) is sequencing-admissible precisely when \(\delta(q_k,a)\) is defined; terminal feasibility may additionally require \(q_n\) to lie in a designated accepting set \(F\subseteq Q\). This representation includes fixed-length recent-history memory by taking \(Q\) to contain the relevant suffixes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequencing memory can be represented by a finite automaton whose current state determines permitted next decisions, the next memory state, and terminal acceptance.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequencing Memory

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-automaton representation correctly matches sequencing memory, including partial transitions and terminal acceptance, but lacks a source and specific locator.

children.title: Visitation Memory
children.top_down_role: State memory recording prior visits or selections relevant to nonrepetition.

assumptions_latex: There is a finite ground set \(V\) of objects.
Each object may be visited at most once, and future admissibility or reward may depend on prior visitation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(S_k\), equivalently its bit mask, is an exact visitation-memory coordinate.

notation.meaning: Indicator vector of the visited set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard subset-state representation for elementary paths, tours, and set-selection dynamic programs.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subset memory for no-repeat visitation and set-dependent continuation rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a decision prefix visiting objects \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\in V\), define the visitation memory by
\[
S_k=\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}\subseteq V.
\]
Equivalently, store its bit mask \(\chi^{S_k}\in\{0,1\}^{|V|}\). A transition that visits \(v\in V\) is no-repeat admissible exactly when \(v\notin S_k\), and it updates the memory by
\[
S_{k+1}=S_k\cup\{v\}.
\]
Any continuation rule depending only on which objects have appeared, rather than their complete order, is determined by \(S_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Visitation memory stores the set, or bit mask, of previously visited objects; membership tests prevent repeats and set union performs the update.
knowledge_statements.title: Visitation Memory

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subset/bit-mask state and no-repeat update are standard and fit visitation memory, but no inspectable citation is provided.

children.title: Memory-State Growth Boundaries
children.top_down_role: State-space expansion caused by retained logical, sequencing, or visitation history.

assumptions_latex: A dynamic program distinguishes all subsets of an \(n\)-element set whenever those subsets induce different feasible or valued continuations.
States with identical future behavior may be merged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact subset memory can require \(2^n\) states, while bounded-window or finite-automaton memory remains polynomial or constant only under additional structure.

notation.meaning: Length of a retained action window

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Counting bound for subset memories and bounded action histories.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case state-count boundary for exact decision-memory representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If every subset of an \(n\)-element ground set yields a distinct continuation class, then any exact visitation-memory representation satisfies
\[
N(n)\ge 2^n,
\]
and the explicit subset representation attains \(N(n)=2^n\). If memory instead retains the last \(h\) actions from an alphabet of size \(d\), its state count is at most
\[
1+d+\cdots+d^h,
\]
which is polynomial in \(d\) for fixed \(h\) but exponential in \(h\). Hence compact memory requires bounded history, symmetry, aggregation, or another equivalence that merges prefixes with identical continuations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact visited-set memory may have exponentially many states. Fixed-window memory is compact only when the retained horizon is bounded or continuation-equivalent histories can be merged.
knowledge_statements.title: Memory-State Growth Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponential subset-state lower bound and bounded-window count fit this complexity-bound leaf, but the nontrivial counting and minimality claims require a cited source with a locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit assignments on a finite variable separator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be the variables shared by a processed subproblem and its unprocessed complement, with finite domains \(D_v\). A separator-assignment state is a vector
\[
\alpha=(\alpha_v)_{v\in S}\in\prod_{v\in S}D_v
\]
that is extendable to a feasible assignment of the processed subproblem. The dynamic-programming table associates with \(\alpha\) the best processed objective value among all such extensions. assumptions_latex: A processed subproblem interacts with the remaining problem only through a finite boundary.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A boundary summary \(\beta(p)\) is a valid interface state exactly when equality of summaries preserves every compatible continuation and its incremental value.

notation.meaning: Boundary-interface summary of a partial solution p

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Sufficient-interface condition standard in decomposition-based dynamic programming.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General finite boundary summaries, including assignments, loads, connectivity, and parity data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each feasible processed partial solution \(p\), let \(\beta(p)\) be finite boundary data. It is a valid boundary-interface state if, whenever \(\beta(p)=\beta(q)\),
\[
\mathcal C(p)=\mathcal C(q)
\]
and every common continuation has the same cross-boundary objective contribution for \(p\) and \(q\). Consequently, among partial solutions with the same interface, the dynamic program may retain only the one with the best internal objective value. The interface may encode separator assignments, residual boundary loads, exposed degrees, parities, or connectivity relations, provided the stated continuation condition holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boundary-interface state is any finite summary that preserves compatible continuations and their cross-boundary values, allowing dominated partial solutions with the same summary to be discarded.

children.title: Interface Equivalence Classes

assumptions_latex: Partial solutions being compared terminate at the same decomposition boundary.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relation \(\sim\) partitions partial solutions into maximal classes that are interchangeable for all future decisions and objective comparisons.

notation.meaning: Feasible continuation set of partial solution p
Incremental value of continuation z after p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-sensitive continuation equivalence at a fixed decomposition interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For partial solutions \(p\) and \(q\) at the same boundary, define
\[
p\sim q
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathcal C(p)=\mathcal C(q)
\ \text{ and }\
g_p(z)=g_q(z)\ \text{ for every }z\in\mathcal C(p).
\]
Then \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation. An exact interface state may be chosen as the equivalence class \([p]_{\sim}\). Any coarser identification can merge partial solutions having different feasible or differently valued continuations, whereas any finer interface representation retains information unnecessary for exact continuation decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two partial solutions are interface-equivalent when they admit the same continuations with identical incremental values; their equivalence class is an exact canonical state.

assumptions_latex: There are stages \(k=0,\ldots,T\) with finite state sets \(S_k\).
Every admissible decision at stage \(k<T\) maps a state in \(S_k\) to a state in \(S_{k+1}\) and has an arc value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible decision sequences correspond to source-to-terminal paths, and their additive objectives equal the associated path values.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard state-transition network representation of finite-horizon dynamic programming.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon deterministic dynamic programs with additive transition objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Construct a directed graph with node set
\[
N=\bigcup_{k=0}^{T}\bigl(\{k\}\times S_k\bigr).
\]
For each admissible decision taking \(s\in S_k\) to \(s'\in S_{k+1}\), include an arc \(((k,s),(k+1,s'))\) carrying that decision and its value \(w_e\). Because every arc advances one layer, the graph is acyclic. Each feasible decision sequence from the initial state determines a directed path to an admissible terminal state, and conversely each such path determines a feasible sequence. For an additive objective, the sequence value is \(\sum_{e\in P}w_e\), possibly plus a terminal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A layered state network places stage states in successive layers and decisions on forward arcs, creating an acyclic graph whose source-to-terminal paths are feasible decision sequences.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: s–t Path Decomposition and Path-Decomposable Subgraph Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the combinatorial objects and modified successor map used in the subsequent polyhedral description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be an acyclic digraph with distinguished nodes \(s,t\). It admits an \(s\)-\(t\) path decomposition if a collection of pairwise interior-node-disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) paths covers every node of \(G\). Its \(s\)-\(t\) path-decomposable subgraph polytope is \(P_G=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^W:W\subseteq V\setminus\{s,t\},\ G[W\cup\{s,t\}]\text{ admits an }s\text{-}t\text{ path decomposition}\}\). For \(S\subseteq V\), let \(\Gamma(S)=\{j\in V:(i,j)\in A\text{ for some }i\in S\}\) and \(\Gamma^*(S)=((\Gamma(S)\setminus\{t\})\cup\Gamma(s))\) if \(t\in\Gamma(S)\), while \(\Gamma^*(S)=\Gamma(S)\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An acyclic digraph with distinguished nodes s and t has an s–t path decomposition when interior-node-disjoint s–t paths cover all its nodes. The associated polytope is the convex hull of incidence vectors of interior-node sets whose induced subgraphs, together with s and t, have such a decomposition. The modified successor set replaces a reachable t by the successors of s.

S\subseteq V.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incidence-matrix formulation of directed shortest paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General-digraph shortest-path formulation and its polyhedral structure; no acyclicity assumption is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a digraph with arc lengths \(\ell_e\), distinct nodes \(s,t\in V\), and at least one directed \(s,t\)-path. Define \(b\in\mathbb R^V\) by \(b_s=-1\), \(b_t=1\), and \(b_v=0\) otherwise. The shortest-path model is \(\min\{\ell^{\mathsf T}x:A_Dx=b,\ x\ge0\}\). Its feasible polyhedron \(Q\) is integral; its vertices are the characteristic vectors of directed \(s,t\)-paths; and \(\operatorname{rec}(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb R^A:A_Dx=0,\ x\ge0\}\), whose extreme rays are generated by characteristic vectors of simple circuits. A circuit \(C\) has negative length exactly when \(\ell(C)=\sum_{e\in C}\ell_e<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a general directed graph containing an s–t path, shortest paths can be modeled by one unit of incidence-matrix flow from s to t. The feasible polyhedron is integral, its vertices represent directed s–t paths, and its recession cone is the circulation cone generated on extreme rays by simple circuits. A circuit is negative-length when its arc lengths sum to a negative value.

children.title: Acyclic Shortest-Path Models
children.top_down_role: Minimization-oriented path representations on ordered state networks.

assumptions_latex: The finite-horizon state-transition graph is acyclic and has designated source \(s\) and terminal set \(F\).
The objective is the sum of transition costs and an optional terminal cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum dynamic-program value equals the length of a shortest directed path from \(s\) to \(F\).

notation.meaning: Minimum cost from the source to node v

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard equivalence between additive minimization dynamic programs and shortest paths in directed acyclic graphs.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive minimization on a finite layered acyclic state network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(d(s)=0\) and \(d(v)=+\infty\) for every other node. Processing nodes in topological order, apply
\[
d(v)=\min_{(u,v)\in E}\bigl\{d(u)+c_{uv}\bigr\}.
\]
If terminal costs are \(h(f)\), the optimal value is
\[
\min_{f\in F}\{d(f)+h(f)\}.
\]
Under the path-sequence correspondence, every feasible decision sequence has exactly the cost of its source-to-terminal path. Predecessors attaining the recurrence reconstruct an optimal integer-decision sequence; unreachable states retain value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An additive minimization dynamic program on an acyclic state network is a shortest-path problem; topological relaxation computes its value and predecessor arcs recover an optimal decision sequence.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum dynamic-program value equals the length of a longest directed path from \(s\) to \(F\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(D(s)=0\) and \(D(v)=-\infty\) for every other node. Processing nodes in topological order, apply
\[
D(v)=\max_{(u,v)\in E}\bigl\{D(u)+w_{uv}\bigr\}.
\]
If terminal rewards are \(h(f)\), the optimal value is
\[
\max_{f\in F}\{D(f)+h(f)\}.
\]
Acyclicity makes the longest-path computation finite even when rewards have arbitrary signs. Under the path-sequence correspondence, maximizing path reward is exactly the original dynamic-program objective, and maximizing predecessor arcs reconstruct an optimal integer-decision sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An additive maximization dynamic program on an acyclic state network is a longest-path problem, solvable by topological recursion with predecessor recovery.

children.title: Objective-Sense Path Duality
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between minimization and maximization path orientations.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and arc weights \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\).
The feasible set \(\mathcal P_{st}\) of directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) paths is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathcal P_{st}} c(P)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{P\in\mathcal P_{st}}[-c(P)]\) and \(\min_{P\in\mathcal P_{st}}c(P)=-\max_{P\in\mathcal P_{st}}[-c(P)]\).

notation.meaning: Total weight of path P, equal to the sum of its arc weights.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite acyclic path models with additive real-valued objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every path \(P\in\mathcal P_{st}\), define \(c(P)=\sum_{e\in P}c(e)\) and the sign-reversed weight \(\bar c(e)=-c(e)\). Then \(\bar c(P)=-c(P)\), so the order of all feasible path values is reversed. Consequently,
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathcal P_{st}}c(P)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{P\in\mathcal P_{st}}\bar c(P),\qquad
\min_{P\in\mathcal P_{st}}c(P)=-\max_{P\in\mathcal P_{st}}\bar c(P).
\]
Thus a shortest-path dynamic program and a longest-path dynamic program represent the same feasible paths after objective negation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating every arc weight converts an acyclic shortest-path model into an equivalent longest-path model, preserving optimal paths and negating the optimal value.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Sense Path Duality

children.title: Implicit State-Transition Systems
children.top_down_role: State networks generated locally rather than materialized in full.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a state set with initial state \(s_0\), and every reachable transition sequence is finite.
For each generated state \(s\), an oracle returns the finite set \(\operatorname{Succ}(s)\) and transition costs \(c(s,u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reachable network and its Bellman values can be generated on demand from \(s_0\), without storing transitions incident to unreachable states.

notation.meaning: Finite set of successor states generated locally from state s.
Set of states reachable from the initial state.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-generated finite-horizon state networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An implicit state-transition system is specified by \((S,s_0,\operatorname{Succ},c)\), rather than by an explicitly listed graph. Its reachable state set is the least set \(R\subseteq S\) satisfying \(s_0\in R\) and \(u\in R\) whenever \(s\in R\) and \(u\in\operatorname{Succ}(s)\). For terminal costs \(g\), the minimization value satisfies \(V(s)=g(s)\) at terminal states and
\[
V(s)=\min_{u\in\operatorname{Succ}(s)}\{c(s,u)+V(u)\}
\]
otherwise. Evaluation need generate only states and transitions reached from \(s_0\); no representation of \(S\setminus R\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A successor oracle generates reachable states and transitions only when needed, permitting Bellman evaluation without materializing the full state network.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit State-Transition Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited chapter-page entry does not establish the successor-oracle representation or its Bellman formula. Terminal states and the domain of the terminal-cost map are also not defined sufficiently to validate the stated recursion.

children.title: Tree Recursion Representations
children.top_down_role: Recursive state organization over parent-child tree structure.

assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite rooted tree whose children precede their parent in a postorder.
Each leaf has a base value, and each internal node has a local combination map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A postorder traversal computes the root value by applying each node's local map once after all child values are available.

notation.meaning: Ordered children of tree node v.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bottom-up representations of finite rooted-tree recursions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T=(N,A)\) be a finite rooted tree. Associate each leaf \(v\) with a base value \(b_v\), and each internal node \(v\), with ordered children \(\operatorname{ch}(v)=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)\), with a map \(F_v\). The tree recursion represents values uniquely by
\[
V_v=b_v\quad\text{for leaves},\qquad V_v=F_v(V_{u_1},\ldots,V_{u_k})\quad\text{for internal nodes}.
\]
Because every nonroot node has exactly one parent, each computed subtree value is passed through a single parent interface. Evaluating nodes in postorder yields the represented root value \(V_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree recursion assigns base values to leaves and combines child values at each internal node, producing the root value by postorder evaluation.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree Recursion Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inventory places the chapter's tree material at Section 5.3, page 83, whereas this record cites page 79. The generic combination maps also lack declared domains and codomains, so the representation needs a directly supporting source and fuller typing.

children.title: Hypergraph Recursion Representations
children.top_down_role: Recursive state organization using hyperarcs with multiple incident components.

assumptions_latex: \(H=(N,\mathcal E)\) is a finite directed acyclic hypergraph with hyperarcs \(e=(T_e,h_e)\).
Each admissible hyperarc combines all values indexed by its tail set \(T_e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed Bellman recursion represents alternatives by incoming hyperarcs and conjunctive subproblems by their multi-node tails.

notation.meaning: Tail set and head node of hyperarc e.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acyclic AND-OR recursions with additive tail aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let every hyperarc \(e\in\mathcal E\) have a finite tail \(T_e\subseteq N\), one head \(h_e\in N\), and cost \(c_e\). Base nodes have prescribed values \(b_v\). For every other node \(v\), define
\[
V_v=\min_{e\in\delta^-(v)}\left\{c_e+\sum_{u\in T_e}V_u\right\}.
\]
Selecting a hyperarc represents one alternative for constructing \(v\), while its entire tail represents subproblems that must all be combined. A topological order of the acyclic dependency relation evaluates every tail before its head. Ordinary tree recursion is recovered when the selected dependencies form a rooted tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed hyperarc combines several predecessor subproblems simultaneously; minimizing over incoming hyperarcs represents alternative decompositions of the same state.
knowledge_statements.title: Hypergraph Recursion Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited source location does not support the specialized acyclic-hypergraph recursion. Nonbase nodes are not assumed to have incoming hyperarcs, and the claim that the displayed additive recursion recovers the preceding arbitrary-map tree recursion is overstated.

children.title: Multi-Predecessor Combination Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces for combining several recursively evaluated predecessor structures.

assumptions_latex: For each state \(v\), \(K_v\) is a finite set of admissible predecessor tuples.
Each tuple has a local cost and a deterministic combination map with a declared common domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A multi-predecessor transition is well-defined exactly when every admitted tuple is domain-compatible and its combined result belongs to the state domain of \(v\).

notation.meaning: Admissible predecessor tuples for state v.
Combination map associated with tuple k at v.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Typed interfaces for conjunctive dynamic-programming transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each target state \(v\), let \(K_v\) contain tuples \(k=(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\) of predecessor states. A multi-predecessor combination interface consists of maps \(C_{v,k}:D_{u_1}\times\cdots\times D_{u_m}\to D_v\) and local costs \(c_{v,k}\). It is compatible when, for every \(k\in K_v\), each supplied predecessor value lies in its declared domain and \(C_{v,k}(x_{u_1},\ldots,x_{u_m})\in D_v\). Under this condition a minimization recursion may set
\[
V_v=\min_{k\in K_v}\{c_{v,k}+C_{v,k}(V_{u_1},\ldots,V_{u_m})\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multi-predecessor interface is valid when every predecessor tuple has matching input domains and its combination map returns a valid value for the target state.
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Predecessor Combination Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited source does not establish this typed multi-predecessor interface. The formula adds a scalar cost to a value in an arbitrary domain and minimizes such values without specifying compatible addition, order, or a nonempty tuple set.

children.title: DP Evaluation-Recovery Interface
children.top_down_role: Evaluation directions and reconstruction interfaces for finite integer dynamic programs.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Sections 7.1.1–7.1.2: Backward and forward dynamic programming

children.title: Evaluation Orientation Pair
children.top_down_role: The two canonical orientations for traversing an ordered state model.

children.title: Forward Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Traversal from initial states toward terminal states.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed acyclic state graph with source \(s\).
Each arc \((u,v)\) has additive cost \(c_{uv}\), and vertices are processed in topological order from \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(d(v)\) equals the minimum cost of an \(s\)-to-\(v\) path for every reachable \(v\).

notation.meaning: Best known cost from source s to vertex v.
Stored predecessor attaining the current value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Source-to-state evaluation on a finite acyclic network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(d(s)=0\), \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\), and leave all predecessor pointers undefined. Process vertices in a topological order beginning at \(s\). For every outgoing arc \((u,v)\), perform the relaxation
\[
\text{if }d(u)+c_{uv}<d(v),\quad d(v)\leftarrow d(u)+c_{uv},\quad p(v)\leftarrow u.
\]
After all reachable vertices are processed, output \(d\). If a target \(t\) is specified, repeatedly following \(p\) from \(t\) to \(s\) recovers an optimal path; an infinite label certifies that the vertex is unreachable from \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process states from the source in topological order, relaxing outgoing transitions; resulting labels give optimal source-to-state costs and predecessor pointers recover paths.
knowledge_statements.title: Forward Evaluation

children.title: Backward Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Traversal from terminal conditions toward initial states.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed acyclic state graph with terminal vertex \(t\).
Each arc \((u,v)\) has additive cost \(c_{uv}\), and vertices are processed in reverse topological order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(J(u)\) equals the minimum cost of a \(u\)-to-\(t\) path for every vertex from which \(t\) is reachable.

notation.meaning: Optimal cost-to-go from vertex u to terminal t.
Stored successor attaining the current value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-to-terminal evaluation on a finite acyclic network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(J(t)=0\) and \(J(u)=+\infty\) for \(u\ne t\). Process vertices in reverse topological order. At each nonterminal vertex \(u\), set
\[
J(u)=\min_{(u,v)\in E}\{c_{uv}+J(v)\},
\]
and store a minimizing successor \(q(u)\) whenever the minimum is finite. Output \(J\). For a specified start vertex \(s\), repeatedly following \(q\) from \(s\) reaches \(t\) along an optimal path; \(J(s)=+\infty\) means that no directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process states backward from the terminal in reverse topological order; cost-to-go labels become optimal and stored successors recover an optimal path.
knowledge_statements.title: Backward Evaluation

children.title: Orientation Reversal Conditions
children.top_down_role: Model features governing equivalence or asymmetry between traversal directions.

assumptions_latex: The state model is a finite directed graph with additive transition costs and designated endpoints \(s\) and \(t\).
Reversing every transition preserves its cost and induces a bijection between feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) paths and reversed \(t\)-to-\(s\) paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Forward evaluation on the reversed model is equivalent to backward evaluation on the original model, with identical path costs and corresponding optimal policies.

notation.meaning: Graph obtained by reversing every arc of G.
Path obtained by reversing the order and direction of P.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reversal of additive finite-state path recursions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G^{\mathrm{rev}}=(V,E^{\mathrm{rev}})\), where \((v,u)\in E^{\mathrm{rev}}\) exactly when \((u,v)\in E\), and assign \(c^{\mathrm{rev}}_{vu}=c_{uv}\). Orientation reversal is valid when terminal and initial conditions are exchanged, transition feasibility is completely captured by the reversed arcs, and path cost is invariant:
\[
\sum_{(u,v)\in P}c_{uv}=\sum_{(v,u)\in P^{\mathrm{rev}}}c^{\mathrm{rev}}_{vu}.
\]
Under these conditions, the original cost-to-go \(J(u)\) equals the reversed graph's minimum cost from \(t\) to \(u\). State-dependent history constraints must therefore be included in the state before reversal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward and backward evaluation are interchangeable when arc reversal bijectively preserves feasible paths, additive costs, and correctly exchanged boundary conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Orientation Reversal Conditions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The path-reversal identity is plausible, but the cited location does not establish the stated reversal conditions or the conclusion about corresponding optimal policies. Policy correspondence is undefined, and the relationship to the acyclic evaluation algorithms is left unclear.

children.title: Bidirectional Search-Join Interface
children.top_down_role: Paired state exploration from opposite ends of a transition system.

children.title: Forward Search Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Partial states generated from the initial side of a transition system.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed state graph with source \(s\).
A forward search has settled all states at depth below \(k\) and generated their outgoing transitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_k\) is precisely the boundary through which every not-yet-settled path generated from \(s\) must pass next.

notation.meaning: States settled by forward search before frontier depth k.
Forward search frontier at depth k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Layer-indexed boundary of a forward state search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R_{<k}^{+}\) denote the states settled from \(s\) before layer or depth \(k\). The forward search frontier is
\[
F_k=\{v\in V\setminus R_{<k}^{+}:\exists u\in R_{<k}^{+}\text{ with }(u,v)\in E\},
\]
with each \(v\in F_k\) carrying the best currently retained forward label and sufficient state information for extension. In a strictly layered network, \(F_k\) is the set of reachable states in layer \(k\). Every generated path from \(s\) that leaves the settled region crosses from \(R_{<k}^{+}\) into \(F_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The forward frontier is the unsettled boundary adjacent to states already reached from the source, together with labels needed for continued extension.
knowledge_statements.title: Forward Search Frontiers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited source location does not support this particular search-frontier definition. In a general directed graph, layer or depth and the settling rule are not defined tightly enough to determine the indexed frontier independently of a specified search procedure.

children.title: Reverse Search Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Partial states generated from the terminal side of a transition system.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed state graph with terminal vertex \(t\).
A reverse search has settled all states at reverse depth below \(k\) and generated their incoming transitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_k\) is precisely the boundary through which every not-yet-settled path generated backward from \(t\) must pass next.

notation.meaning: States settled by reverse search before frontier depth k.
Reverse search frontier at depth k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Layer-indexed boundary of a reverse state search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R_{<k}^{-}\) denote the states settled backward from \(t\) before reverse layer or depth \(k\). The reverse search frontier is
\[
B_k=\{u\in V\setminus R_{<k}^{-}:\exists v\in R_{<k}^{-}\text{ with }(u,v)\in E\},
\]
with each \(u\in B_k\) carrying the best retained cost-to-go label and sufficient state information for backward extension. In a strictly layered network, \(B_k\) consists of states in the corresponding reverse layer that can reach \(t\). Every backward-generated path leaving the settled reverse region enters \(B_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reverse frontier is the unsettled boundary adjacent to states known to reach the terminal, together with labels needed for backward extension.
knowledge_statements.title: Reverse Search Frontiers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited source location does not support this reverse-frontier formalization. Reverse depth, settling, and layer correspondence require a specified search procedure or a strictly layered model.

children.title: Joining Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Compatibility structures used to connect opposite evaluation frontiers.

assumptions_latex: Forward labels \(d^+(x)\\) and reverse labels \(d^-(y)\) are exact for their represented partial paths.
A compatibility predicate \(K(x,y)\) is true exactly when the two partial states can be concatenated feasibly, with correction cost \(\gamma(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimizing the join expression over compatible frontier pairs yields the best complete path represented by the two frontiers.

notation.meaning: Compatibility predicate for a forward and reverse frontier state.
Cost introduced or corrected when joining x and y.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact joining of compatible forward and reverse partial solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) and \(B\) be forward and reverse frontiers. A joining interface specifies a predicate \(K:F\times B\to\{0,1\}\), a concatenation operation for pairs satisfying \(K(x,y)=1\), and a correction term \(\gamma(x,y)\) that prevents omitted or double-counted join costs. The best complete value represented by the frontiers is
\[
Z_{F,B}=\min_{\substack{x\in F,\ y\in B\\K(x,y)=1}}\{d^+(x)+\gamma(x,y)+d^-(y)\}.
\]
If every represented feasible complete path has a compatible decomposition and every compatible pair concatenates feasibly, then \(Z_{F,B}\) is exact over all complete paths covered by the two searches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A join interface tests frontier-state compatibility, concatenates compatible partial solutions, and combines their labels with any necessary boundary-cost correction.
knowledge_statements.title: Joining Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited dynamic-programming chapter location does not substantiate the specialized bidirectional joining formula or its completeness conditions. In addition, the first assumption contains a malformed delimiter after d^+(x), which must be repaired once an appropriate source is supplied.

children.title: Join Compatibility Failures
children.top_down_role: Boundary cases where retained frontier information cannot validate a complete solution.

assumptions_latex: A proposed bidirectional join tests only equality of the current location.
Feasibility also depends on a resource value that the frontier state does not retain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Location equality alone can accept an infeasible concatenation; exact joining requires retaining sufficient resource information or strengthening the compatibility predicate.

notation.meaning: Resource used by the forward and reverse partial paths.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by joining resource-incomplete frontier states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a resource-constrained path problem with capacity \(Q=10\). A forward partial path reaches join vertex \(v\) using \(r^+=6\), and a reverse partial path represents a continuation from \(v\) to the terminal requiring \(r^-=6\). A join rule that checks only the common vertex declares the pair compatible, although the concatenated path uses \(r^++r^-=12>Q\) and is infeasible. Therefore, projecting frontier states onto location alone does not support an exact join. Compatibility must at least enforce \(r^++r^-\le Q\), with analogous conditions for every history-dependent constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joining partial paths solely by common location can create infeasible solutions when omitted resource histories conflict; compatibility must test all coupling constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Join Compatibility Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The numerical incompatibility example is internally coherent and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the cited page does not support resource-aware bidirectional joins. The generalization to every history-dependent constraint therefore lacks adequate evidence.

children.title: Decision Recovery Storage Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Storage and recomputation interfaces for recovering an optimizing integer decision sequence.

children.title: Predecessor Storage
children.top_down_role: Persistent predecessor information retained during dynamic-program evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Predecessor Storage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointer storage for a finite layered minimization dynamic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the recurrence be \(V_i(s)=\min_{(r,a)\in P_i(s)}\{V_{i-1}(r)+c_i(r,a,s)\}\). Initialize the pointer table as empty. Whenever a reachable state \(s\in S_i\) is evaluated, choose one minimizing pair and store \(\pi_i(s)=(r,a)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{(r,a)\in P_i(s)}\{V_{i-1}(r)+c_i(r,a,s)\}\). After selecting an optimal terminal state, output its value together with the stored pointers needed for backward reconstruction. One pointer record is stored for each reached noninitial state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: During evaluation, store one minimizing predecessor and action for every reached state; these pointers later recover an optimal decision sequence.
assumptions_latex: \(S_0,\ldots,S_n\) and every predecessor set \(P_i(s)\) are finite.
An optimal terminal state exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stored pointer chain identifies an optimal path from a terminal state to an initial state.

notation.meaning: optimal value at stage i and state s
feasible predecessor-action pairs entering state s

children.title: Decision Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovery of an optimizing integer decision sequence from evaluated states.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backward reconstruction from stored optimal-predecessor pointers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\geq 1\), let \(S_0,\ldots,S_n\) be the stage-state sets, and let \(s_n\in S_n\) be an optimal terminal state. Set \(i=n\). While \(i\geq 1\), read the stored pointer \(\pi_i(s_i)=(s_{i-1},a_i)\), record \(a_i\), and decrement \(i\). After reaching \(s_0\in S_0\), output \((a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) in forward order. If every stored pointer is a feasible predecessor-action pair attaining the Bellman minimum at its state, the reconstructed state-decision sequence is feasible and attains \(V_n(s_n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from an optimal terminal state, follow feasible Bellman-minimizing pointers backward and output the recovered actions in forward order; the result is an optimal decision sequence.
assumptions_latex: For every state encountered during backtracking, \(\pi_i(s_i)=(s_{i-1},a_i)\) is stored, is feasible, and attains the Bellman minimum defining \(V_i(s_i)\).
The terminal state \(s_n\in S_n\) has optimal terminal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output sequence \((a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) is feasible and attains the optimal terminal value \(V_n(s_n)\).

notation.meaning: stored predecessor-action map at stage i
optimal state-value function at stage i

children.title: Recomputation-Based Recovery
children.top_down_role: Solution recovery using renewed state evaluation instead of full predecessor retention.

knowledge_statements.title: Recomputation-Based Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal-path recovery without retaining predecessor pointers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Retain the value tables but no predecessor table. Starting from an optimal terminal state \(s_n\), for \(i=n,n-1,\ldots,1\), scan \(P_i(s_i)\) until finding \((s_{i-1},a_i)\) satisfying \(V_i(s_i)=V_{i-1}(s_{i-1})+c_i(s_{i-1},a_i,s_i)\). Record \(a_i\), continue from \(s_{i-1}\), and finally reverse the actions. If value tables were discarded, recompute the required earlier layers before performing the same equality test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recover decisions by rescanning transitions that realize each Bellman equality, recomputing discarded value layers when necessary.
assumptions_latex: All transition costs and required value entries can be evaluated exactly.
Each finite minimum defining a state on the optimal path is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recovered decisions form an optimal state path ending at \(s_n\).

notation.meaning: incoming predecessor-action pairs for state s
stored or recomputed optimal state value

children.title: Storage–Recovery Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Memory implications of alternative solution-recovery interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Storage–Recovery Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint bounds for pointer-based and scan-based recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\sum_{i=1}^n|R_i|\), where \(R_i\) is the set of reached states at stage \(i\), and let \(d_i\) be the number of incoming transitions inspected at the recovered stage-\(i\) state. Storing one constant-word predecessor record per reached state uses \(\Theta(M)\) additional words and permits \(O(n)\) recovery time. Storing no pointers uses no such \(\Theta(M)\) table, but recovery from retained values requires \(O(\sum_{i=1}^n d_i)\) transition inspections, plus any work needed to recompute discarded value layers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointers cost linear storage and enable linear-stage backtracking; omitting them saves that table but requires transition scans and possibly value recomputation.
assumptions_latex: A predecessor and action fit in \(O(1)\) machine words.
Value-table storage is accounted for separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointer storage exchanges \(\Theta(M)\) additional words for recovery time \(O(n)\), whereas pointer-free recovery incurs transition-inspection or recomputation work.

notation.meaning: incoming transitions inspected at recovered stage i

children.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Tractability-Approximation Frontier
children.top_down_role: How encoding, numerical ranges, state dimension, and scaling determine the complexity role of integer dynamic programs.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Sections 18.5–18.6: Dynamic programming applied to knapsack and integer linear programming
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6: Complexity and Problem Reductions
Classical dynamic-programming and approximation chapters

children.title: Encoding-Range Complexity Interface
children.top_down_role: The distinction between compact input encoding and the numerical domains indexing states.

children.title: Controlled-Magnitude Encoding Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes in which numerical state ranges remain controlled by the input representation.

children.title: Unary-Encoding Regimes
children.top_down_role: Pseudo-polynomial state ranges under unary numerical input representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Unary-Encoding Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of pseudo-polynomial bounds under unary numerical encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an exact dynamic program runs in time \(p(N,U)\) and space \(q(N,U)\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are polynomials, \(N\) is the nonnumeric input length, and \(U\) bounds every nonnegative integer magnitude governing the state range. If these integers are encoded in unary and the total input length is \(L\), then \(N\leq L\) and \(U\leq L\). Consequently, its time is at most \(p(L,L)\) and its space at most \(q(L,L)\), both polynomial in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudo-polynomial dynamic program becomes polynomial-time and polynomial-space when its range-controlling integers are encoded in unary.
assumptions_latex: The number of numerical parameters is polynomially bounded by the input length.
Arithmetic on values of magnitude \(U\) has polynomial bit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unary encoding converts the bounds \(p(N,U)\) and \(q(N,U)\) into polynomial bounds in \(L\).

children.title: Bounded-Magnitude Regimes
children.top_down_role: State ranges controlled by explicit bounds on numerical magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Magnitude Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial solvability when numerical magnitudes are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an exact dynamic program have time \(p(L,U)\) and space \(q(L,U)\), with \(p\) and \(q\) polynomial and \(L\) the binary input length. On any instance class satisfying \(U\leq r(L)\) for a fixed polynomial \(r\), substitution gives time \(p(L,r(L))\) and space \(q(L,r(L))\). Thus a pseudo-polynomial algorithm is polynomial on a bounded-magnitude regime, even though the same algorithm need not be polynomial on unrestricted binary-encoded instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pseudo-polynomial dynamic programming is polynomial on instance families whose controlling numerical magnitudes are polynomially bounded by input length.
assumptions_latex: The dynamic-program state range is bounded by the parameter \(U\).
Bit-operation costs are polynomial in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(U\leq r(L)\), both \(p(L,U)\) and \(q(L,U)\) are polynomial in \(L\).

children.title: Numerical-Range Control
children.top_down_role: Connections between input representation and reachable state-domain size.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical-Range Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-count criterion for polynomial dynamic-program complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a dynamic program whose state is an integer vector \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_d)\) with \(0\leq s_j\leq R_j\), the full rectangular state grid contains at most \(\prod_{j=1}^d(R_j+1)\) states per layer. Numerical-range control holds when \(d\) is fixed and each \(R_j\leq p_j(L)\) for a fixed polynomial \(p_j\). Under polynomial transition work per state and polynomially many layers, this condition yields polynomial total time and storage in input length \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-dimensional DP has polynomially many states when every coordinate range is polynomially bounded in the input length.
assumptions_latex: The number of layers is polynomial in \(L\).
Transition processing per state is polynomial in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed \(d\) and bounds \(R_j\leq p_j(L)\) imply a polynomial state-space and polynomial DP resource bounds.

notation.meaning: range bound for state coordinate j

children.title: Binary-Encoded Large-Magnitude Regimes
children.top_down_role: Compactly encoded instances whose numerical state ranges are large.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary-Encoded Large-Magnitude Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential input-length behavior of magnitude-indexed tables under binary encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a capacity-indexed dynamic program for binary knapsack that, for each of \(n\) items, processes every capacity index \(b\in\{0,\ldots,B\}\). It performs \(\Theta(nB)\) table updates and uses \(\Theta(B)\) storage when rolling layers are used. If \(B\) has binary length \(m=\lceil\log_2(B+1)\rceil\), the family \(B=2^m-1\) requires \(\Theta(n2^m)\) updates and \(\Theta(2^m)\) storage. Thus this explicitly magnitude-indexed implementation is not polynomially bounded in \(m\) on unrestricted binary-encoded instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implementation that explicitly processes every capacity index uses a number of updates and storage locations exponential in the binary capacity length when the capacity is unrestricted.
assumptions_latex: For every item, the implementation processes each index in \(\{0,ldots,B\}\).
The computational measure counts table updates and stored table entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(B=2^m-1\), the implementation requires \(\Theta(n2^m)\) table updates and \(\Theta(2^m)\) rolling-layer storage.

children.title: Arithmetic Grid-Compression Calculus
children.top_down_role: Arithmetic reductions that shrink reachable integer grids.

children.title: Common-Factor Normalization
children.top_down_role: Reduction of integer state coordinates through shared arithmetic factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Factor Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar-grid compression for integer resource recurrences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_1,\ldots,a_n,B\) be nonnegative integers and let \(g=\gcd(a_1,\ldots,a_n)>0\). For binary decisions \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\), define \(a_i'=a_i/g\) and \(B'=\lfloor B/g\rfloor\). Then \[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\leq B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_{i=1}^n a_i'x_i\leq B'.\] Every attainable resource total is a multiple of \(g\), so indexing the dynamic program by normalized totals preserves feasible decisions and objective values while dividing the largest resource index by approximately \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divide all resource increments by their gcd and floor-scale the capacity; feasibility and objective values are unchanged while the DP grid shrinks.
assumptions_latex: At least one resource coefficient \(a_i\) is positive.
The objective depends on decisions but is not altered by resource-unit scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original and normalized resource inequalities define the same binary decisions.

notation.meaning: greatest common divisor of resource coefficients

children.title: Lattice Scaling
children.top_down_role: Re-expression of reachable states on a coarser integer lattice.

knowledge_statements.title: Lattice Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate normalization of vector-valued DP states on an affine lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let all reachable resource states lie in the affine lattice \(s_0+H\mathbb Z^d\), where \(H\in\mathbb Q^{d\times d}\) is nonsingular. Assign each state the integer coordinate \(z=H^{-1}(s-s_0)\in\mathbb Z^d\). If a transition adds \(h=Hk\) with \(k\in\mathbb Z^d\), then \(s\mapsto s+h\) is represented exactly by \(z\mapsto z+k\). Thus the coordinate transformation is bijective on the affine lattice and preserves transition incidence, path costs, and optimal values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Express affine-lattice states in integer lattice coordinates; transitions and optimal paths are preserved while redundant grid spacing disappears.
assumptions_latex: The lattice basis matrix \(H\) is nonsingular.
Every permitted state increment belongs to \(H\mathbb Z^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \(s\mapsto H^{-1}(s-s_0)\) gives an exact integer-coordinate representation of the dynamic program.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine-lattice coordinate statement is mathematically plausible, but the sole citation is only a chapter-opening page and has not been shown to support this specialized multidimensional lattice formulation or its preservation claims.

children.title: Reachable-Grid Compression
children.top_down_role: State-domain shrinkage resulting from arithmetic regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Reachable-Grid Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse dynamic programming over reachable states only.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(R_0\) with the feasible initial states and their values. For each stage \(i=1,\ldots,n\), initialize an empty associative map for \(R_i\). For every \(r\in R_{i-1}\) and feasible action \(a\), generate \(s=T_i(r,a)\) and update its entry by \(V_i(s)\leftarrow\min\{V_i(s),V_{i-1}(r)+c_i(r,a)\}\).
