Store no entry for an ungenerated grid point. After the last stage, return the best admissible terminal entry, or infeasibility if none exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generate and store only states reachable from the preceding layer, merging duplicate states by their best value.
assumptions_latex: Each feasible action set can be enumerated.
State equality and associative-map operations are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sparse recurrence returns the same optimal value as full-grid enumeration while storing only generated states.

notation.meaning: best value associated with a reachable state

children.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Complexity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Complexity regimes determining when pseudo-polynomial state enumeration is structurally plausible.

children.title: Weak-Hardness Solvability Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Problem families whose hardness is compatible with numerical-range dynamic programs.

children.title: Weak-Hardness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Integer problem families exhibiting hardness tied to numerical magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Hardness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of binary NP-hardness with pseudo-polynomial solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a numerical decision problem be NP-hard under binary encoding and admit an exact algorithm with running time polynomial in the structural input length \(N\) and the largest numerical magnitude \(U\). The algorithm may require exponential time in binary input length because \(U\) can be exponential in \(\log U\), yet it runs in polynomial time when the numerical data are unary encoded or polynomially bounded. This is the characteristic algorithmic regime associated with weak, rather than strong, numerical hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weakly hard numerical problems may be NP-hard in binary encoding yet exactly solvable in pseudo-polynomial time and polynomially in unary regimes.
assumptions_latex: The numerical parameters are nonnegative integers.
The exact algorithm has a bound polynomial in \(N\) and \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Binary NP-hardness is compatible with pseudo-polynomial solvability and polynomial solvability under unary or bounded-magnitude encoding.

notation.meaning: order of the binary encoding length of U

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatibility claim is broadly standard, but the relationship between pseudo-polynomial solvability and classification as weak rather than strong numerical hardness requires a directly supporting complexity source and careful definitional qualification. The cited chapter-opening page is insufficiently confirmed.

children.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Solvability
children.top_down_role: Dynamic-program solvability measured through numerical state ranges.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Solvability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity measured in instance length and numerical magnitudes, rather than binary encoding length alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integer optimization problem is pseudo-polynomially solvable if there exist an algorithm and a polynomial \(p\) such that every instance \(I\) is solved in time \(p(L(I),M(I))\), where \(L(I)\) is the binary encoding length and \(M(I)\) is the largest absolute value among designated integer data. The dependence on \(M(I)\) may be polynomial even though \(\log(1+M(I))\) contributes to \(L(I)\); consequently, this definition does not imply polynomial time in the ordinary bit model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solvability is pseudo-polynomial when runtime is polynomial in both input length and designated integer magnitudes, although it may be exponential in their binary encoding lengths.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) has finitely encoded integer numerical data.
\(M(I)\ge 1\) bounds the absolute values of the designated data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(I)\le p(L(I),M(I))\) for some polynomial \(p\).

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of instance I

children.title: Numerical-Range Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Structural compatibility between weak hardness and numerical-range enumeration.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical-Range Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition under which a magnitude-dependent dynamic program becomes pseudo-polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an integer-programming dynamic program have runtime bounded by \(p(L,R)\), where \(L\) is the binary input length, \(R\) is the cardinality or width of its numerical state range, and \(p\) is a polynomial. The formulation is numerically range-compatible when \(R\le q(L,M)\) for a polynomial \(q\) and a designated maximum input magnitude \(M\). Under this condition its runtime is polynomial in \(L\) and \(M\), hence pseudo-polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A range-based dynamic program is compatible when its state-range width is polynomially bounded by input length and designated numerical magnitudes.
assumptions_latex: \(T\le p(L,R)\) for a polynomial \(p\).
\(R\le q(L,M)\) for a polynomial \(q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\le p(L,q(L,M))=\operatorname{poly}(L,M)\).

children.title: Strong-Hardness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Problem families for which unrestricted pseudo-polynomial solvability is excluded by stronger hardness.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Hardness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard bit-model boundary for strongly NP-hard integer optimization families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi\) be an integer optimization problem that remains NP-hard when every numerical datum is bounded by a polynomial in the binary input length. If \(\Pi\) admitted an exact pseudo-polynomial algorithm with runtime \(p(L,M)\), then on those bounded-data instances its runtime would be polynomial in \(L\). Thus strong NP-hardness excludes an exact pseudo-polynomial algorithm for all instances of \(\Pi\), unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly NP-hard problem cannot have an unrestricted exact pseudo-polynomial algorithm unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi\) is strongly NP-hard.
\(T(I)\le p(L(I),M(I))\) is assumed for a polynomial \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\Rightarrow\Pi\) has no exact pseudo-polynomial algorithm.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The standard strong-NP-hardness boundary is stated correctly and failure_boundary fits the container, but the record has no citation. An authoritative complexity source defining strong NP-hardness and its exclusion of pseudo-polynomial algorithms is required.

children.title: Fixed-Coordinate Dimension Regimes
children.top_down_role: Recoveries obtained by bounding the number of tracked integer coordinates.

children.title: Fixed Resource-Dimension Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dynamic programs with a bounded number of tracked resource coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Resource-Dimension Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-grid bound when the number of tracked nonnegative resources is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a layered dynamic program whose state records \(m\) cumulative integer resource consumptions. Suppose coordinate \(j\) always lies in \(\{0,\ldots,B_j\}\). Then each layer contains at most \(\prod_{j=1}^{m}(B_j+1)\) states. If \(m\) is fixed and every state has at most \(D\) feasible outgoing decisions processed in constant time, the runtime over \(n\) layers is \(O\!\left(nD\prod_{j=1}^{m}(B_j+1)\right)\), which is pseudo-polynomial in the resource bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a fixed number of bounded integer resources, the state grid and transition runtime are polynomial in the resource bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) is independent of the input.
\(0\le s_j\le B_j\) for every reachable state coordinate.
Each state has at most \(D\) constant-time transitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|S_i|\le\prod_{j=1}^{m}(B_j+1)\) and \(T=O\!\left(nD\prod_{j=1}^{m}(B_j+1)\right)\).

notation.meaning: upper bound on resource coordinate j

children.title: Fixed Constraint-Dimension Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dynamic programs with a bounded number of tracked constraint activities.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Constraint-Dimension Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State bound for a fixed number of tracked integral constraint activities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a dynamic program for nonnegative integral decisions whose state is the partial activity vector of \(q\) packing constraints \(Ax\le b\), with \(A\ge0\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^q\). Every feasible state belongs to \(\prod_{k=1}^{q}\{0,\ldots,b_k\}\), so a layer has at most \(\prod_{k=1}^{q}(b_k+1)\) states. For fixed \(q\), bounded branching \(D\), and \(n\) layers, enumeration takes \(O\!\left(nD\prod_{k=1}^{q}(b_k+1)\right)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed number of nonnegative integral packing constraints yields a state count polynomial in their right-hand sides.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z_+^{q\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^q\), and decisions are nonnegative integral.
\(q\) is fixed.
At most \(D\) constant-time transitions are examined per state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|S_i|\le\prod_{k=1}^{q}(b_k+1)\) and \(T=O\!\left(nD\prod_{k=1}^{q}(b_k+1)\right)\).

notation.meaning: reachable partial-activity states at layer i

children.title: Combined Coordinate Bounds
children.top_down_role: Tractability effects from simultaneous bounds on multiple state-coordinate families.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Coordinate Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product bound for fixed-dimensional states with distinct coordinate intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every state of a layered integer-programming dynamic program be a vector in \(\mathbb Z^d\), and suppose coordinate \(j\) is restricted to the integer interval \([L_j,U_j]\). Every layer then has at most \(N=\prod_{j=1}^{d}(U_j-L_j+1)\) states. If \(d\) is fixed, there are \(n\) layers, and at most \(D\) constant-time transitions are examined from each state, the total runtime is \(O(nDN)\) and the two-layer storage requirement is \(O(N)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying the widths of fixed-dimensional coordinate intervals bounds both the state count and the resulting dynamic-program runtime.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) is fixed and \(L_j,U_j\in\mathbb Z\) with \(L_j\le U_j\).
Each state has at most \(D\) constant-time candidate transitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|S_i|\le N=\prod_{j=1}^{d}(U_j-L_j+1)\), \(T=O(nDN)\), and two-layer space is \(O(N)\).

notation.meaning: cardinality of the enclosing state box

children.title: Bounded-Numerics Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Regimes controlled by bounds on coefficients, right-hand sides, or reachable activities.

children.title: Bounded-Coefficient Regimes
children.top_down_role: State-space behavior under bounded integer coefficients.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Coefficient Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Magnitude condition converting coefficient-indexed state spaces into polynomial-size spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integral formulation \(Ax\le b\), define \(\Delta=\max_{i,j}|A_{ij}|\). A coefficient-indexed dynamic program is in a bounded-coefficient regime when \(\Delta\le q(L)\) for a polynomial \(q\) in the binary input length \(L\), or when \(\Delta\) is a fixed constant. If its state and transition counts are polynomial in \(L\), \(\Delta\), and other polynomially bounded parameters, then substituting this bound yields polynomial-time solvability in the ordinary bit model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coefficient dependence becomes ordinary polynomial dependence when all integral coefficients are polynomially bounded in the input length.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is integral and finitely encoded.
The algorithmic bound is polynomial in \(L\), \(\Delta\), and polynomially bounded auxiliary parameters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta\le q(L)\Rightarrow T=\operatorname{poly}(L)\).

children.title: Bounded-Range Regimes
children.top_down_role: State-space behavior under bounded reachable numerical domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Range Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-width condition for every integer coordinate used to index DP states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let coordinate \(j\) of every reachable state lie in an integer interval \([L_j,U_j]\), and write \(W_j=U_j-L_j+1\). A layered dynamic program is in a bounded-range regime when \(\prod_{j=1}^{d}W_j\le q(L)\) for some polynomial \(q\) in the binary input length \(L\). If the number of layers and the lookup, branching, and transition-processing work per state are polynomially bounded in \(L\), then exhaustive processing of the enclosing state ranges runs in polynomial time in the ordinary bit model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A layered DP has a bounded-range regime when the product of its coordinate widths is polynomial in binary input length; with polynomially many layers and polynomial per-state work, exhaustive processing is polynomial-time.
assumptions_latex: Every reachable state lies in \(\prod_{j=1}^{d}([L_j,U_j]\cap\mathbb Z)\).
\(\prod_{j=1}^{d}W_j\le q(L)\) for a polynomial \(q\).
The number of layers and the total lookup, branching, and transition-processing work per state are polynomially bounded in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T=\operatorname{poly}(L)\).

notation.meaning: number of integer values in state coordinate j

children.title: Bounded Right-Hand-Side Regimes
children.top_down_role: State-space behavior under bounded constraint limits or demands.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Right-Hand-Side Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Packing-form condition that bounds partial-activity states by right-hand-side magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax\le b\) with \(A\ge0\), \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^m\), and nonnegative integral decisions, a dynamic program tracking partial constraint activities is in a bounded right-hand-side regime when \(m\) is fixed and every \(b_i\le q(L)\) for a polynomial \(q\). Its enclosing state grid has at most \(\prod_{i=1}^{m}(b_i+1)\le(q(L)+1)^m\) points, hence is polynomially bounded in the binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-dimensional packing DPs have polynomially many activity states when every right-hand side is polynomially bounded in input length.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z_+^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^m\), and decisions are nonnegative integral.
\(m\) is fixed and \(b_i\le q(L)\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|S_k|\le\prod_{i=1}^{m}(b_i+1)\le(q(L)+1)^m=\operatorname{poly}(L)\).

notation.meaning: reachable partial-activity states after layer k

children.title: State-Space Complexity Measures
children.top_down_role: Structural quantities governing evaluation work, storage, and frontier growth.

children.title: State-Transition Count Measures
children.top_down_role: Complexity measured through generated states and feasible transitions.

children.title: Reachable-State Counts
children.top_down_role: Evaluation size measured by states reachable from valid initial conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Reachable-State Counts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive state-count measure for a layered dynamic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a layered dynamic program, let \(S_i\) be the set of distinct states reachable after processing layer \(i\). If initialization and processing of each stored state, excluding examination of its outgoing transitions, take expected \(O(1)\) time, then the state-processing work is \(O\!\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n}|S_i|\right)\). With rolling storage for two consecutive layers, the number of simultaneously stored state records is at most \(\max_{0\le i<n}(|S_i|+|S_{i+1}|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant expected work per reachable state gives processing time proportional to the total reachable-state count, while two-layer rolling storage depends on the largest pair of consecutive layers.
assumptions_latex: The dynamic program has layers \(0,\ldots,n\).
Initialization and nontransition processing take expected \(O(1)\) time per stored state.
Rolling storage retains only two consecutive layers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{state}}=O\!\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n}|S_i|\right)\) and \(M=O\!\left(\max_{0\le i<n}(|S_i|+|S_{i+1}|)\right)\).

notation.meaning: distinct states reachable at layer i
number of simultaneously stored state records

children.title: Feasible-Transition Counts
children.top_down_role: Evaluation work measured by admissible arcs between generated states.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Transition Counts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transition-sensitive runtime bound for explicit layered-state propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_i\subseteq S_i\times S_{i+1}\) be the feasible transitions from layer \(i\) to layer \(i+1\). If each feasible transition is generated, feasibility-checked, and relaxed in \(O(1)\) time, and state initialization costs \(O(|S_i|)\) at layer \(i\), then the complete dynamic program runs in \(O\!\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n}|S_i|+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}|E_i|\right)\) time. This bound counts only feasible generated transitions, not rejected candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When feasible transitions are generated directly and processed in constant time, runtime is linear in reachable states plus feasible transitions.
assumptions_latex: \(S_i\) and \(E_i\) are represented explicitly.
The transition generator outputs the feasible members of \(E_i\) directly.
Generation, feasibility checking, and relaxation cost \(O(1)\) per feasible transition.

children.title: Sparse Reachability Effects
children.top_down_role: Complexity reductions arising when only a small portion of the nominal state network is reachable.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Reachability Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive improvement when reachable states sparsely occupy the enclosing numerical grid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_i\) be the finite enclosing grid of possible states at layer \(i\), and let \(S_i\subseteq G_i\) be the reachable subset. Suppose a sparse implementation stores only \(S_i\), generates at most \(D_i\) candidate transitions per reachable state, processes each candidate in expected \(O(1)\) time, and uses expected constant-time hashing. Its expected runtime is \(O\!\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}D_i|S_i|+\sum_{i=0}^{n}|S_i|\right)\). A dense implementation that visits every point of each enclosing grid incurs \(\Omega\!\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n}|G_i|\right)\) state visits; sparse processing is advantageous when the reachable sets are much smaller than their enclosing grids.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With constant expected work per generated candidate, sparse storage replaces dependence on every point of the enclosing grids by dependence on reachable states and candidates generated from them.
assumptions_latex: \(S_i\subseteq G_i\) for every layer \(i\).
Hash-table lookup and insertion take expected \(O(1)\) time.
At most \(D_i\) candidates are generated per reachable state in layer \(i\), and generating, checking, and processing each candidate take expected \(O(1)\) time.
The compared dense implementation visits every point of each \(G_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{sparse}}=O\!\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}D_i|S_i|+\sum_{i=0}^{n}|S_i|\right)\), whereas dense state visitation is \(\Omega\!\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n}|G_i|\right)\).

notation.meaning: enclosing state grid at layer i
maximum candidate transitions generated per reachable state

children.title: Dimension-Range Growth Coupling
children.top_down_role: State growth caused by multiple independently tracked numerical coordinates.

children.title: Resource-Dimension Growth
children.top_down_role: State-space expansion caused by additional tracked resource coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Dimension Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-count growth for an integer-resource dynamic program with bounded coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the resource state after each stage belong to \(S\subseteq\prod_{j=1}^{d}\{0,1,\ldots,R_j\}\). A tabular dynamic program storing at most one value per state uses at most \[|S|\leq\prod_{j=1}^{d}(R_j+1)\] entries per layer. If every stored state examines at most \(b\) transitions, a layer requires \(O\!\left(b\prod_{j=1}^{d}(R_j+1)\right)\) transition evaluations. Thus the method is polynomial in the coordinate ranges for fixed \(d\), but generally exponential in \(d\) when the ranges exceed one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded resource grid has at most the product of its coordinate ranges plus one; fixed dimension yields pseudo-polynomial growth, while variable dimension can cause exponential growth.
assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\) and \(R_j\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\) for every \(j\).
The dynamic program stores at most one value for each reachable resource vector.
Each stored state has at most \(b\) examined transitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|S|\leq\prod_{j=1}^{d}(R_j+1)\), with per-layer work \(O\!\left(b\prod_{j=1}^{d}(R_j+1)\right)\).

notation.meaning: maximum value of resource coordinate j
maximum transitions examined per stored state

children.title: Coordinate-Range Products
children.top_down_role: Nominal state-domain size induced by products of coordinate ranges.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate-Range Products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cartesian-product representation of bounded integer resource states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integer bounds \(L_j\leq U_j\), define the full resource grid by \[G=\prod_{j=1}^{d}\bigl([L_j,U_j]\cap\mathbb{Z}\bigr).\] Its cardinality is exactly \[|G|=\prod_{j=1}^{d}(U_j-L_j+1).\] Any reachable state set \(S\subseteq G\) therefore satisfies \(|S|\leq |G|\). Equality holds precisely when every grid vector is reachable and retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full bounded integer resource grid has cardinality equal to the product of its coordinate-range lengths; any reachable-state set is no larger.
assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\).
\(L_j,U_j\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(L_j\leq U_j\) for every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|G|=\prod_{j=1}^{d}(U_j-L_j+1)\) and \(|S|\leq |G|\) for every \(S\subseteq G\).

children.title: Dimension–Range Interaction
children.top_down_role: Joint influence of coordinate count and numerical extent on state growth.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension–Range Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform-range specialization of multidimensional resource-state growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every resource coordinate takes values in \(\{0,1,\ldots,R\}\). The full state grid contains \((R+1)^d\) vectors. Consequently, a table-based dynamic program with \(T\) stages and at most \(b\) transitions per state has worst-case time \(O\!\left(Tb(R+1)^d\right)\) and two-layer space \(O\!\left((R+1)^d\right)\). The bounds are polynomial in \(R\) when \(d\) is fixed, but exponential in \(d\) for every fixed \(R\geq 1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With d resource coordinates of common range R, table size is a power of R+1: polynomial in R for fixed d but exponential in variable d.
assumptions_latex: \(T,d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\) and \(R\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\).
At most two consecutive layers are stored.
Each state examines at most \(b\) transitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Time is \(O\!\left(Tb(R+1)^d\right)\) and two-layer space is \(O\!\left((R+1)^d\right)\).

children.title: Antichain-Width Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity governed by collections of mutually incomparable partial solutions.

children.title: Frontier Width
children.top_down_role: Maximum size of an active or retained dynamic-program frontier.

assumptions_latex: \((P,\preceq)\) is a finite partially ordered set.
\(T\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\), and \(S_t\subseteq P\) is the generated state set for each \(t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W=\max_{0\leq t\leq T}|F_t|\), where \(F_t\) is the set of minimal elements of \(S_t\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum nondominated-layer size under a specified dominance order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((P,\preceq)\) be a finite partially ordered state space, and let \(S_t\subseteq P\) be the states generated at stage \(t\). For minimization dominance, define the retained frontier by \[F_t=\{s\in S_t: \nexists u\in S_t\setminus\{s\}\text{ with }u\preceq s\}.\] The frontier width of the dynamic program is \[W=\max_{0\leq t\leq T}|F_t|.\] It is the maximum number of pairwise incomparable nondominated states simultaneously retained at any stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Frontier width is the largest number of nondominated, mutually incomparable states retained in any dynamic-programming layer.
knowledge_statements.title: Frontier Width

children.title: Nondominated Antichains
children.top_down_role: Mutually incomparable partial solutions retained under dominance filtering.

assumptions_latex: \((P,\preceq)\) is a partially ordered set.
\(S\subseteq P\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is an antichain and \(|F|\leq\operatorname{width}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic structure of a dominance-pruned dynamic-programming frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((P,\preceq)\) be a partially ordered state space and \(S\subseteq P\) be finite. Its minimization frontier \[F=\{s\in S:\nexists u\in S\setminus\{s\}\text{ with }u\preceq s\}\] is an antichain: for distinct \(x,y\in F\), neither \(x\preceq y\) nor \(y\preceq x\) holds. Hence \(|F|\leq\operatorname{width}(P)\), where \(\operatorname{width}(P)\) is the maximum cardinality of an antichain in \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimal nondominated states are pairwise incomparable, so their number cannot exceed the width of the ambient state poset.
knowledge_statements.title: Nondominated Antichains

children.title: Incomparability Growth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem structures producing large collections of mutually incomparable labels.

knowledge_statements.title: Incomparability Growth Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frontier growth in product orders as dimension or coordinate range varies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the product poset \(P=\{0,1,\ldots,R\}^{d}\) ordered coordinatewise, every rank level \[A_k=\left\{x\in P:\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_j=k\right\}\] is an antichain. Therefore \(\operatorname{width}(P)\geq\max_k|A_k|\). Since the \((dR+1)\) rank levels partition \(P\), \[\max_k|A_k|\geq\frac{(R+1)^d}{dR+1}.\] Thus dominance pruning can still retain exponentially many states as \(d\) grows, even though comparable states are discarded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product grid contains a rank-level antichain of at least its total size divided by the number of ranks, permitting exponential frontier growth in dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\) and \(R\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\).
The order on \(P\) is coordinatewise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{width}(P)\geq (R+1)^d/(dR+1)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank levels are antichains, the averaging bound is correct, and the exponential-in-dimension conclusion follows for fixed positive R. The complexity_bound kind fits the growth-regime leaf. No citation is supplied for the antichain-width claim, so source support is required.

children.title: Time–Space Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Recomputation, checkpointing, and sparse exploration regimes that exchange memory for evaluation work.

knowledge_statements.title: Time–Space Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkpointing and recomputation for a layered deterministic dynamic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a deterministic layered recurrence \(V_t=\Phi_t(V_{t-1})\) for \(t=1,\ldots,T\), where one layer occupies \(M\) memory words and costs at most \(C\) operations to compute. Storing every layer uses \(O(TM)\) space and \(O(TC)\) time. Storing only the current layer uses \(O(M)\) space for the terminal value, but reconstructing a full predecessor trajectory by restarting from the initial layer before each backward decision uses at most \(O(T^2C)\) time. Intermediate checkpoints interpolate between these endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keeping all layers supports linear-time reconstruction with large memory; retaining only a current layer saves space but may require quadratic-time recomputation of a trajectory.
assumptions_latex: The recurrence \(V_t=\Phi_t(V_{t-1})\) is deterministic and reproducible.
Each layer requires at most \(M\) words and \(C\) operations.
A predecessor decision can be recovered after recomputing its layer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Full storage costs \(O(TM)\) space and \(O(TC)\) time; restart-based reconstruction costs \(O(M)\) space and at most \(O(T^2C)\) time.

notation.meaning: operations needed to compute one layer

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The endpoint time-space estimates are coherent under the explicit restart-based reconstruction assumption, and principle is an appropriate kind for this topic container. The cited chapter-opening page does not specifically identify checkpointing or the quadratic recomputation bound; a supporting section, theorem, or page is needed.

children.title: State-Scaling Approximation Interface
children.top_down_role: Approximation structures obtained by modifying the numerical state domains of pseudo-polynomial dynamic programs.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Approximation algorithms following classical dynamic programming

children.title: Objective-Coordinate Scaling Family
children.top_down_role: State-range reduction through scaled objective coordinates.

children.title: Profit Scaling
children.top_down_role: Compression of profit-indexed state domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Profit Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard profit rounding for a nonnegative-profit knapsack dynamic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\) items with profits \(p_i\geq0\), weights \(w_i\geq0\), capacity \(B\), and scale \(K>0\), set \(q_i=\lfloor p_i/K\rfloor\). Initialize \(D_0(0)=0\) and \(D_0(q)=+\infty\) for \(q>0\). Update \[D_i(q)=\min\{D_{i-1}(q),D_{i-1}(q-q_i)+w_i\},\] omitting the second term when \(q<q_i\). Output a subset attaining the largest \(q\) with \(D_n(q)\leq B\). For any subset \(S\), its rounded value satisfies \(K\sum_{i\in S}q_i\leq\sum_{i\in S}p_i<K\sum_{i\in S}q_i+nK\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Round nonnegative profits down by a common scale, run a minimum-weight dynamic program over scaled profit, and return the largest feasible scaled-profit state.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq1}\), \(p_i,w_i\geq0\), and \(B,K>0\).
Each item may be selected at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output maximizes scaled profit subject to capacity, and every subset loses less than \(nK\) profit through rounding.

notation.meaning: scaled integer profit of item i
minimum weight attaining scaled profit q using the first i items

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaled-profit recurrence and additive rounding inequality are correct for 0-1 items with nonnegative profits, and algorithm fits the leaf. The supplied general dynamic-programming chapter locator does not specifically support profit scaling, so a precise scaling or knapsack-approximation source is required.

children.title: Cost Scaling
children.top_down_role: Compression of cost-indexed state domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upward rounding of nonnegative additive costs for a budgeted dynamic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given nonnegative costs \(c_i\), budget \(B\), and quantum \(K>0\), define \(\widehat c_i=\lceil c_i/K\rceil\) and \(\widehat B=\lfloor B/K\rfloor\). Run the original budget-indexed recurrence with integer costs \(\widehat c_i\) and budget \(\widehat B\), then output its selected set \(S\). Because \(c_i\leq K\widehat c_i\), every scaled-feasible output satisfies \[\sum_{i\in S}c_i\leq K\sum_{i\in S}\widehat c_i\leq K\widehat B\leq B.\] Moreover, \(0\leq K\widehat c_i-c_i<K\) for each item.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Round nonnegative costs upward and the budget downward, solve the compressed integer-cost dynamic program, and preserve feasibility for the original budget.
assumptions_latex: The selected-set cost is additive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every set feasible for the scaled budget is feasible for the original budget, with per-item rounding excess below \(K\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The upward-cost and downward-budget scaling preserves original feasibility, and the per-item rounding bound is correct. Algorithm is suitable for the cost-scaling leaf. The cited general dynamic-programming locator does not specifically support this scaling construction, so a more precise source is required.

children.title: Objective-Coordinate Compression
children.top_down_role: State-range reduction obtained through modified objective coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Coordinate Compression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bucket map and additive-error bound for a nonnegative objective coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z=
obreak\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i x_i\) with \(p_i\geq0\) and \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\). For quantum \(K>0\), replace each coefficient by \(q_i=\lfloor p_i/K\rfloor\) and represent a partial solution by the compressed coordinate \(\widehat z=
obreak\sum_i q_i x_i\). Then \[K\widehat z\leq z<K\widehat z+K\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\leq K\widehat z+nK.\] Hence states sharing \(\widehat z\) lie within an objective interval of width at most \(nK\), while the coordinate range decreases to at most \(
obreak\sum_i q_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Floor-scaled objective coefficients merge nearby objective states; the reconstructed value underestimates the true value by less than one quantum per selected item.
assumptions_latex: The objective is additive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq z-K\widehat z<nK\), and the compressed coordinate ranges from \(0\) to \(\sum_i q_i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compressed-coordinate representation and additive error bound are correct, and representation matches the leaf's mathematical role. The generic dynamic-programming locator does not specifically support objective-coordinate compression; a scaling or approximation source with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Sign-Sensitive Scaling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scaling behavior affected by objective sign conventions or mixed objective contributions.

assumptions_latex: \(K>0\), \(0<\varepsilon<K\), and \(0<\delta<K-\varepsilon\).
Scaling uses \(q_i=\lfloor p_i/K\rfloor\) for signed coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under unrestricted sign cancellation, the relative reconstruction error \(\lvert z-K\sum_i q_i\rvert/\lvert z\rvert\) is unbounded over instances with \(z\neq 0\).

notation.meaning: positive perturbation used in the signed coefficients

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of multiplicative guarantees under cancellation between positive and negative objective terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(K>0\) and use floor scaling \(q_i=\lfloor p_i/K\rfloor\). For signed profits, choose \(0<\varepsilon<K\) and \(0<\delta<K-\varepsilon\), and take two selected terms \(p_1=K-\varepsilon\) and \(p_2=-K+\varepsilon+\delta\). Their true sum is \(z=\delta>0\), while \(q_1=0\), \(q_2=-1\), and the reconstructed scaled sum is \(K(q_1+q_2)=-K\). Hence the relative reconstruction error is \[(K+\delta)/\delta,\] which is unbounded as \(\delta\to 0\) with \(K\) fixed. Thus bounded additive coefficient errors do not yield a uniform multiplicative approximation when positive and negative terms may cancel; additional sign, positivity, or lower-bound assumptions are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Signed objective terms can nearly cancel, so bounded additive rounding errors can produce unbounded relative reconstruction error; multiplicative scaling guarantees therefore require additional positivity or lower-bound assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Sensitive Scaling Regimes

children.title: Resource-State Aggregation Family
children.top_down_role: Approximate aggregation of numerical resource states.

children.title: Resource Rounding
children.top_down_role: Approximate modification of numerical resource coordinates through rounding.

assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\), \(a_i\geq 0\), \(B\geq 0\), and \(K>0\).
Resource consumption is additive and each item is used at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every output item set \(I\) satisfies \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i\leq B\), while \(0\leq Kr_i-a_i<K\) for each item.

notation.meaning: reachable scaled-resource states after i items
item set represented by an output state

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservative upward rounding of nonnegative resource consumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\) nonnegative resource increments \(a_i\), capacity \(B\), and quantum \(K>0\), set \(r_i=\lceil a_i/K\rceil\) and \(R=\lfloor B/K\rfloor\). Initialize the reachable set \(S_0=\{0\}\). For each item, update \[S_i=S_{i-1}\cup\{s+r_i:s\in S_{i-1},\ s+r_i\leq R\},\] retaining associated objective values according to the original recurrence. Output an item set \(I\) represented by a state in \(S_n\). Since \(a_i\leq Kr_i\), every retained item set satisfies \[\sum_{i\in I}a_i\leq K\sum_{i\in I}r_i\leq KR\leq B.\] The rounding excess satisfies \(0\leq Kr_i-a_i<K\) for every item.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Round resource use upward, scale capacity downward, and run the resulting integer-state recurrence; every retained item set remains feasible for the original capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource Rounding

children.title: Resource Bucketing
children.top_down_role: Grouping of resource values into shared state classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource Bucketing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform aggregation of a nonnegative integer resource state in a finite dynamic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the exact resource state be \(r\in\{0,1,\ldots,R\}\), and fix a bucket width \(\Delta\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\). Downward resource bucketing replaces \(r\) by \(b_\Delta(r)=\lfloor r/\Delta\rfloor\), whose bucket represents \(B_k=\{r:k\Delta\le r<\min\{(k+1)\Delta,R+1\}\}\). A bucketed dynamic program stores one label for each \(k\in\{0,\ldots,\lfloor R/\Delta\rfloor\}\), together with an explicitly chosen representative or dominance rule for \(B_k\). Thus the resource coordinate has at most \(\lfloor R/\Delta\rfloor+1\) aggregate states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resource bucketing maps consecutive resource levels into width-Δ classes, reducing the resource coordinate to at most floor(R/Δ)+1 aggregate states.
assumptions_latex: \(R\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\)
\(\Delta\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert b_\Delta(\{0,\ldots,R\})\rvert=\lfloor R/\Delta\rfloor+1\).

children.title: Aggregation-Granularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: State-space effects associated with alternative aggregation resolutions.

assumptions_latex: \(R\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\)
\(\Delta\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_\Delta=\lfloor R/\Delta\rfloor+1\) and \(0\le r-\Delta\lfloor r/\Delta\rfloor<\Delta\) for every \(r\in\{0,\ldots,R\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tradeoff between uniform bucket width, state count, and resource-coordinate distortion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the resource range \(\{0,\ldots,R\}\) and integer width \(\Delta>0\), uniform downward bucketing has \(N_\Delta=\lfloor R/\Delta\rfloor+1\) states and satisfies \(0\le r-\Delta\lfloor r/\Delta\rfloor<\Delta\) for every \(r\in\{0,\ldots,R\}\). Hence \(\Delta=1\) is the exact regime, \(1<\Delta<R+1\) is a nontrivial aggregation regime, and \(\Delta\ge R+1\) is the single-bucket regime. Increasing \(\Delta\) weakly decreases \(N_\Delta\), while the uniform additive-distortion bound is less than \(\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Width one is exact; intermediate widths trade fewer states for an additive distortion of less than the bucket width; widths at least R+1 collapse all resource levels into one state.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation-Granularity Regimes

children.title: Feasibility-Loss Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where resource aggregation can obscure feasibility distinctions.

assumptions_latex: \(C\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\)
For the counterexample, \(\Delta\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\).
Aggregate acceptance is determined by \(\widehat r(x)\le C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An upper surrogate \(\widehat r(x)\ge r(x)\) is feasibility-safe under aggregate acceptance, whereas a downward-rounded lower surrogate need not be.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility boundary for replacing exact resource use by rounded aggregate use.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a capacity constraint \(r(x)\le C\). If aggregation uses an upper surrogate \(\widehat r(x)\ge r(x)\), then \(\widehat r(x)\le C\) implies true feasibility, although truly feasible solutions may be discarded. In contrast, let \(\Delta\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\) and use the downward-rounded surrogate \(\widehat r(x)=\Delta\lfloor r(x)/\Delta\rfloor\), which satisfies \(0\le r(x)-\widehat r(x)<\Delta\). With \(C=\Delta\) and a one-item selection having \(r(x)=2\Delta-1\), one obtains \(\widehat r(x)=\Delta\le C\) although \(r(x)>C\). Thus downward rounding crosses the exact-feasibility boundary unless capacity is tightened or exact resource use is rechecked.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper resource surrogates preserve feasibility but may reject feasible solutions; downward-rounded lower surrogates can admit infeasible solutions unless capacity is tightened or exact use is rechecked.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Loss Boundaries

children.title: Exactness-Approximation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Separation between exact arithmetic normalization and state modifications that change the optimization guarantee.

children.title: Exact Arithmetic Normalization
children.top_down_role: State-domain transformations preserving the original optimization guarantee.

assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\)
\(a_1,ldots,a_n,C\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\)
\(D\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) is a common multiple of the denominators of \(a_1,ldots,a_n,C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\le C\iff\sum_{i=1}^n Da_i x_i\le DC\).

notation.meaning: positive common divisor used for optional reduction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact integer normalization of rational resource data before dynamic programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_1,\ldots,a_n,C\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\), and let \(D\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) be a common multiple of their denominators. Define \(A_i=Da_i\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(B=DC\). For every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\le C\) if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^n A_i x_i\le B\). If \(g\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) divides every member of \(\{A_1,\ldots,A_n,B\}\), then dividing all of them by \(g\) also preserves this equivalence. These transformations change the integer state scale but neither the feasible decision set nor objective values that are left unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clearing rational denominators and optionally dividing all integer coefficients and the capacity by a positive common divisor yields an equivalent integer-capacity model without approximation.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Arithmetic Normalization

children.title: Approximation-Inducing State Modification
children.top_down_role: State-domain changes that alter attainable objective or feasibility guarantees.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a finite exact state space.
\(T:S\to\widehat S\) is the aggregation map.
The aggregated recurrence observes no state information beyond \(T(s)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(T(s)=T(t)\) while \(s\) and \(t\) have different continuation-outcome sets, a recurrence using only \(T(s)\) cannot represent both exact sets without additional information.

notation.meaning: exact continuation-outcome set from state s

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion distinguishing information-losing state modification from exact state aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite exact dynamic-programming state space, let \(T:S\to\widehat S\) be a state map, and let \(\mathcal C(s)\) denote the set of feasible continuations from \(s\), each paired with its incremental value. If \(T(s)=T(t)\) implies \(\mathcal C(s)=\mathcal C(t)\) for all reachable \(s,t\in S\), then replacing each state by its image under \(T\) preserves these continuation outcomes. If some merged reachable pair satisfies \(\mathcal C(s)\ne\mathcal C(t)\), a recurrence whose only state information is \(T(s)\) cannot represent both exact continuation-outcome sets; exactness then requires additional distinguishing labels or a corrective exact check, and omitting them can induce approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregation preserves all continuation outcomes when every pair of merged reachable states has the same feasible continuations and incremental values. If a merged pair differs, additional labels or an exact corrective check are required to retain that information.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Inducing State Modification

children.title: Guarantee-Change Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural separation between exact state compression and approximation.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite nonempty feasible set.
\(f:F\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) is the maximization objective.
For the displayed multiplicative example, \(\varepsilon\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactness requires \(\widehat x\in F\) and \(f(\widehat x)=z^*\); otherwise any valid weaker guarantee must state its feasibility or approximation allowance explicitly.

notation.meaning: output of the modified-state dynamic program

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between exact optimization and approximation after modifying dynamic-programming states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a finite nonempty feasible decision set, let \(f:F\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and let \(z^*=\max_{x\in F}f(x)\). A modified-state dynamic program retains an exact guarantee only if its output \(\widehat x\) is certified to satisfy \(\widehat x\in F\) and \(f(\widehat x)=z^*\). If aggregation merges states with unequal continuation values, the value equality need not hold; if aggregation can understate resource use, membership in \(F\) need not hold. Beyond this boundary, a valid guarantee must explicitly state what remains, such as feasibility together with \(f(\widehat x)\ge(1-\varepsilon)z^*\) for a specified \(\varepsilon\in[0,1]\), or a quantified constraint-violation bound. Reduced state count alone supplies neither guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state-modified algorithm is exact only when its output is feasible and optimal. If modification can change continuation values or feasibility, any remaining approximation or violation guarantee must be stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.title: Guarantee-Change Boundary

children.title: Capacity-Weight State Representations
children.top_down_role: Knapsack and subset-sum state models indexed by consumed or remaining capacity.

children.title: Capacity-Indexed Knapsack Dynamic Programs
children.top_down_role: Knapsack state models indexed by available or used capacity.

assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\)
\(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\)
\(p_i\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\)
\(C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n(C)=\max\{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le C,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\).

notation.meaning: maximum profit using the first i items under capacity c

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-one knapsack recurrence indexed by an available-capacity upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), weights \(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), profits \(p_i\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and capacity \(C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), set \(F_0(c)=0\) for \(c\in\{0,\ldots,C\}\). For \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), set \(F_i(c)=F_{i-1}(c)\) when \(c<w_i\), and set \(F_i(c)=\max\{F_{i-1}(c),p_i+F_{i-1}(c-w_i)\}\) when \(c\ge w_i\). Output \(F_n(C)\). An optimal subset can be recovered by tracing maximizing alternatives when the required predecessor information is retained. The value table requires \(O(nC)\) arithmetic operations and comparisons and can be evaluated with \(O(C)\) working memory when only the optimal value is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The capacity-indexed zero-one knapsack dynamic program stores the best profit obtainable from the first items under each capacity bound and updates by excluding or including the next item.
knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Indexed Knapsack Dynamic Programs

children.title: Weight-Indexed Knapsack Dynamic Programs
children.top_down_role: Knapsack state models indexed by attainable cumulative weight.

assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\)
\(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\)
\(p_i\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\)
\(C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{0\le q\le C}G_n(q)=\max\{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le C,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\).

notation.meaning: best profit with exact weight q using the first i items

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-one knapsack recurrence indexed by exact accumulated weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), weights \(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), profits \(p_i\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and capacity \(C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), initialize \(G_0(0)=0\) and \(G_0(q)=-\infty\) for \(q\in\{1,\ldots,C\}\). For \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(q\in\{0,\ldots,C\}\), set \(G_i(q)=\max\{G_{i-1}(q),p_i+G_{i-1}(q-w_i)\}\), interpreting the second term as \(-\infty\) when \(q<w_i\). Output \(\max_{0\le q\le C}G_n(q)\). Here \(G_i(q)\) is the best profit among subsets of the first \(i\) items having exact total weight \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This zero-one knapsack dynamic program stores the best profit for each exact accumulated weight and maximizes over all weights not exceeding capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Indexed Knapsack Dynamic Programs

children.title: Consumed-Capacity States
children.top_down_role: State coordinates recording capacity already used.

assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\)
\(w_j\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) for \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\)
\(C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_{i+1}=q_i+w_{i+1}x_{i+1}\) with feasible state domain \(q_{i+1}\in\{0,\ldots,C\}\).

notation.meaning: capacity consumed after the first i decisions
binary selection decision for item j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward resource-state representation by total capacity already consumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For decisions on the first \(i\) items, define the consumed-capacity state \(q_i=\sum_{j=1}^i w_jx_j\). Its feasible domain is \(\{0,\ldots,C\}\). Including item \(i+1\) sends \(q_i\) to \(q_i+w_{i+1}\) when \(q_i+w_{i+1}\le C\), while exclusion leaves the state unchanged. Because all weights are positive, a complete selection is feasible exactly when its reached consumed-capacity states remain at most \(C\). Different partial selections may reach the same \(q_i\); an optimizing dynamic program may merge their state labels only while retaining the appropriate best objective label for that state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consumed capacity is accumulated selected weight. Inclusion adds the next item's weight, exclusion leaves the state unchanged, and states above capacity are infeasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Consumed-Capacity States

children.title: Residual-Capacity States
children.top_down_role: State coordinates recording capacity remaining.

assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\)
\(w_j\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) for \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\)
\(C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\)

notation.meaning: capacity remaining after the first i decisions
capacity consumed after the first i decisions
binary selection decision for item j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent knapsack state representation by capacity remaining after partial decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For decisions on the first \(i\) items, define consumed capacity \(q_i=\sum_{j=1}^i w_jx_j\) and residual capacity \(r_i=C-\sum_{j=1}^i w_jx_j=C-q_i\). The feasible residual-state domain is \(\{0,\ldots,C\}\). Including item \(i+1\) is allowed exactly when \(w_{i+1}\le r_i\), producing \(r_{i+1}=r_i-w_{i+1}\); exclusion gives \(r_{i+1}=r_i\). The mapping \(r_i=C-q_i\) is a bijection between the feasible residual-capacity and consumed-capacity state values, so either representation gives the same feasible transitions and optimal value when labels are transformed accordingly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual capacity is total capacity minus accumulated selected weight. Inclusion subtracts the next weight and is allowed only when enough capacity remains; this is equivalent to the consumed-capacity representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Capacity States

children.title: Objective-Indexed Knapsack Representations
children.top_down_role: Dual state orientations indexed by accumulated objective value.

children.title: Value-Indexed Knapsack Dynamic Programs
children.top_down_role: Knapsack state models indexed by accumulated value.

assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\)
\(v_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\)
\(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\)
\(C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{t\in\{0,\ldots,V\}:H_n(t)\le C\}=\max\{\sum_{i=1}^n v_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le C,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\).

notation.meaning: minimum weight attaining value at least t with the first i items

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Knapsack recurrence minimizing weight needed to attain each value threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), integer values \(v_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), weights \(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and capacity \(C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), let \(V=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i\). Initialize \(H_0(0)=0\) and \(H_0(t)=+\infty\) for \(t\in\{1,\ldots,V\}\). For \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(t\in\{0,\ldots,V\}\), set \(H_i(t)=\min\{H_{i-1}(t),w_i+H_{i-1}(\max\{0,t-v_i\})\}\). Then \(H_i(t)\) is the minimum weight of a subset of the first \(i\) items whose total value is at least \(t\). Output the largest \(t\in\{0,\ldots,V\}\) satisfying \(H_n(t)\le C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value-indexed dynamic program stores the minimum weight needed to attain each integer value threshold and returns the largest threshold that fits within capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Value-Indexed Knapsack Dynamic Programs

children.title: Profit-Indexed Knapsack Dynamic Programs
children.top_down_role: Knapsack state models indexed by attainable profit.

assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\)
\(p_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\)
\(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\)
\(C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{q\in\{0,\ldots,P\}:M_n(q)\le C\}=\max\{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le C,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\).

notation.meaning: minimum weight attaining exact profit q with the first i items

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Knapsack recurrence minimizing weight for each exact attainable integer profit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), profits \(p_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), weights \(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and capacity \(C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), let \(P=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\). Initialize \(M_0(0)=0\) and \(M_0(q)=+\infty\) for \(q\in\{1,\ldots,P\}\). For \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(q\in\{0,\ldots,P\}\), set \(M_i(q)=\min\{M_{i-1}(q),w_i+M_{i-1}(q-p_i)\}\), interpreting the second term as \(+\infty\) when \(q<p_i\). Output the largest \(q\in\{0,\ldots,P\}\) satisfying \(M_n(q)\le C\). Here \(M_i(q)\) is the minimum weight of a subset of the first \(i\) items having exact total profit \(q\), and the recurrence requires \(O(nP)\) arithmetic operations and comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The profit-indexed dynamic program stores the minimum weight for every exact integer profit and returns the greatest attainable profit whose weight does not exceed capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Profit-Indexed Knapsack Dynamic Programs

children.title: Objective-Indexed Reachability
children.top_down_role: Reachability structure over attainable objective-coordinate levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Indexed Reachability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-weight representation indexed by exact integral objective value for zero–one knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For items indexed by \(i=1,\ldots,n\) and each \(p\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), define \(R_i(p)\) as the minimum total weight of a subset of the first \(i\) items having total profit exactly \(p\), with value \(+\infty\) when no such subset exists. Initialize \(R_0(0)=0\) and \(R_0(p)=+\infty\) for \(p>0\). Then
\[
R_i(p)=\min\{R_{i-1}(p),\;w_i+R_{i-1}(p-v_i)\},
\]
where the second term is omitted when \(p<v_i\). For capacity \(W\), the optimal profit equals \(\max\{p\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:R_n(p)\le W\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every nonnegative integer profit, store the least weight attaining that exact profit. Excluding or including the current item gives the recurrence; the largest indexed profit whose stored weight fits is optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) and \(v_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for every item \(i\).
\(W\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), and each item may be selected at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(W)=\max\{p\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:R_n(p)\le W\}\).

notation.meaning: minimum weight attaining exact profit p using the first i items

children.title: Item-Multiplicity Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Canonical knapsack variants distinguished by admissible item multiplicities.

children.title: Zero–One Multiplicity Variants
children.top_down_role: Selection structures allowing at most one copy of each item.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero–One Multiplicity Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-indexed dynamic program when every item has multiplicity zero or one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F_i(c)\) be the maximum profit obtainable from the first \(i\) items with total weight at most \(c\). Initialize \(F_0(c)=0\) for every \(c=0,\ldots,W\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), update
\[
F_i(c)=
\begin{cases}
F_{i-1}(c),&c<w_i,\\
\max\{F_{i-1}(c),\,v_i+F_{i-1}(c-w_i)\},&c\ge w_i.
\end{cases}
\]
The use of the preceding layer in the inclusion term prevents repeated selection of item \(i\). Output \(F_n(W)\); predecessor choices recover an optimal subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each item and capacity, compare excluding the item with including it once. Reading the previous item layer enforces zero–one multiplicity.
assumptions_latex: \(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), \(v_i\in\mathbb R\), and \(W\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).
Decision variables satisfy \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n(W)=\max\{\sum_{i=1}^n v_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le W,\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\}\).

notation.meaning: best profit using the first i items within capacity c

children.title: Bounded Multiplicity Variants
children.top_down_role: Selection structures with finite item-specific copy limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Multiplicity Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-indexed recurrence for item-specific finite multiplicity bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let item \(i\) be usable at most \(u_i\) times, and let \(F_i(c)\) denote the maximum profit obtainable from the first \(i\) item types within capacity \(c\). Set \(F_0(c)=0\). For \(i=1,
\ldots,n\) and \(c=0,\ldots,W\), compute
\[
F_i(c)=\max_{0\le k\le\min\{u_i,\lfloor c/w_i\rfloor\}}
\{F_{i-1}(c-k w_i)+k v_i\}.
\]
Output \(F_n(W)\). Storing an attaining value of \(k\) at each state permits reconstruction of an optimal bounded-multiplicity solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each state, enumerate every feasible number of copies of the current item type and combine it with the preceding item layer.
assumptions_latex: \(w_i,u_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), \(v_i\in\mathbb R\), and \(W\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).
Decision variables satisfy \(x_i\in\{0,1,\ldots,u_i\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n(W)=\max\{\sum_i v_i x_i:\sum_i w_i x_i\le W,\ 0\le x_i\le u_i,\ x_i\in\mathbb Z\}\).

notation.meaning: maximum permitted number of copies of item type i
best profit from the first i item types within capacity c

children.title: Unbounded Multiplicity Variants
children.top_down_role: Selection structures permitting unrestricted repeated item use within resource limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Multiplicity Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-indexed recurrence allowing arbitrarily many copies of each item type.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F_i(c)\) be the maximum profit obtainable from the first \(i\) item types within capacity \(c\). Initialize \(F_0(c)=0\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), set \(F_i(c)=F_{i-1}(c)\) when \(c<w_i\), and otherwise compute
\[
F_i(c)=\max\{F_{i-1}(c),\;v_i+F_i(c-w_i)\}.
\]
The second term reads the current layer, so item \(i\) may be selected repeatedly. Evaluate capacities in nondecreasing order and output \(F_n(W)\); stored predecessor choices recover multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare excluding the item type with adding one copy to a current-layer state. Increasing capacity order permits unlimited reuse.
assumptions_latex: \(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), \(v_i\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and \(W\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).
Decision variables satisfy \(x_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_n(W)=\max\{\sum_i v_i x_i:\sum_i w_i x_i\le W,\ x_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\}\).

notation.meaning: best profit from the first i item types within capacity c

children.title: Multiplicity-Regime Transitions
children.top_down_role: State-model changes across zero–one, bounded, or unbounded copy regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity-Regime Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: How multiplicity bounds specialize bounded-knapsack states and alter one-array update order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bounded model \(0\le x_i\le u_i\) specializes to zero–one knapsack when \(u_i=1\). For a fixed capacity \(W\), it has the same feasible solutions as the unbounded model whenever \(u_i\ge\lfloor W/w_i\rfloor\) for every \(i\). In a one-array capacity implementation, processing \(c\) in decreasing order for each item enforces zero–one use, while processing \(c\) in increasing order implements unbounded reuse. General finite bounds require an explicit bounded transition or an equivalent bounded-item decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounds of one give zero–one knapsack; sufficiently large bounds are effectively unbounded. Decreasing versus increasing capacity order determines whether current-item states can be reused.
assumptions_latex: \(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), \(u_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and \(W\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).
All regimes use the same weights, profits, and capacity constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_i=1\) yields zero–one multiplicity, while \(u_i\ge\lfloor W/w_i\rfloor\) makes the upper bound redundant at capacity \(W\).

notation.meaning: finite multiplicity bound for item type i
capacity used to determine effective multiplicity

children.title: Choice-Class Knapsack Variants
children.top_down_role: Knapsack states organized around choice classes or partitions.

children.title: Grouped Knapsack Variants
children.top_down_role: Knapsack structures partitioning items into selection groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Grouped Knapsack Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Knapsack with mutually exclusive selections inside prescribed item groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the item set be partitioned into nonempty groups \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\). The grouped zero–one knapsack problem is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{i\in G_j}v_i x_i:
\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{i\in G_j}w_i x_i\le W,
\ \sum_{i\in G_j}x_i\le1\ \text{for every }j,
\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.
\]
Thus each group contributes either no item or exactly one of its members. Replacing selected group inequalities by equalities defines mandatory-choice groups without changing the capacity coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Items are partitioned into groups, and at most one item may be selected from each group while all selections share one capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) partition a finite item set.
\(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), \(v_i\in\mathbb R\), and \(W\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible solution satisfies \(\lvert\{i\in G_j:x_i=1\}\rvert\le1\) for each group \(j\).

notation.meaning: the j-th mutually exclusive item group
binary selection variable for item i

children.title: Multiple-Choice Knapsack Variants
children.top_down_role: Knapsack structures imposing class-specific choice restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Choice Knapsack Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Grouped knapsack requiring one selected alternative from every choice class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) partition the alternatives. The multiple-choice knapsack problem is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{i\in G_j}v_i x_i:
\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{i\in G_j}w_i x_i\le W,
\ \sum_{i\in G_j}x_i=1\ \text{for every }j,
\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.
\]
Each feasible solution therefore chooses exactly one alternative from every class. An optional-choice class can be represented by adjoining a dummy alternative of weight and profit zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly one alternative is chosen from each class, subject to the shared capacity. A zero-weight, zero-profit dummy converts optional classes to this form.
assumptions_latex: \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) partition a finite set of alternatives.
\(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), \(v_i\in\mathbb R\), and \(W\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible solution satisfies \(\lvert\{i\in G_j:x_i=1\}\rvert=1\) for each class \(j\).

notation.meaning: binary selection variable for alternative i

children.title: Choice-Class State Interfaces
children.top_down_role: State organization around completed, active, or remaining choice classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Choice-Class State Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic-programming interface that consumes one complete choice class per stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F_j(c)\) be the maximum profit after processing classes \(G_1,\ldots,G_j\) with capacity at most \(c\), where item \(i\) has weight \(w_i\) and profit \(v_i\). Set \(F_0(c)=0\). For optional-choice classes, update
\[
F_j(c)=\max\left(\{F_{j-1}(c)\}\cup
\{F_{j-1}(c-w_i)+v_i:i\in G_j,\ w_i\le c\}\right).
\]
For mandatory-choice classes, omit \(F_{j-1}(c)\) and assign \(-\infty\) when no member fits. The interface reads only the preceding class layer, thereby preventing two alternatives from the same class. Output \(F_m(W)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each stage processes one complete choice class and evaluates its alternatives against the preceding class layer. Retaining the preceding state permits an optional class; omitting it requires one fitting alternative and prevents selecting two members of the class.
assumptions_latex: The finite classes \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) are pairwise disjoint.
\(w_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), \(v_i\in\mathbb R\), and \(W\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_m(W)\) is the optimal grouped-knapsack value under optional or mandatory class semantics, according to the stated transition.

notation.meaning: best value after the first j choice classes within capacity c
choice class processed at stage j

children.title: Multidimensional Knapsack Dynamic Programs
children.top_down_role: Knapsack state spaces tracking several resource capacities.

knowledge_statements.title: Multidimensional Knapsack Dynamic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-vector dynamic program for knapsack with several integral resource constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d,n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\). For each item \(i=1,\ldots,n\), let \(a_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{d}\) be its consumption vector and let \(v_i\in\mathbb R\) be its profit; let \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{d}\) be the capacity vector. For every \(c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{d}\) satisfying \(c\le b\), define \(F_i(c)\) as the best profit using the first \(i\) items at componentwise capacity \(c\). Initialize \(F_0(c)=0\). Then
\[
F_i(c)=\max\bigl(\{F_{i-1}(c)\}\cup
\{v_i+F_{i-1}(c-a_i):a_i\le c\}\bigr).
\]
All vector inequalities are componentwise. Output \(F_n(b)\); predecessor choices recover an optimal zero–one packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive number of resources, index states by nonnegative integral capacity vectors. Each item is excluded or included once when every resource component permits inclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(d,n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), \(a_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{d}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{d}\), and \(v_i\in\mathbb R\).
Each item has a zero–one selection variable.

notation.meaning: best profit at integral capacity vector c after i items

children.title: Subset-Sum Reachability Structures
children.top_down_role: Reachability-oriented dynamic programs for attainable subset totals.

knowledge_statements.title: Subset-Sum Reachability Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean dynamic-programming representation of reachable subset sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) and target bound \(T\), define \(R_i(s)\) to mean that some subset of \(\{1,\ldots,i\}\) has sum exactly \(s\). Initialize \(R_0(0)=\mathrm{true}\) and \(R_0(s)=\mathrm{false}\) for \(s>0\). Then, for \(0\le s\le T\),
\[
R_i(s)=R_{i-1}(s)\lor\bigl(s\ge a_i\land R_{i-1}(s-a_i)\bigr).
\]
Consequently, a target \(T\) is attainable exactly when \(R_n(T)\) is true. A one-array implementation updates sums in decreasing order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Boolean state records whether each exact sum is attainable. Each new item preserves old sums and creates shifted sums, with decreasing updates enforcing single use.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\).
\(T\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), and each input number may be used at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_n(T)\) is true if and only if \(T=\sum_{i\in S}a_i\) for some \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).

notation.meaning: Boolean reachability of exact sum s using the first i inputs
largest represented sum and queried target

children.title: Subset-Sum Counting Variants
children.top_down_role: Dynamic-program state structures for counting selections that realize target totals.

knowledge_statements.title: Subset-Sum Counting Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic program counting index-distinct subsets with each exact sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), let \(C_i(s)\) be the number of subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,i\}\) whose elements have total value exactly \(s\). Initialize \(C_0(0)=1\) and \(C_0(s)=0\) for \(s>0\). For \(0\le s\le T\), compute
\[
C_i(s)=C_{i-1}(s)+
\begin{cases}
C_{i-1}(s-a_i),&s\ge a_i,\\
0,&s<a_i.
\end{cases}
\]
The two terms count disjoint classes of subsets excluding and including index \(i\). Output \(C_n(T)\), or retain all states to obtain the complete distribution of subset sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace Boolean reachability by integer counts. Excluding and including the current index partition the subsets, so their counts add.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) and \(T\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).
Subsets are distinguished by indices, even when input values coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_n(T)=\lvert\{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}:\sum_{i\in S}a_i=T\}\rvert\).

notation.meaning: number of index subsets of the first i inputs summing to s

children.title: Single-Resource Separable Integer Programs
children.top_down_role: Separable integer decisions linked by one aggregate resource.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Resource Separable Integer Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic program for finite integer domains coupled by one integral resource bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider minimizing a separable cost over finite integer domains \(D_i\) subject to one resource bound. Let \(V_i(c)\) be the minimum cost for decisions \(1,\ldots,i\) using at most resource \(c\). Set \(V_0(c)=0\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\) and \(c=0,\ldots,B\), compute
\[
V_i(c)=\min_{\substack{x\in D_i\\a_i(x)\le c}}
\{V_{i-1}(c-a_i(x))+f_i(x)\},
\]
with the minimum of an empty set equal to \(+\infty\). Output \(V_n(B)\); stored minimizers reconstruct an optimal integer allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process one separable decision at a time, indexing states by the available resource allowance. Each transition selects a domain value, subtracts its resource use from that allowance, and adds its cost.
assumptions_latex: Each \(D_i\subset\mathbb Z\) is finite and nonempty.
\(a_i:D_i\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), \(f_i:D_i\to\mathbb R\), and \(B\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_n(B)=\min\{\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i):\sum_{i=1}^n a_i(x_i)\le B,\ x_i\in D_i\}\).

notation.meaning: finite integer domain of decision i
resource consumed by value x of decision i
minimum separable cost after i decisions within resource allowance c

children.title: Multi-Resource Separable Integer Programs
children.top_down_role: Separable integer decisions linked by several aggregate resources.

assumptions_latex: \(n,m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\), each decision set \(X_i\subset\mathbb{Z}\) is finite, and each cost \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb{R}\).
Resource coefficients satisfy \(a_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{m}\) and the capacity vector satisfies \(b\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{m}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimizer is any feasible \(x^*\) attaining \(\min\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x_i):x_i\in X_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i x_i\le b\}\).

notation.meaning: resource-consumption vector per unit of component i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain, inequality-constrained formulation with several integer resource coordinates.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A multi-resource separable integer program has the form
\[\min_{x}\ \sum_{i=1}^{n} f_i(x_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i x_i\le b,\qquad x_i\in X_i.\]
The inequality is componentwise in \(\mathbb{Z}^{m}\). For dynamic programming, define \(V_k(r)\) as the minimum cost of the first \(k\) components using at most resource vector \(r\). Then \(V_0(r)=0\) and
\[V_k(r)=\min_{q\in X_k:\,a_kq\le r}\{V_{k-1}(r-a_kq)+f_k(q)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable integer program is multi-resource when independent integer choices are linked by a vector of aggregate capacity inequalities.

children.title: Separable-Cost Curvature Regimes

children.title: Convex Separable-Cost Regimes
children.top_down_role: Integer resource-allocation structures with convex component costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Separable-Cost Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete convexity on bounded integer intervals, expressed through marginal costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\prod_{i=1}^{n}X_i\to\mathbb{R}\) be defined by \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x_i)\). It is in the convex separable-cost regime when, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the forward differences \(\Delta f_i(k)=f_i(k+1)-f_i(k)\) satisfy \(\Delta f_i(k+1)\ge\Delta f_i(k)\) for every \(k\in\{\ell_i,\ldots,u_i-2\}\). Equivalently, \(f_i(k+1)-2f_i(k)+f_i(k-1)\ge0\) for every \(k\in\{\ell_i+1,\ldots,u_i-1\}\). Thus the discrete marginal cost of successive units is nondecreasing on each component domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable cost is in the discrete-convex regime exactly when every component has nondecreasing forward marginal costs, equivalently nonnegative interior second differences.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\), and \(X_i=\{\ell_i,\ell_i+1,\ldots,u_i\}\subset\mathbb{Z}\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
Each \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is convex separable exactly when \(\Delta f_i(k+1)\ge\Delta f_i(k)\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and every \(k\in\{\ell_i,\ldots,u_i-2\}\).

notation.meaning: lower and upper integer bounds for component i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary identified by loss of monotonicity in discrete marginal costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The curvature regimes are separated by monotonicity of the forward differences. If \(\Delta f(k)\) is nondecreasing, \(f\) is discretely convex; if it is nonincreasing, \(f\) is discretely concave. For the concrete cost
\[f(0)=0,\quad f(1)=0,\quad f(2)=2,\quad f(3)=3,\]
the forward differences are \((0,2,1)\), hence neither monotonicity condition holds. Consequently, an allocation rule justified by globally ordered marginal costs cannot be inferred, although exhaustive finite-state dynamic programming remains valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When discrete marginal costs are not monotone, the cost lies in neither curvature regime and curvature-based marginal allocation rules no longer apply.
