children.top_down_role: Classical regeneration-interval and shortest-path organizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncapacitated Single-Item Lot-Sizing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical deterministic uncapacitated model with fixed setups and linear holding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the zero-inventory ordering property, production in period \(i\) may cover the consecutive demands in periods \(i,\ldots,j\). For \(1\le i\le j\le T\), associate the regeneration interval with arc \((i,j+1)\) and cost \(C_{ij}=K_i+c_iD_{ij}+\sum_{t=i}^{j}h_t\sum_{s=t+1}^{j}d_s\), where \(D_{ij}=\sum_{t=i}^{j}d_t\). The shortest-path recursion is \[F(0)=0,\qquad F(j)=\min_{1\le i\le j}\{F(i-1)+C_{ij}\},\qquad j=1,\ldots,T.\] A minimizing predecessor sequence identifies the setup periods and their consecutive demand blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical deterministic uncapacitated single-item lot-sizing optimum is a shortest path whose arcs represent consecutive demand blocks supplied from one setup period.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\), and deterministic demands satisfy \(d_t\ge0\) for every \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\).
Production capacity is unlimited, backlogging is forbidden, and initial and required terminal inventories are zero.
For every \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\), production has setup cost \(K_t\ge0\), unit cost \(c_t\in\mathbb{R}\), and nonnegative per-unit holding cost \(h_t\ge0\) from period \(t\) to period \(t+1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum lot-sizing cost equals the shortest-path distance from node \(1\) to node \(T+1\) in the regeneration-interval network.

notation.meaning: total demand from period i through period j
cost of producing in period i for demands i through j

children.title: Capacitated Lot-Sizing State Models
children.top_down_role: Inventory and capacity states induced by binding production limits.

assumptions_latex: Demands, production capacities, and inventories are integer-valued over periods \(1,ldots,T\).
Production satisfies \(0\le q_t\le U_t\), and backlogging is forbidden.
The one-period cost \(g_t(q_t,I_t)\) includes all production, setup, and holding charges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum total cost is \(V_T(I_T^{\mathrm{req}})\), with infeasible states assigned \(+\infty\).

notation.meaning: minimum cost through period t ending at inventory s

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: inventory balance with bounded production yields the canonical finite-state lot-sizing recurrence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon inventory-state recursion with binding per-period production capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given initial inventory \(I_0\), the state transition is
\[I_t=I_{t-1}+q_t-d_t,\qquad 0\le q_t\le U_t,\qquad I_t\ge0.\]
Initialize \(V_0(I_0)=0\) and all other initial states at \(+\infty\). For each reachable integer inventory \(s\), update
\[V_t(s)=\min_{0\le q\le U_t:\,s-q+d_t\ge0}\{V_{t-1}(s-q+d_t)+g_t(q,s)\}.\]
After period \(T\), output the required terminal-state value, commonly \(V_T(0)\), and recover production decisions from minimizing predecessors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacities make end-of-period inventory a necessary state; bounded production choices generate the exact Bellman transition.
knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated Lot-Sizing State Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inventory-state recurrence is plausible and its algorithm kind fits the state-model leaf, but the exact capacitated formulation and its terminal-state claim have no citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Lot-Sizing Constraint Variants
children.top_down_role: State extensions induced by delayed demand, setup logic, and service restrictions.

children.title: Backlogging Variants
children.top_down_role: Lot-sizing states supporting delayed demand fulfillment.

assumptions_latex: Demand and production quantities are integer-valued.
Unmet demand may be carried forward and incurs a specified backlog cost.
The inventory balance is enforced in every period.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Allowing \(I_t<0\) extends the inventory-state dynamic program exactly, with backlog equal to \((-I_t)_{+}\).

notation.meaning: net inventory, negative when demand is backlogged
minimum cost through period t at net inventory s

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: signed inventory is the canonical state representation for deterministic backlogging
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic lot sizing with signed inventory and explicit backlog penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Replace the nonnegative-inventory restriction by the signed balance
\[I_t=I_{t-1}+q_t-d_t,\qquad I_t\in\mathcal{I}_t\subset\mathbb{Z}.\]
Positive \(I_t\) is stock and negative \(I_t\) represents backlog \(B_t=(-I_t)_{+}\). With period cost \(g_t(q,I_t)\) containing holding and backlog charges, initialize \(V_0(I_0)=0\) and update
\[V_t(s)=\min_{q:\,s-q+d_t\in\mathcal{I}_{t-1}}\{V_{t-1}(s-q+d_t)+g_t(q,s)\}.\]
The output is the prescribed terminal-state value, often \(V_T(0)\), with predecessors giving production and backlog trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backlogging is represented by negative net inventory, so the usual inventory recursion remains exact after adding backlog costs and signed state bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Backlogging Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Signed inventory is a standard representation of deterministic backlogging, but the exact Bellman formulation, state bounds, and terminal-state claim lack a variant-specific citation.

children.title: Setup Variants
children.top_down_role: Lot-sizing states incorporating setup-dependent production choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Setup Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-charge production setups linked to positive integer lot quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\), a fixed-charge setup variant introduces \(y_t\in\{0,1\}\) and imposes \[0\le q_t\le U_ty_t.\] Its period production cost is \(K_ty_t+c_tq_t\). Because \(K_t\ge0\), an optimal solution can choose \(y_t=\mathbf{1}_{\{q_t>0\}}\); hence the equivalent quantity-only cost is \[c_tq_t+K_t\mathbf{1}_{\{q_t>0\}}.\] This period cost can be used in an inventory-state Bellman transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-charge setup variant uses a binary variable linked to production quantity and charges a fixed cost exactly when production is positive.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\), and for every \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\), production satisfies \(q_t\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\) and setup satisfies \(y_t\in\{0,1\}\).
For every \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\), \(U_t\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\) is a valid production upper bound, \(K_t\ge0\) is the fixed setup cost, and \(c_t\in\mathbb{R}\) is the unit production cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\), the constraint \(0\le q_t\le U_ty_t\) together with the charge \(K_ty_t\) models a fixed production setup, and an optimal solution can choose \(y_t=\mathbf{1}_{\{q_t>0\}}\).

notation.meaning: binary setup indicator in period t
valid upper bound on period-t production
fixed setup cost in period t
unit production cost in period t

children.title: Service-Restriction Variants
children.top_down_role: Lot-sizing states reflecting service-level or timing restrictions.

assumptions_latex: Net inventory \(I_t\) is integer-valued and backlog is \(B_t=(-I_t)_{+}\).
A deterministic service limit \(L_t\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\) is specified for every period.
Inventory balance holds over the finite horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The service restriction is satisfied exactly when every reachable state obeys \(I_t\ge-L_t\).

notation.meaning: maximum permitted backlog after period t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a hard deterministic service restriction is representable as a periodwise backlog bound
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard periodwise backlog limits as a deterministic service-level variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the hard-backlog interpretation of service, impose
\[B_t=(-I_t)_{+}\le L_t,\qquad t=1,ldots,T.\]
Equivalently, admissible inventory states satisfy \(I_t\ge-L_t\). An inventory-state dynamic program enforces the restriction by deleting every transition whose successor state violates this inequality. This condition is specific to a hard backlog cap; fill-rate, waiting-time, and chance-constrained service criteria are different variants and generally require cumulative, age-structured, or probabilistic state information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hard deterministic service requirement bounds each period's backlog, equivalently imposing a lower bound on every reachable net-inventory state.
knowledge_statements.title: Service-Restriction Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hard-backlog-cap condition is mathematically plausible and appropriately distinguished from other service metrics, but it has no citation. The horizon expression also contains the malformed text 'ldots' instead of the intended TeX ellipsis and must be repaired after sourcing.

children.title: Combined Variant States
children.top_down_role: State extensions supporting simultaneous backlog, setup, or service features.

assumptions_latex: All inventory, demand, production, and service-budget quantities are integer-valued.
The next state is determined by the current state and current production/setup decision.
The finite state and action sets encode all capacity, backlog, setup, and service restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bellman recursion on \((I_t,z_t,r_t)\) is exact whenever this augmented state is Markov sufficient for all future costs and constraints.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: combined constraints require the Cartesian-product state of their future-relevant summaries
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Augmented Markov states combining inventory, setup mode, and service allowance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the augmented state be \(s_t=(I_t,z_t,r_t)\), where \(I_t\) records net inventory, \(z_t\) records any setup mode affecting future costs, and \(r_t\) records remaining cumulative service allowance. Initialize \(V_0(s_0)=0\). For each period, use
\[V_t(s')=\min_{s,q,y:\,T_t(s,q,y)=s'}\{V_{t-1}(s)+g_t(s,q,y)\},\]
where \(T_t\) enforces inventory balance, capacity, setup logic, backlog rules, and service-budget consumption. Output the least value among admissible terminal states and recover decisions through minimizing predecessors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When variants interact, the exact state combines every summary affecting future feasibility or cost, such as inventory, setup mode, and remaining service allowance.
knowledge_statements.title: Combined Variant States

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Markov-sufficiency principle is plausible, but no source supports this particular augmented state. The transition and service-allowance update are abstract enough that exactness cannot be checked for the stated combined variants.

children.title: Multi-Item Coupled Lot-Sizing
children.top_down_role: Shared-capacity models requiring multidimensional states or decomposition.

assumptions_latex: There are \(J\) items with integer demands \(d_{jt}\), productions \(q_{jt}\), and inventories \(I_{jt}\).
Period \(t\) has shared capacity \(\sum_{j=1}^{J}a_{jt}q_{jt}\le C_t\).
The one-period cost \(g_t(q_t,I_t)\) is evaluable on a finite feasible action set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vector-state recurrence yields the exact optimum; coupling prevents independent itemwise dynamic programs unless the shared constraints are relaxed or decomposed.

notation.meaning: vector of item inventories after period t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: shared capacity couples item actions and induces a vector-inventory Bellman state
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon multi-item lot sizing with shared per-period production capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The state is the inventory vector \(I_t=(I_{1t},ldots,I_{Jt})\), with componentwise balance
\[I_{jt}=I_{j,t-1}+q_{jt}-d_{jt}.\]
At period \(t\), admissible production vectors satisfy \(q_t\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{J}\) and \(\sum_{j=1}^{J}a_{jt}q_{jt}\le C_t\). Initialize the prescribed state \(V_0(I_0)=0\), then update
\[V_t(I')=\min_{q_t:\,I'-q_t+d_t\text{ admissible}}\{V_{t-1}(I'-q_t+d_t)+g_t(q_t,I')\}.\]
The desired terminal-state value is returned, with infeasible states assigned \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared capacity couples item production decisions, so an exact lot-sizing dynamic program generally uses the full vector of item inventories as its state.
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Item Coupled Lot-Sizing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vector-inventory state and shared-capacity coupling are plausible, but the exact recurrence and decomposition assertion lack a multi-item lot-sizing citation. The inventory-vector ellipsis is also malformed as 'ldots' and requires repair once the statement is sourced.

children.title: Tree-Structured Selection DP Family
children.top_down_role: Integer selection problems whose recursive structure is supplied by a rooted tree or bounded interface.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Section 5.3: An Optimal Subtree of a Tree
Dynamic programming algorithms for trees

children.title: Optimal Subtree Selection
children.top_down_role: Rooted subtree-selection models with recursively combined choices.

assumptions_latex: \(T=(V,E)\) is a finite tree rooted at \(r\).
Each vertex \(v\in V\) has weight \(w_v\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(r)\) is the maximum weight of an ancestor-closed vertex set containing \(r\).

notation.meaning: optimal value for a selected subtree rooted at v and containing v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Root-containing, ancestor-closed version on a finite rooted tree.

source_refs.locator: 5.3 An Optimal Subtree of a Tree p. 83

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Process vertices in postorder. For every leaf \(v\), set \(F(v)=w_v\). For every nonleaf vertex, set \[F(v)=w_v+\sum_{u\in C(v)}\max\{0,F(u)\}.\] Reconstruct a selected set by including \(r\) and, whenever an included vertex \(v\) has child \(u\), including the optimal subtree at \(u\) exactly when \(F(u)>0\); either choice is optimal when \(F(u)=0\). The resulting set is connected, contains \(r\), and maximizes \(\sum_{v\in S}w_v\) over all ancestor-closed \(S\subseteq V\) containing \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Postorder recursion retains a child subtree exactly when its optimal contribution is positive, producing a maximum-weight ancestor-closed subtree containing the root.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal Subtree Selection

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3 An Optimal Subtree of a Tree p. 83

children.title: Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack Family
children.top_down_role: Resource-limited selection over tree precedence structures.

children.title: Tree Knapsack
children.top_down_role: Resource-limited selection organized by rooted tree structure.

assumptions_latex: \(T=(V,E)\) is a finite tree rooted at \(r\).
Vertex profits satisfy \(p_v\in\mathbb{R}\), costs satisfy \(a_v\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\), and \(B\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is \(\max\{\sum_{v\in V}p_vx_v:x\in\mathcal{K}(T,B)\}\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ancestor-closed vertex selection with one integral resource budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The rooted tree-knapsack feasible family is \[\mathcal{K}(T,B)=\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^{V}:x_v\le x_{\pi(v)}\ \text{for every }v\ne r,\quad \sum_{v\in V}a_vx_v\le B\right\}.\] A tree-knapsack problem maximizes \(\sum_{v\in V}p_vx_v\) over this family. Thus selecting any nonroot vertex forces selection of every vertex on its path to the root, while the total integral cost cannot exceed \(B\). Requiring a nonempty solution or mandatory root is expressed by adding \(x_r=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tree knapsack maximizes vertex profit under a budget while requiring every selected vertex's ancestors to be selected.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree Knapsack

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is a standard definition of rooted tree knapsack and fits the container, but no inspectable source is cited.

children.title: Precedence-Constrained Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection structures governed by predecessor eligibility restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(T=(V,E)\) is a finite rooted tree.
A binary variable \(x_v\) indicates whether vertex \(v\) is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A selection is precedence-feasible exactly when \(x_v\le x_{pi(v)}\) for every \(v\ne r\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parent-before-child precedence on binary selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The parent-before-child precedence condition is \[x_v\le x_{\pi(v)}\qquad(v\in V\setminus\{r\}).\] Equivalently, \(S\subseteq V\) is feasible when \(v\in S\) implies that every ancestor of \(v\), including \(\pi(v)\), also lies in \(S\). Hence every nonempty feasible set contains the root and induces a connected rooted subtree. Conversely, every vertex set containing the root and closed under taking parents satisfies all displayed inequalities, so the inequality and ancestor-closure descriptions define the same feasible family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parent-before-child precedence is equivalent to ancestor closure: selecting a vertex forces selection of every ancestor up to the root.
knowledge_statements.title: Precedence-Constrained Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ancestor-closure equivalence is standard and the condition kind fits, but it lacks a citation. The conclusion also uses x_{pi(v)} instead of the defined x_{\pi(v)}.

children.title: Resource-Limited Tree Selection
children.top_down_role: Tree-structured selection combining resource limits with hierarchical eligibility.

assumptions_latex: \(T=(V,E)\) is a finite rooted tree with integral costs \(a_v\ge 0\) and profits \(p_v\in\mathbb{R}\).
The available budget is \(B\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The root-table value \(\max_{0\le b\le B}D_r(b)\) is the optimal resource-limited ancestor-closed selection value.

notation.meaning: best profit of a selected subtree rooted at v using exactly b units

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudopolynomial budget-indexed dynamic program for integral costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(D_v(a_v)=p_v\) and \(D_v(b)=-\infty\) for other \(b\). Process each child \(u\in C(v)\) after computing its table, and replace the current table \(Q\) by \[Q'(b)=\max_{0\le t\le b}\left\{Q(b-t)+\max\{0,D_u(t)\}\right\},\] where the zero alternative means omitting the entire child subtree and infeasible entries have value \(-\infty\). After all children are merged, set \(D_v=Q\). Output \(\max\{0,D_r(b):0\le b\le B\}\), or omit zero when selection of the root is mandatory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A budget-indexed table combines child subtrees by knapsack convolution, with each child either omitted or included through its own feasible table.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Limited Tree Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the algorithm. Moreover, D_v(b) is defined for exactly b units, while max{0,D_u(t)} permits omission after assigning a positive t to the child; omission should consume zero resource or the tables should instead be defined for usage at most b.

children.title: Bounded-Interface Graph Dynamic Programs
children.top_down_role: Extensions governed by separator size rather than numerical resource ranges.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) has a rooted tree decomposition whose bags have size at most \(k+1\).
Each local decision has a finite domain of size at most \(q\), and objective and constraints decompose over bags.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimization problem is solvable by bag dynamic programming using \(O(q^{k+1})\) interface states per bag.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain optimization over a supplied bounded-width tree decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each decomposition node \(t\) and assignment \(\sigma\in[q]^{X_t}\), store the best value attainable in the subgraph represented below \(t\) among solutions agreeing with \(\sigma\) on \(X_t\). Introduce, forget, and join operations update these values by local feasibility checks, maximization over forgotten coordinates, and addition of compatible child values with duplicated bag contributions removed. The separator property ensures that two processed regions interact only through their common bag assignment. Consequently, the state count is at most \(q^{k+1}\) per bag and depends exponentially on interface size rather than on numerical resource magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-width decomposition permits dynamic programming over separator assignments, with exponentially many states in interface size but no resource-range indexing.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Interface Graph Dynamic Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-interface principle fits the node, but no source is supplied and “objective and constraints decompose over bags” is too informal to guarantee the stated introduce/forget/join program and state bound.

children.title: One-Dimensional Cutting Patterns
children.top_down_role: Knapsack-structured pattern generation for one-dimensional stock.

assumptions_latex: Stock length \(L\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) and item lengths \(\ell_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) are given for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible one-dimensional cutting patterns are exactly the vectors in \(\mathcal{P}(L,\ell)\).

notation.meaning: number of items of type i cut from one stock piece

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard one-dimensional cutting-stock pattern representation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-length, single-stock-piece pattern model without kerf or setup losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A one-dimensional cutting pattern is represented by a vector \(a\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{m}\), where \(a_i\) counts pieces of length \(\ell_i\). Its feasibility condition is \[\mathcal{P}(L,\ell)=\left\{a\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{m}:\sum_{i=1}^{m}\ell_i a_i\le L\right\}.\] If a pattern has value \(c_i\) per produced item, maximum-value pattern generation is the unbounded integer knapsack \(\max\{\sum_i c_i a_i:a\in\mathcal{P}(L,\ell)\}\). A capacity-indexed dynamic program therefore generates an optimal pattern whenever lengths are integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cutting pattern is a nonnegative integer item-count vector whose total length fits in one stock piece; pattern generation is unbounded knapsack.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Dimensional Cutting Patterns

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The single-stock pattern representation and its unbounded-knapsack specialization are standard and locally appropriate, but they have no cited source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pattern formulation and column generation for one-dimensional cutting stock
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Knapsack-structured pattern formulation and its restricted-master pricing certificate. The pricing condition is sufficient for full-LP optimality; the extract does not establish the converse for an arbitrary optimal restricted-master dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W>0\), \(0<w_i\le W\), \(b_i\in\mathbb Z_+\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(\mathcal S=\{s\in\mathbb Z_+^m:\sum_{i=1}^m w_i s_i\le W\}\). The cutting-stock pattern formulation is \(\min\{\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}x_s:\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}s_i x_s\ge b_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ x\in\mathbb Z_+^{\mathcal S}\}\), whose LP dual is \(\max\{\sum_i b_i u_i:\sum_i s_i u_i\le1\ (s\in\mathcal S),\ u\ge0\}\). For \(\mathcal S'\subseteq\mathcal S\), let \((\bar x,\bar u)\) be an optimal primal-dual pair for the restricted LP. If \(\max_{s\in\mathcal S}\sum_i\bar u_i s_i\le1\), then \(\bar u\) is feasible for the full dual and \(\bar x\), extended by zero outside \(\mathcal S'\), is optimal for the full LP. If the maximum exceeds \(1\), any maximizer \(s^*\) indexes a most-violated full-dual constraint and a column to add to the restricted master.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cutting pattern is a nonnegative integer vector of roll counts whose total width does not exceed the stock width. The pattern model minimizes the number of stock rolls while meeting all demands. Given an optimal dual solution of a restricted LP master, a knapsack pricing value at most one certifies optimality for the full LP. If the value exceeds one, an optimal pricing pattern gives a most-violated omitted dual constraint and a column to add. The extract supports this certificate direction, not an unconditional converse.
assumptions_latex: m\in\mathbb Z_{>0}
0<w_i\le W\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)
b_i\in\mathbb Z_+\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)
\mathcal S'\subseteq\mathcal S
(\bar x,\bar u)\text{ is an optimal primal-dual pair for the LP restricted to }\mathcal S'
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{s\in\mathcal S}\sum_{i=1}^m\bar u_i s_i\le1\ \Longrightarrow\ \bar x\text{ is optimal for the full LP};\qquad \max_{s\in\mathcal S}\sum_{i=1}^m\bar u_i s_i>1\ \Longrightarrow\ s^*\text{ supplies a most-violated dual constraint and a column to add.}

children.title: Bounded-Demand Patterns
children.top_down_role: Pattern states respecting finite demand limits for item types.

assumptions_latex: Item lengths \(\ell_i\), stock length \(L\), and demand caps \(d_i\) are nonnegative integers, with \(\ell_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A vector is a bounded-demand pattern exactly when it belongs to \(\mathcal{P}_d(L,\ell)\).

notation.meaning: available demand cap for item type i

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-pattern production cannot exceed residual demand by item type.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bounded-demand pattern family is \[\mathcal{P}_d(L,\ell)=\left\{a\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{m}:\sum_{i=1}^{m}\ell_i a_i\le L,\quad 0\le a_i\le d_i\ \text{for all }i\right\}.\] Thus each coordinate is bounded both by its demand cap and implicitly by stock capacity. When \(d_i=0\), type \(i\) cannot occur; when \(d_i\ge\lfloor L/\ell_i\rfloor\), its explicit cap is redundant. Optimizing a linear pattern value over this family is a bounded integer-knapsack problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-demand cutting pattern fits within stock capacity and uses no more than the available demand of any item type.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Demand Patterns

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-demand pattern definition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no inspectable citation is provided.

children.title: Multiplicity-Constrained Patterns
children.top_down_role: Pattern states respecting copy limits within individual patterns.

assumptions_latex: For each item type \(i\), an allowed finite multiplicity set \(M_i\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\) contains \(0\).
Item lengths satisfy \(\ell_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), with stock length \(L\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pattern \(a\) is multiplicity-feasible exactly when \(a_i\in M_i\) for every \(i\) and \(\sum_i\ell_i a_i\le L\).

notation.meaning: allowed counts of item type i in one pattern

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite allowed-multiplicity generalization of bounded patterns
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrary finite allowed count sets, including batch and parity restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The multiplicity-constrained pattern family is \[\mathcal{P}_M=\left\{a\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{m}:a_i\in M_i\ \text{for every }i,\quad \sum_{i=1}^{m}\ell_i a_i\le L\right\}.\] This includes upper bounds through \(M_i=\{0,1,\ldots,d_i\}\), binary occurrence through \(M_i=\{0,1\}\), and fixed-batch restrictions through sets such as \(M_i=\{0,b_i,2b_i,\ldots,k_ib_i\}\). Because membership is coordinatewise, a dynamic program may enumerate the allowed multiplicity of each type while retaining only capacity-feasible transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplicity-constrained patterns restrict each item count to a prescribed finite set, allowing bounds, binary use, parity, or batch-size rules.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity-Constrained Patterns

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite allowed-multiplicity formulation fits the title and definition kind, but its generalization and dynamic-programming assertion lack a source.

children.title: Demand-Cap State Coordinates
children.top_down_role: State coordinates retaining remaining demand or pattern-level copy allowances.

assumptions_latex: Demand caps satisfy \(d_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\) for \(i=1,,m\).
Patterns are constructed by transitions that add one item of a chosen type.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vector \(s\) is sufficient to enforce every per-type cap during pattern construction.

notation.meaning: counts already used in the partial pattern
unit vector for item type i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact count-vector state for capped pattern generation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact per-type count coordinates for enforcing residual-demand caps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a partial pattern by a demand-cap state \[s\in\prod_{i=1}^{m}\{0,1,\ldots,d_i\},\] where \(s_i\) is the number of type-\(i\) items already included. Adding an item of type \(i\) applies the transition \(s\mapsto s+e_i\), permitted only when \(s_i<d_i\) and the resulting pattern remains resource-feasible. The residual availability is \(d-s\). Since any two partial patterns with the same resource usage and the same vector \(s\) admit identical future multiplicity choices, these coordinates are sufficient for exact enforcement of all demand caps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A count-vector state records usage of every item type; incrementing a coordinate is allowed only below its demand cap.
knowledge_statements.title: Demand-Cap State Coordinates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The count-vector representation is appropriate, but no source is cited. The assumption range “i=1,,m” must also be corrected to “i=1,\ldots,m”.

children.title: Multi-Coordinate Pattern States
children.top_down_role: Pattern states tracking several capacities or compatibility attributes.

children.title: Multi-Resource Pattern States
children.top_down_role: Pattern states carrying several capacity dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Resource Pattern States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive, integral resource consumption in a fixed number of coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a partial pattern by its resource-usage vector \[b=\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_i x_i\in\prod_{j=1}^{k}\{0,1,\ldots,B_j\},\] where \(x_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) is the current multiplicity of item type \(i\). Adding one item of type \(i\) applies \(b\mapsto b+a_i\) and is feasible exactly when \(b+a_i\le B\) componentwise. For additive resource constraints, two partial patterns with the same vector \(b\) have identical remaining resource capacities \(B-b\); hence future resource feasibility depends on the past only through \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multi-resource state records every used capacity coordinate; an item transition is feasible when the updated vector stays componentwise within capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(m,k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) are the numbers of item types and resources, respectively.
Each item type \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) consumes \(a_{ji}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) units of resource \(j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\).
Resource capacities satisfy \(B_j\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) for \(j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vector \(b\) is a sufficient resource state for additive multi-resource pattern feasibility.

notation.meaning: resource-consumption vector of item type i
resource usage of a partial pattern

children.title: Multi-Attribute Compatibility States
children.top_down_role: Pattern states carrying multiple compatibility or classification attributes.

assumptions_latex: Each item has attributes from finite domains.
Compatibility of extending a partial pattern depends only on a finite summary state and the next item's attributes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The state \(q\) exactly distinguishes partial patterns having different feasible continuations under the specified compatibility rules.

notation.meaning: partial transition on adding item i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-state encoding of attribute compatibility
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state compatibility rules for attributes of items in one pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a finite state set \(Q\), initial state \(q_0\), and partial transition map \(\delta:Q\times\{1,\ldots,m\}\rightharpoonup Q\). Initialize the empty pattern at \(q_0\). When item type \(i\) is appended to a partial pattern in state \(q\), reject the transition if \(\delta(q,i)\) is undefined; otherwise replace \(q\) by \(\delta(q,i)\). A state is exact when two partial patterns assigned the same \(q\) admit precisely the same compatible future item sequences. Dynamic programming may then retain the best partial-pattern value for each resource state and compatibility state pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite compatibility state summarizes relevant item attributes; undefined transitions reject incompatible additions, while equal states have identical feasible continuations.
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Attribute Compatibility States

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-state construction is plausible but uncited. Its mathematical role is a state representation, not an algorithm: no complete optimization procedure, processing order, or output specification is given.

children.title: Resource–Attribute Coupling
children.top_down_role: Pattern families where capacity dimensions interact with compatibility attributes.

assumptions_latex: Resource usage lies in an integral capacity box \(0\le b\le B\).
Compatibility is represented by a finite state \(q\in Q\) with partial transitions \(\delta(q,i)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A transition is feasible exactly when both \(b+a_i\le B\) and \(\delta(q,i)\) is defined.

notation.meaning: resource vector consumed by item type i
compatibility transition after adding type i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: product-state coupling of resource and compatibility transitions
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint transitions when attribute feasibility and resource use must be tracked together.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Use the product state \((b,q)\), where \(b\) records additive resource usage and \(q\) records attribute compatibility. Adding item type \(i\) is permitted exactly when \[b+a_i\le B\quad\text{componentwise}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\delta(q,i)\ \text{is defined}.\] The successor is then \((b+a_i,\delta(q,i))\). Neither marginal state is generally sufficient: equal resource vectors can have different compatible continuations, and equal compatibility states can have different remaining capacities. The product state is sufficient whenever resource increments depend only on the chosen item and compatibility evolution depends only on \((q,i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resource-attribute coupling uses product states; adding an item must simultaneously respect capacity and define a valid compatibility transition.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource–Attribute Coupling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product-state transition condition fits resource–attribute coupling and is internally coherent, but no source supports the sufficiency and marginal-insufficiency claims.

children.title: Sequence-Dependent Patterns
children.top_down_role: Pattern dynamic programs retaining order-dependent information.

assumptions_latex: Item types form a finite set \(I\), each item \(i\in I\) has integer resource use \(w_i\ge 0\), and capacity is \(W\in\mathbb Z_+\).
Appending item \(j\) after item \(i\) incurs integer transition use \(s_{ij}\ge 0\); a distinguished symbol \(0\) denotes the initial predecessor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(W,0)\) gives the optimal feasible sequence value.

notation.meaning: best value attainable with used capacity c and final type i
value of selecting an item of type j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward labeling DP with the last selected type retained in the state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(F(0,0)=0\) and \(F(c,i)=-\infty\) for every other state \((c,i)\). From each finite label \(F(c,i)\), append a type \(j\in I\) whenever \(c+s_{ij}+w_j\le W\), and perform the update \[F(c+s_{ij}+w_j,j)\leftarrow\max\{F(c+s_{ij}+w_j,j),F(c,i)+p_j\}.\] Process states in nondecreasing used capacity when every append has positive total use. The optimum over sequences fitting one stock object is \(\max_{0\le c\le W,\,i\in I\cup\{0\}}F(c,i)\); predecessor pointers recover an optimal ordered pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retaining the last item type makes transition consumption available to the recurrence, so feasible ordered patterns can be generated by forward dynamic programming.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequence-Dependent Patterns

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the sequence-dependent recurrence. Moreover, F(W,0) is not the stated optimum: the recurrence never returns to predecessor 0, and the statement instead maximizes over all capacities and final types. Strictly positive append consumption or another finiteness condition is also required to exclude zero-consumption cycles. The plain statement omits the claimed optimization and recovery details.

children.title: Cutting-Stock Pattern Structures
children.top_down_role: Pattern dynamic programs organized around feasible cuts from stock units.

assumptions_latex: Stock length is \(W\in\mathbb Z_+\); item lengths and demands satisfy \(w_i\in\mathbb Z_+\) and \(d_i\in\mathbb Z_+\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integer master problem selects a minimum-cardinality multiset of feasible cutting patterns satisfying all demands.

notation.meaning: set of feasible one-stock cutting patterns
multiplicity of item i in pattern p
number of stock objects cut according to pattern p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gilmore-Gomory-style integer pattern representation for one-dimensional cutting stock.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Cutting Stock: Formulations with Many Variables p. 48

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the feasible pattern set by \[\mathcal P=\left\{a\in\mathbb Z_+^m:\sum_{i=1}^m w_i a_i\le W\right\}.\] For each \(p\in\mathcal P\), let \(a_{ip}\) be its multiplicity of type \(i\). The minimum-stock cutting problem has the pattern representation \[\min\left\{\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}y_p:\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}a_{ip}y_p\ge d_i\ \text{for all }i,\ y_p\in\mathbb Z_+\ \text{for all }p\right\}.\] A capacity-indexed knapsack dynamic program generates or prices columns because membership in \(\mathcal P\) is exactly the single-stock integer capacity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cutting-stock solution is an integer multiset of feasible one-stock patterns whose combined item multiplicities cover every demand.
knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Stock Pattern Structures

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Cutting Stock: Formulations with Many Variables p. 48

children.title: Packing Feasibility Pattern Structures
children.top_down_role: Pattern dynamic programs organized around feasible placement within resource containers.

assumptions_latex: There are \(m\) item types and \(q\) nonnegative integer resource coordinates.
Type \(i\) uses vector \(a_i\in\mathbb Z_+^q\), and one container has capacity \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A multiplicity vector is a feasible packing pattern exactly when its total resource vector does not exceed \(b\) componentwise.

notation.meaning: multiplicity vector of a packing pattern

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive multi-resource feasibility for one-container integer packing patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=[a_1\ \cdots\ a_m]\in\mathbb Z_+^{q\times m}\). The set of feasible one-container packing patterns is \[\mathcal P(b)=\{x\in\mathbb Z_+^m:Ax\le b\},\] where the inequality is componentwise. Equivalently, starting at resource state \(r=0\), a pattern is feasible precisely when its items can be appended through transitions \(r\mapsto r+a_i\) that remain in \(\{r\in\mathbb Z_+^q:r\le b\}\). Since addition is commutative and all resource uses are nonnegative, every ordering of the same multiplicity vector reaches the same terminal state \(Ax\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A packing pattern is feasible exactly when the componentwise sum of its item resource vectors stays within the container capacity vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Packing Feasibility Pattern Structures

children.title: Constraint-Row Activity Dynamic Programs
children.top_down_role: States indexed by partial activities across integer constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Row Activity Dynamic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Layered activity-state DP for bounded, nonnegative integer linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(F_0(0)=0\) and \(F_0(r)=-\infty\) for every \(r\ne 0\). For \(j=1,\ldots,n\) and every \(r\in\mathbb Z_+^m\) satisfying \(r\le b\), compute \[F_j(r)=\max_{k\in\{0,\ldots,u_j\}:\,ka_j\le r}\left\{F_{j-1}(r-ka_j)+c_jk\right\}.\] Infeasible predecessor labels have value \(-\infty\). For every state \(r\), \(F_j(r)\) is the best objective value among assignments to variables \(1,\ldots,j\) having row activity \(r\). The optimal value is \(\max_{r\in\mathbb Z_+^m:\,r\le b}F_n(r)\), and stored maximizing choices recover an optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm processes one bounded integer variable per layer and records the best partial objective for every attainable constraint-row activity vector; maximizing the final labels gives the ILP optimum.
assumptions_latex: Consider \(\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le b,\ 0\le x\le u,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb Z_+^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^m\), \(u\in\mathbb Z_+^n\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \(r\), the label \(F_n(r)\) equals the best objective among feasible integer vectors with \(Ax=r\), and maximizing these labels yields the optimal value.

notation.meaning: best value after processing variables 1 through j with activity r

children.title: Residual Right-Hand-Side Dynamic Programs
children.top_down_role: States indexed by remaining integer requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Right-Hand-Side Dynamic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backward residual-capacity DP for bounded, nonnegative integer linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(\rho\in\mathbb Z_+^m\) satisfying \(\rho\le b\), initialize \(G_{n+1}(\rho)=0\). For \(j=n,n-1,\ldots,1\), compute \[G_j(\rho)=\max_{k\in\{0,\ldots,u_j\}:\,ka_j\le\rho}\left\{c_jk+G_{j+1}(\rho-ka_j)\right\}.\] The transition subtracts the row activity consumed by the selected multiplicity of variable \(j\). The output is \(G_1(b)\), and stored maximizing choices recover an optimizer. The state set is finite because each coordinate of \(\rho\) lies between zero and the corresponding coordinate of \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm indexes states by remaining row capacities and processes each bounded integer variable by subtracting its selected row activity; the initial residual state gives the ILP optimum.
assumptions_latex: Consider \(\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le b,\ 0\le x\le u,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb Z_+^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^m\), \(u\in\mathbb Z_+^n\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The initial-state label \(G_1(b)\) equals the optimal integer-program value.

notation.meaning: best value using variables j through n under residual capacity rho

children.title: Group-Relaxation States
children.top_down_role: Finite arithmetic states induced by group relaxations.

assumptions_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite abelian group, let \(g_1,\ldots,g_n,g_0\in G\), and let \(c\in\mathbb R_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The group-relaxation state is the accumulated group element, with feasibility determined by reaching \(g_0\).

notation.meaning: group element contributed by one unit of variable j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-group state model for a nonnegative integer group relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the group relaxation \[\min\left\{c^Tx:\sum_{j=1}^n g_jx_j=g_0\ \text{in }G,\ x\in\mathbb Z_+^n\right\},\] a group-relaxation state is an element \(g\in G\) representing the accumulated sum \(\sum_{j=1}^n g_jx_j\). Selecting one additional unit of variable \(j\) induces the transition \(g\mapsto g+g_j\) with cost \(c_j\). The initial state is the identity element \(0_G\), and the accepting state is \(g_0\). Thus a feasible walk from \(0_G\) to \(g_0\) encodes a feasible nonnegative integer vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A group-relaxation state records the finite-group sum accumulated by selected integer variables; feasible solutions end at the prescribed group element.
knowledge_statements.title: Group-Relaxation States

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-group state formulation is plausible and the definition kind fits the container, but no inspectable citation supports the particular group-relaxation formulation or its DP interpretation.

children.title: Congruence-Class States
children.top_down_role: Finite states indexed by residue or congruence classes.

assumptions_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb Z^{r\times r}\) be nonsingular and let \(L=M\mathbb Z^r\) be its full-rank sublattice of \(\mathbb Z^r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Congruence-class states are the finitely many cosets in \(\mathbb Z^r/L\).

notation.meaning: full-rank integer lattice generated by M
finite quotient group of congruence classes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quotient-lattice states induced by a nonsingular integer basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z,z'\in\mathbb Z^r\), define \(z\equiv z'\pmod L\) if and only if \(z-z'\in L\). A congruence-class state is the coset \([z]_L=z+L\) in the quotient \(\mathbb Z^r/L\). The quotient contains exactly \(|\det M|\) states. If an integer decision contributes a vector \(a_j\in\mathbb Z^r\), then adding one unit of that decision maps \([z]_L\) to \([z+a_j]_L\). Consequently, an equality required only modulo \(L\) is enforced by specifying a target coset rather than retaining the full integer activity vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer activity vectors equivalent modulo a full-rank lattice share one state; the resulting quotient has absolute determinant many states.
knowledge_statements.title: Congruence-Class States

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quotient-lattice construction and determinant cardinality are mathematically standard, but the record supplies no source for their use as congruence-class DP states.

children.title: Group–Congruence Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between group-based state spaces and residue-class state spaces.

assumptions_latex: Let \(L=M\mathbb Z^r\) for a nonsingular integer matrix \(M\), and let \(G=\mathbb Z^r/L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quotient map identifies lattice congruence states and finite-group states bijectively, preserving additive transitions.

notation.meaning: quotient homomorphism sending z to its lattice coset

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical correspondence between quotient-lattice congruence states and finite abelian group states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The quotient map \(\pi:\mathbb Z^r\to G\), defined by \(\pi(z)=[z]_L\), is a surjective group homomorphism with kernel \(L\). Hence \(z\equiv z'\pmod L\) if and only if \(\pi(z)=\pi(z')\), and every congruence class corresponds to exactly one element of \(G\). Moreover, for every transition vector \(a_j\in\mathbb Z^r\), \[\pi(z+a_j)=\pi(z)+\pi(a_j).\] Therefore a dynamic program whose state is the congruence class of accumulated activity is the same state graph as the group-relaxation dynamic program on \(G\), up to relabeling of vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting integer activities by a lattice produces a finite abelian group, and the quotient map preserves every additive DP transition.
knowledge_statements.title: Group–Congruence Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quotient correspondence is plausible, but no source supports the asserted identification with a group-relaxation state graph. The statement also contains proof-style derivational text that should be removed when a sourced replacement is prepared.

children.title: Generic ILP-DP Applicability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Coefficient, dimension, and boundedness conditions governing finite generic state models.

knowledge_statements.title: Generic ILP-DP Applicability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finiteness and pseudopolynomial limits of generic row-activity dynamic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every reachable activity coordinate is integral and coordinate \(k\) lies in \(\{0,\ldots,B_k\}\), then a full row-activity table has at most \(\prod_{k=1}^m(B_k+1)\) states per variable layer. The construction is finite but generally pseudopolynomial because this bound depends on coefficient and right-hand-side magnitudes rather than their binary encoding lengths. If an indispensable state coordinate has no finite reachable bound, direct state enumeration need not terminate. With negative coefficients, the finite box \(\prod_{k=1}^m\{0,\ldots,B_k\}\) is not automatically invariant under transitions, so valid finite bounds or a different state representation are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generic ILP dynamic programming has a finite state table only when all retained integral activity coordinates have finite reachable ranges, and its table size is generally pseudopolynomial in numerical magnitudes.
assumptions_latex: A generic activity-state construction is applied to an integer linear program with integer coefficient matrix \(A\).
The construction retains \(m\in\mathbb Z_+\) activity coordinates, and \(B_k\in\mathbb Z_+\) denotes a proposed finite upper bound for coordinate \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite exact enumeration requires finite reachable activity or residual ranges; otherwise the generic state construction may be infinite or only pseudopolynomial.

notation.meaning: number of constraint rows retained as state coordinates
finite nonnegative integer upper bound on state coordinate k

children.title: Dominance Frontier Calculus
children.top_down_role: Partial-order mechanisms for retaining only states with distinct competitive continuations.

children.title: Scalar-Resource Dominance
children.top_down_role: Dominance over states with one ordered resource coordinate.

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar-Resource Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe label dominance for one monotone resource in a maximization DP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a fixed DP stage and continuation-relevant discrete state, define \(P\succeq Q\) when \(r_P\le r_Q\) and \(v_P\ge v_Q\). Under resource-monotone continuation feasibility and history-independent continuation rewards, \(P\succeq Q\) implies that deleting \(Q\) preserves the optimal value. At least one inequality must be strict for strict dominance between distinct resource-value pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the same stage and discrete state, a label using no more scalar resource and having no lower value safely dominates and permits removal of the other label.
assumptions_latex: Two labels \(P,Q\) represent the same DP stage and continuation-relevant discrete state.
The problem is a maximization problem; \(r_P,r_Q\in\mathbb R_+\) are used scalar resources and \(v_P,v_Q\in\mathbb R\) are accumulated values.
Every continuation feasible at used-resource level \(r_Q\) is feasible at every used-resource level at most \(r_Q\), and its incremental value is independent of label history.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(r_P\le r_Q\) and \(v_P\ge v_Q\), label \(Q\) may be discarded without changing the optimal value.

notation.meaning: used scalar resource of label P
accumulated objective value of label P

children.title: Pareto Resource Dominance
children.top_down_role: Componentwise dominance over multi-resource states.

knowledge_statements.title: Pareto Resource Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto pruning under componentwise monotone resource consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a fixed DP stage and continuation-relevant discrete state, define \(P\succeq Q\) when \(r_{P,k}\le r_{Q,k}\) for every \(k=1,\ldots,q\) and \(v_P\ge v_Q\). Under componentwise resource-monotone continuation feasibility and history-independent continuation rewards, \(P\succeq Q\) implies that \(Q\) may be pruned without changing the optimal value. The retained Pareto frontier consists of labels not dominated under this partial order; incomparable labels generally must both be retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the same stage and discrete state, a label using no more of every resource and having no lower value safely dominates and permits removal of the other label.
assumptions_latex: Labels \(P,Q\) share the same DP stage and continuation-relevant discrete state.
The problem is a maximization problem with \(r_P,r_Q\in\mathbb R_+^q\) and \(v_P,v_Q\in\mathbb R\).
Continuation feasibility is componentwise resource-monotone, and continuation rewards are independent of discarded label history.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(r_P\le r_Q\) componentwise and \(v_P\ge v_Q\), label \(Q\) may be removed without changing the optimal value.

children.title: Completion-Bound Dominance
children.top_down_role: Dominance strengthened by bounds on feasible continuations.

assumptions_latex: Labels \(P,Q\) share a DP stage and all state information required to characterize their feasible continuation sets \(\mathcal C(P)\) and \(\mathcal C(Q)\).
For each feasible continuation \(z\), its incremental maximization reward is \(\Delta(z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(v_Q+U(Q)\le v_P+L(P)\), no completion through \(Q\) can beat the certified completion through \(P\).

notation.meaning: valid upper bound on continuation reward from label Q
reward of a known feasible continuation from label P
feasible continuation set of label P

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound-based pruning certificate for maximization labels with characterized continuations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(U(Q)\) satisfies \(\Delta(z)\le U(Q)\) for every \(z\in\mathcal C(Q)\), and suppose a known continuation \(\hat z\in\mathcal C(P)\) has \(\Delta(\hat z)=L(P)\). Then every completion through \(Q\) has value at most \(v_Q+U(Q)\), while \(P\) has a verified completion of value \(v_P+L(P)\). Therefore the inequality \[v_Q+U(Q)\le v_P+L(P)\] certifies that \(Q\) cannot yield a strictly better incumbent and may be discarded when only an optimal value or one optimizer is required. The validity of both bounds is part of the certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A label is prunable when an upper bound on all its completions is no better than a feasible completion certified from another label.
knowledge_statements.title: Completion-Bound Dominance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bound comparison is a plausible pruning certificate and the certificate kind fits the container, but it has no source. Its statement also includes a proof-style derivation; a sourced revision should state only the bound validity conditions and pruning consequence.

children.title: Dominance Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Weak orders, contextual feasibility, and large antichains that limit pruning.

knowledge_statements.title: Dominance Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when state dominance cannot safely or substantially reduce a dynamic-programming layer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_t\) be a finite state layer in a minimization dynamic program, and let \(s\preceq_t s'\) mean that state \(s\) is proposed to dominate state \(s'\). Deleting \(s'\) is certified by this comparison only if every feasible continuation \(q\) from \(s'\) is feasible from \(s\) and satisfies \(g_t(s)+c(q\mid s)\le g_t(s')+c(q\mid s')\). If either condition fails, the comparison alone does not justify deleting \(s'\). Even for a sound dominance relation, every state not dominated by another retained state must remain under dominance-only pruning; in particular, if \(S_t\) is pairwise incomparable, no state can be removed and the retained layer has size \(|S_t|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dominance comparison is safe only when it preserves every continuation and does not worsen its total cost. Sound dominance may still provide no reduction when the entire layer is an antichain.
assumptions_latex: \(S_t\) is finite and the dynamic program is a minimization problem.
\(g_t(s)\) is the best prefix cost stored at state \(s\).
\(c(q\mid s)\) is the incremental cost of continuation \(q\) from state \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of continuation preservation or cost monotonicity prevents the proposed comparison from certifying deletion, and a pairwise-incomparable layer cannot be reduced by dominance alone.

notation.meaning: State s is proposed to dominate state s' at layer t.
Best accumulated prefix cost at state s.
Incremental cost of continuation q from state s.

children.title: Exact State Reduction
children.top_down_role: State transformations and filters preserving feasible continuation behavior and exact optimization.

children.title: State Viability Filtering
children.top_down_role: Removal of unreachable states and states without feasible completions.

children.title: Forward Reachability Filtering
children.top_down_role: Removal based on accessibility from admissible initial states.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward Reachability Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact removal of states unreachable from the initial layer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For layered state sets \(S_0,\ldots,S_T\), initial states \(I\subseteq S_0\), admissible decisions \(A_t(s)\), and transition maps \(F_t\), initialize \(R_0=I\). For \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\), compute \[R_{t+1}=\{F_t(s,a)\in S_{t+1}:s\in R_t,\ a\in A_t(s)\}.\] Replace each layer by \(S_t\cap R_t\), retaining predecessor or value information only for those states. A removed state has no admissible path from \(I\), so it cannot occur in any feasible complete decision sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagate states forward from the initial set and delete every state never reached by an admissible prefix.
assumptions_latex: \(F_t(s,a)\) exactly represents every admissible transition between consecutive layers.
\(I\) contains every permitted initial state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Filtering to \(S_t\cap R_t\) preserves every feasible complete path and therefore preserves the optimum.

notation.meaning: States reachable at layer t from an admissible initial state.
Admissible decisions from state s at layer t.

children.title: Feasible-Completion Filtering
children.top_down_role: Removal based on the absence of admissible terminal continuations.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Completion Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact backward removal of states having no feasible terminal continuation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\subseteq S_T\) be the acceptable terminal states. Initialize \(C_T=G\). For \(t=T-1,\ldots,0\), compute \[C_t=\{s\in S_t:\exists a\in A_t(s)\text{ with }F_t(s,a)\in C_{t+1}\}.\] Retain only states in \(C_t\) and transitions whose successor belongs to \(C_{t+1}\). Every removed state lacks an admissible suffix ending in \(G\), so no feasible complete decision sequence can pass through it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Work backward from acceptable terminal states and delete any state from which no feasible completion exists.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) exactly describes terminal feasibility.
\(A_t(s)\) and \(F_t\) enumerate all admissible outgoing transitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Restricting layer \(t\) to \(C_t\) preserves exactly the states admitting a feasible terminal completion.

notation.meaning: States at layer t admitting an admissible terminal completion.

children.title: Bidirectional Viability Filtering
children.top_down_role: State retention using both initial accessibility and terminal viability.

knowledge_statements.title: Bidirectional Viability Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact viability filtering by intersecting forward-reachable and backward-completable states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For layered state sets \(S_0,\ldots,S_T\), initial states \(I\subseteq S_0\), acceptable terminal states \(G\subseteq S_T\), admissible decisions \(A_t(s)\), and transition maps \(F_t\), compute \(R_0=I\) and \[R_{t+1}=\{F_t(s,a)\in S_{t+1}:s\in R_t,\ a\in A_t(s)\}\] for \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\). Compute \(C_T=G\) and \[C_t=\{s\in S_t:\exists a\in A_t(s)\text{ such that }F_t(s,a)\in C_{t+1}\}\] for \(t=T-1,\ldots,0\). Define \(V_t=R_t\cap C_t\), and retain exactly the states in \(V_t\) and transitions \((s,a)\) for which \(s\in V_t\) and \(F_t(s,a)\in V_{t+1}\). A state in \(S_t\) lies on an admissible path from \(I\) to \(G\) if and only if it belongs to \(V_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersect forward-reachable states with backward-completable states to retain exactly the states and transitions lying on feasible complete paths.
assumptions_latex: \(F_t(s,a)\) exactly represents every admissible transition between consecutive layers.
\(I\) and \(G\) exactly specify initial and terminal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_t=R_t\cap C_t\) is precisely the viable portion of layer \(t\).

notation.meaning: States at layer t admitting an acceptable terminal completion.
States at layer t lying on complete feasible paths.
Admissible decisions from state s at layer t.

children.title: Equivalent-State Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Merging states with equivalent continuation sets and values.

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent-State Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an exact quotient condition for merging dynamic-programming states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For states \(s,s'\in S_t\), write \(s\sim_t s'\) when their feasible continuation sets coincide and every common continuation \(q\) has the same incremental cost: \[Q_t(s)=Q_t(s')\quad\text{and}\quad c_t(q\mid s)=c_t(q\mid s')\ \text{for all }q\in Q_t(s).\] If each equivalence class stores the best prefix cost \(\min\{g_t(u):u\in[s]_{\sim_t}\}\), replacing \(S_t\) by the quotient \(S_t/{\sim_t}\) preserves the optimal value and permits reconstruction from a minimizing representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: States may be merged when they have identical feasible continuations and identical continuation costs, while retaining the best prefix representative.
assumptions_latex: The objective decomposes into stored prefix cost plus continuation cost.
\(\sim_t\) is evaluated within a single layer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quotient dynamic program on \(S_t/{\sim_t}\) has the same optimal value as the unaggregated program.

notation.meaning: Incremental cost of continuation q from state s.

children.title: Resource-Window Tightening
children.top_down_role: Narrowing state domains with forward and backward feasibility information.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Window Tightening
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tightens scalar resource domains using necessary prefix and suffix feasibility bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scalar resource state \(r\) at layer \(t\), compute bounds \(L_t^{F}\le r\le U_t^{F}\) satisfied by every forward-reachable prefix and bounds \(L_t^{B}\le r\le U_t^{B}\) satisfied by every state admitting a feasible suffix. Replace the resource domain by \[W_t=[\max\{L_t^{F},L_t^{B}\},\min\{U_t^{F},U_t^{B}\}]\cap D_t.\] If the lower endpoint exceeds the upper endpoint, declare the layer infeasible. Otherwise discard states outside \(W_t\); all viable states remain, although holes inside the interval may still be infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersect necessary forward and backward resource bounds, deleting values outside the resulting window without removing viable states.
assumptions_latex: All four bounds are valid necessary conditions for their respective reachability directions.
\(D_t\) is the original scalar resource domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every viable resource value lies in \(W_t\), and \(W_t=\varnothing\) certifies infeasibility.

notation.meaning: Original resource domain at layer t.

children.title: Decision-Order Width Control
children.top_down_role: Ordering choices that change intermediate state width without changing the model.

children.title: Decision Ordering
children.top_down_role: Sequencing choices among staged decisions in a dynamic program.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision Ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates the ordering of decision blocks to exactness and intermediate state width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_1,\ldots,B_m\) be finite decision blocks and let \(\pi\) be a permutation. Construct a layered dynamic program that processes blocks in order \(B_{\pi(1)},\ldots,B_{\pi(m)}\), with each state retaining a sufficient signature for constraints and objective terms crossing the processed-unprocessed boundary. Every such order is exact when its signature is sufficient. Its computational burden depends on \(W(\pi)=\max_t|S_t^{\pi}|\); therefore an ordering minimizing \(W(\pi)\), or a valid upper bound on it, controls peak intermediate width without changing the feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any decision-block order is exact with sufficient states, but choosing an order with smaller peak layer width reduces resource use.
assumptions_latex: Each block has a finite domain.
The state signature preserves all information needed by unprocessed constraints and objective terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Decision ordering affects \(W(\pi)\) and computational cost, but not correctness under a sufficient state representation.

notation.meaning: State layer after processing t blocks under order pi.
Maximum intermediate state count under order pi.

children.title: Variable Ordering
children.top_down_role: Sequencing choices among integer variables represented by stages.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable Ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specializes width control to permutations of individual integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite-domain variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), let \(\pi\) specify the order in which assignments are introduced. After assigning \(x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(t)}\), merge partial assignments only when their retained signatures induce identical feasible and costed continuations. The resulting dynamic program is exact for every permutation \(\pi\). However, the layer width \(W_t(\pi)\) equals the number of distinct reachable signatures, so different permutations can produce exponentially different maximum widths even though they represent the same optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable order preserves exactness when signatures are sufficient, yet can change the number of distinct intermediate states exponentially.
assumptions_latex: Every variable has a finite domain.
State equivalence preserves all feasible continuation sets and continuation costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The permutation \(\pi\) may change \(\max_t W_t(\pi)\) but does not change the optimal value.

notation.meaning: Number of distinct reachable signatures after t assignments.

children.title: Intermediate-Width Ordering Criteria
children.top_down_role: Ordering criteria focused on limiting intermediate state-space width.

knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate-Width Ordering Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluates an ordering through layer widths and transition branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an ordering \(\pi\), let \(W_t(\pi)=|S_t^{\pi}|\) and let \(b_t(\pi)\) bound the number of decisions examined from each state at layer \(t\). If a transition and its value update take constant time, a forward tabulation requires \[O\!\left(\sum_{t=0}^{m-1}W_t(\pi)b_t(\pi)\right)\] time and \(O(\max_t W_t(\pi))\) memory when only adjacent layers are stored. Thus valid ordering criteria include minimizing peak width, total weighted width, or certified upper bounds on either quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orderings can be ranked by peak layer width or branching-weighted total width, which bound memory and running time respectively.
assumptions_latex: Each generated transition and value update costs \(O(1)\).
Only the current and next layers are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Time is \(O(\sum_t W_t(\pi)b_t(\pi))\) and memory is \(O(\max_t W_t(\pi))\).

notation.meaning: Number of retained states at layer t.
Maximum examined branching per state at layer t.

children.title: DP Storage-Execution Architecture
children.top_down_role: Memory layouts and evaluation organizations for explicit and sparse state spaces.

children.title: Density-Adaptive State Storage
children.top_down_role: Storage choices based on the density of reachable states.

children.title: Dense State Tables
children.top_down_role: Array-oriented storage for state spaces with high occupancy.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense State Tables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Array representation for a finite, directly indexable state universe.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U_t\) be a finite state universe with a bijective index map \(i_t:U_t\to\{0,\ldots,M_t-1\}\). A dense table stores one value at every index, using a distinguished sentinel for unreachable states. Initialization and a complete scan cost \(\Theta(M_t)\), storage costs \(\Theta(M_t)\), and lookup or replacement costs \(O(1)\) in the unit-cost random-access model. If \(R_t\subseteq U_t\) is the reachable set, unused entries number \(M_t-|R_t|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense table allocates every possible state index, giving constant-time access but space proportional to the whole state universe.
assumptions_latex: States admit a collision-free constant-time index map.
The computation uses a unit-cost random-access memory model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dense storage uses \(\Theta(M_t)\) memory and supports \(O(1)\) indexed access.

notation.meaning: Finite universe of possible layer-t states.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct-address table complexity in the unit-cost RAM model
