children.title: Resource-Cost Dominance Order
children.top_down_role: Dominance comparisons over label cost and resource vectors.

children.title: Resource Dominance
children.top_down_role: Label comparisons over resource-consumption vectors.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the componentwise resource preorder between labels at a common state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\in\mathbb{N}\) be positive, and let two labels \(L_1,L_2\) terminate at the same network vertex and have identical nonresource state. For resource vectors \(r(L_i)\in\mathbb{R}^q\), where every component is consumption to be minimized, define \(L_1\preceq_r L_2\) precisely when \(r_k(L_1)\le r_k(L_2)\) for every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\). Strict resource dominance holds when this relation holds and at least one component inequality is strict. This preorder compares resource states only; without an accompanying cost or continuation-compatibility condition, it does not by itself justify deleting \(L_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the same state, one label resource-dominates another when it consumes no more of every resource, with strictness when at least one resource consumption is smaller.
assumptions_latex: \(q\in\mathbb{N}\) is positive.
All resource coordinates use the convention that smaller consumption is preferable.
The compared labels have the same endpoint and nonresource state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_1\preceq_r L_2\iff r_k(L_1)\le r_k(L_2)\) for every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\).

children.title: Cost Dominance
children.top_down_role: Label comparisons over accumulated or reduced-cost measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines objective-cost comparison for labels sharing the same resource and contextual state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_1,L_2\) be labels at the same vertex with identical resource vector and identical continuation-relevant state. In a minimization problem, \(L_1\) cost-dominates \(L_2\) when \(g(L_1)\le g(L_2)\), and it strictly cost-dominates \(L_2\) when \(g(L_1)<g(L_2)\). Because every continuation feasible for one label is then feasible for the other and contributes the same incremental cost, replacing \(L_2\) by \(L_1\) cannot increase the objective value of any common completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among labels with identical resource and contextual states, the label with no greater accumulated cost dominates the other.
assumptions_latex: The objective is minimized and continuation costs are additive.
The compared labels have identical endpoint, resource vector, and continuation-relevant state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(L_1)\le g(L_2)\) implies that \(L_1\) cost-dominates \(L_2\).

notation.meaning: Accumulated objective cost of label L.

children.title: Joint Resource–Cost Dominance
children.top_down_role: Label comparisons combining resource status with cost status.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Resource–Cost Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the standard safe label-elimination rule under monotone resources and compatible continuations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_1,L_2\) terminate at the same vertex with compatible contextual states. Suppose \(g(L_1)\le g(L_2)\), \(r(L_1)\le r(L_2)\) componentwise, and every feasible continuation of \(L_2\) is also feasible for \(L_1\). If continuation costs and resource consumptions are additive and resource feasibility is downward closed, then applying any continuation of \(L_2\) to \(L_1\) produces a feasible complete path of no greater total cost and no greater resource consumption. Hence \(L_2\) may be discarded without changing the optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A label can be deleted when another compatible label has no greater cost or resource use and admits all its continuations.
assumptions_latex: Continuation costs and resource consumptions are additive.
Resource feasibility is downward closed under componentwise reduction.
The continuation set of \(L_2\) is contained in that of \(L_1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(L_1)\le g(L_2)\) and \(r(L_1)\le r(L_2)\) imply safe deletion of \(L_2\) under continuation compatibility.

children.title: Dominance Tradeoff Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Nondominated label sets arising from resource–cost tradeoffs.

knowledge_statements.title: Dominance Tradeoff Frontiers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the surviving label set through the Pareto frontier of its cost-resource vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\in\mathbb{N}\) be positive. For compatible labels \(\mathcal{L}_v\) ending at vertex \(v\), associate \(z(L)=(g(L),r(L))\in\mathbb{R}^{q+1}\). Define the dominance tradeoff frontier of vectors by \[\mathcal{Z}_v=\{z(L):L\in\mathcal{L}_v,\ \nexists L'\in\mathcal{L}_v\text{ such that }z(L')\le z(L)\text{ and }z(L')\ne z(L)\}.\] The corresponding frontier labels are \(\mathcal{F}_v=\{L\in\mathcal{L}_v:z(L)\in\mathcal{Z}_v\}\). Under the hypotheses supporting joint resource-cost dominance, retaining one compatible representative of each distinct vector in \(\mathcal{Z}_v\) and deleting dominated labels preserves at least one optimal completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The vector frontier consists of the componentwise minimal joint cost-resource vectors, and the associated frontier labels are exactly those attaining these vectors.
assumptions_latex: \(q\in\mathbb{N}\) is positive.
Labels in \(\mathcal{L}_v\) share vertex \(v\) and compatible continuation-relevant state.
Joint resource-cost dominance is valid for the label system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{Z}_v\) is the set of minimal elements of \(\{(g(L),r(L)):L\in\mathcal{L}_v\}\) under componentwise order, and \(\mathcal{F}_v\) is its preimage in \(\mathcal{L}_v\).

notation.meaning: Nondominated cost-resource vector frontier at vertex v.
Labels attaining vectors on the frontier.
Compatible labels ending at vertex v.

children.title: Completion Bounds for Labels
children.top_down_role: Destination-side bounds used to discard noncompetitive partial paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Completion Bounds for Labels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bounds the best destination completion and certifies incumbent-based label deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each label \(L\), let \(h(L)\) satisfy \(h(L)\le c(P)\) for every feasible continuation \(P\) from the state of \(L\) to the destination. If no feasible continuation exists, a valid infeasibility certificate may set \(h(L)=+\infty\). With accumulated cost \(g(L)\) and incumbent value \(U\), the inequality \(g(L)+h(L)\ge U\) certifies that no completion of \(L\) can improve the incumbent. The certificate is checked by validating the lower-bound property of \(h\), the accumulated cost, and the displayed inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid lower bound on every completion cost certifies deletion when accumulated cost plus that bound reaches the incumbent value.
assumptions_latex: The objective is minimized and decomposes into accumulated and continuation costs.
\(U\) is the value of a feasible incumbent solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(L)+h(L)\ge U\) certifies that label \(L\) has no completion with value below \(U\).

notation.meaning: Lower bound on feasible completion cost.

source_refs.locator: 2.7 Primal Bounds: Greedy and Local Search p. 34

source_witnesses.locator: 2.7 Primal Bounds: Greedy and Local Search p. 34

children.title: Resource-Network Preprocessing Calculus
children.top_down_role: Graph reduction and resource-window tightening before or during labeling.

children.title: Network Preprocessing
children.top_down_role: Graph-level reduction of nodes, arcs, or connectivity regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Preprocessing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletes vertices and arcs excluded by valid reachability, resource, or objective bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a directed network \(G=(V,A)\), source \(s\), destination \(t\), valid forward and backward resource bounds, completion-cost bounds, and incumbent \(U\). Initialize the active subnetwork \(G'=G\). Delete any vertex or arc that lies on no \(s\)-to-\(t\) walk satisfying the necessary resource bounds, or whose valid lower bound on total path cost is at least \(U\). Recompute affected bounds and repeat until no deletion occurs. Output the reduced subnetwork \(G'\). Because every deletion is supported by a necessary feasibility condition or a valid objective lower bound, every path capable of improving \(U\) remains in \(G'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly remove vertices and arcs that cannot belong to any resource-feasible path improving the incumbent, and return the resulting subnetwork.
assumptions_latex: All feasibility tests used for deletion are necessary conditions.
All objective tests use valid lower bounds.
\(U\) is the value of a feasible incumbent path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output subnetwork \(G'\) contains every feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) path with objective value below \(U\).

children.title: Resource Preprocessing
children.top_down_role: Tightening of resource ranges or feasibility information.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource Preprocessing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computes necessary forward and backward resource bounds before label expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a directed network \(G=(V,A)\) with nonnegative additive resource vectors \(a_e\in\mathbb{R}_+^q\), source \(s\), and destination \(t\). For each resource coordinate \(k\), compute \(d_k^-(v)\), the minimum coordinate-\(k\) consumption of an \(s\)-to-\(v\) path, and \(d_k^+(v)\), the minimum coordinate-\(k\) consumption of a \(v\)-to-\(t\) path. Store these values as necessary resource bounds. A label reaching \(v\) with consumption \(r\) can be rejected whenever \(r_k+d_k^+(v)\) exceeds the permitted coordinate-\(k\) upper bound for some \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute coordinatewise minimum resource consumptions to and from every vertex, then use them as necessary feasibility tests for labels.
assumptions_latex: Arc resource consumptions are additive and componentwise nonnegative.
Each resource has a specified upper bound at the destination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_k+d_k^+(v)>b_k\) for some \(k\) certifies that a label at \(v\) cannot be feasibly completed.

notation.meaning: Minimum source-to-v consumption of resource k.
Minimum v-to-destination consumption of resource k.

children.title: Resource-Window Tightening
children.top_down_role: Narrowing feasible resource intervals before or during labeling.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Window Tightening
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tightens vertex resource intervals using valid forward and backward consumption bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For resource coordinate \(k\), suppose a label at vertex \(v\) must satisfy the current window \([\ell_k(v),u_k(v)]\), the destination limit is \(b_k\), and valid forward and backward lower bounds are \(d_k^-(v)\) and \(d_k^+(v)\). Replace the window by \[\ell'_k(v)=\max\{\ell_k(v),d_k^-(v)\},\qquad u'_k(v)=\min\{u_k(v),b_k-d_k^+(v)\}.\] Repeat over vertices and resources after propagating changed bounds. If \(\ell'_k(v)>u'_k(v)\) for any coordinate, delete \(v\); otherwise retain the tightened window, which contains every resource value realizable by a feasible source-to-destination path through \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersect each vertex’s resource window with necessary forward reachability and backward completion bounds, deleting vertices whose windows become empty.
assumptions_latex: Resource consumptions are additive and componentwise nonnegative.
The forward and backward quantities are valid lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible path through \(v\) reaches it with resource coordinate in \([\ell'_k(v),u'_k(v)]\).

notation.meaning: Current resource window at vertex v.
Forward and backward resource lower bounds.

children.title: Dynamic Preprocessing
children.top_down_role: Preprocessing updates performed during label exploration.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Preprocessing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reapplies safe reductions as incumbents and reachable label states change during an exhaustive label search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the active network, resource windows, completion bounds, incumbent \(U\), and label queue. During an exhaustive label search, whenever \(U\), a resource window, or the reachable label-state set changes, recompute every affected lower bound. Delete an active label \(L\) if it violates a necessary feasibility condition or satisfies \(g(L)+h(L)\ge U\). Delete an arc or vertex only when no remaining reachable label can use it in a feasible completion with value below \(U\). Propagate each deletion until no bound or active set changes, and then continue generating every feasible, nonpruned label extension. When the queue is empty, output the incumbent. If the label expansion is exhaustive and every reduction is valid, the output incumbent is optimal for the modeled problem whenever a feasible incumbent exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: During exhaustive label search, recompute affected bounds and safely remove labels or network elements as stronger information becomes available; queue exhaustion then certifies the incumbent when all nonpruned extensions have been generated.
assumptions_latex: Every updated completion bound remains valid.
Every structural deletion is justified for all reachable label states.
\(U\) is always the value of a feasible incumbent.
Every feasible label extension not removed by a valid reduction is eventually generated and processed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dynamic reductions preserve every completion with value below the current \(U\); under exhaustive label expansion, queue exhaustion certifies optimality of the final feasible incumbent for the modeled problem.

notation.meaning: Valid completion-cost lower bound for label L.

children.title: Context-Dependent Dominance
children.top_down_role: Dominance criteria depending on visitation memory, uncertainty, or compatible continuations.

knowledge_statements.title: Context-Dependent Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines dominance through inclusion of feasible continuations rather than resource-cost coordinates alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a label \(L\), let \(\mathcal{C}(L)\) denote the set of continuations permitted by its endpoint, visitation memory, uncertainty state, and other continuation-relevant context. A label \(L_1\) context-dependently dominates \(L_2\) when \(\mathcal{C}(L_2)\subseteq\mathcal{C}(L_1)\) and, for every \(P\in\mathcal{C}(L_2)\), completing \(L_1\) with \(P\) is feasible and has total cost no greater than completing \(L_2\) with \(P\). Under this definition, \(L_2\) may be removed even when a coordinatewise resource-cost comparison is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One label dominates another when it admits all of the other’s continuations and realizes each at no greater total cost.
assumptions_latex: Both labels terminate at endpoints from which the same continuation objects can be compared.
The context stored in each label determines its permitted continuation set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{C}(L_2)\subseteq\mathcal{C}(L_1)\) with no-greater completion cost makes deletion of \(L_2\) safe.

notation.meaning: Set of feasible continuations compatible with label L.

children.title: Elementarity Management
children.top_down_role: Exact and relaxed mechanisms controlling repeated visits in path-labeling dynamic programs.

children.title: Exact Visited-Set States
children.top_down_role: Labels retaining complete visitation information.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Visited-Set States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents elementary-path labels by retaining their complete set of visited vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an elementary-path labeling dynamic program on \(G=(V,A)\), represent a label by \(L=(v,S,r,g)\), where \(v\in V\) is the current vertex, \(S\subseteq V\) is exactly the set of vertices already visited, \(r\) is the accumulated resource vector, and \(g\) is accumulated cost. An extension along \((v,w)\in A\) is allowed only if \(w\notin S\) and the updated resources are feasible; it creates \(L'=(w,S\cup\{w\},r+a_{vw},g+c_{vw})\). Consequently, every generated label encodes an elementary partial path, and every elementary feasible path has a corresponding sequence of such states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Store the complete visited set in each label and permit extension only to unvisited vertices, thereby enforcing elementarity exactly.
assumptions_latex: The path must visit each vertex at most once.
Arc costs and resource consumptions are additive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transition condition \(w\notin S\) makes generated partial paths elementary and preserves all feasible elementary paths.

notation.meaning: Exact set of vertices visited by the partial path.

children.title: Neighborhood-Memory Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Localized visitation memory used to reduce state growth.

knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood-Memory Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The standard neighborhood-memory representation for relaxed elementary-path labeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a directed graph and choose neighborhoods \(N_v\subseteq V\) with \(v\in N_v\) for every \(v\in V\). A label ending at \(i\) stores a memory set \(M\subseteq N_i\). Extension along \((i,j)\in A\) is permitted only when \(j\notin M\), after which the memory is updated by \[M'=(M\cap N_j)\cup\{j\}.\] Thus a previously visited vertex is protected against repetition only while it remains in the current neighborhood memory. Taking \(N_v=V\) for every \(v\) recovers exact visited-set elementarity; smaller neighborhoods define relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A label remembers only locally selected visited vertices. Extension forbids remembered vertices, intersects memory with the next neighborhood, and becomes exact when every neighborhood is the full vertex set.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
\(v\in N_v\subseteq V\) for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M'=(M\cap N_j)\cup\{j\}\), and \(N_v=V\) for all \(v\) yields exact elementarity.

notation.meaning: Neighborhood whose visited vertices remain remembered at vertex v.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically coherent and fits the neighborhood-memory leaf, but no citation is supplied for the specialized memory semantics and update rule. An inspectable routing or ng-route source with a section, definition, or page locator is required.

children.title: Decremental State-Space Relaxation
children.top_down_role: Adaptive restoration of visitation distinctions.

knowledge_statements.title: Decremental State-Space Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive refinement of a relaxed labeling state space until a returned route is elementary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite graph and an initial collection of visitation memories defining a relaxation of elementary paths. Solve the relaxed labeling problem and obtain an optimal walk \(P\). If \(P\) is elementary, output \(P\). Otherwise choose a vertex repeated by \(P\) and enlarge at least one relevant memory or neighborhood so that the witnessed repeated-vertex segment is infeasible in the next relaxation; then resolve. Never remove a previously restored distinction. If every refinement is chosen from a finite family whose maximal member stores the exact visited set, the procedure terminates after finitely many refinements with either an elementary optimum or infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated vertices in a relaxed optimum trigger permanent memory refinements. A finite refinement family ending at exact visited sets guarantees finite termination.
assumptions_latex: The graph and refinement family are finite.
Each refinement strictly removes the witnessed non-elementary walk without removing any elementary path.
The maximal state distinguishes the exact visited set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The refinement sequence terminates finitely and returns an elementary optimum or certifies infeasibility.

notation.meaning: Current optimal walk in the relaxed state space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the adaptive-refinement leaf, but the finite-termination claim and the stated refinement conditions require a source for the intended decremental state-space relaxation variant. No citation is present.

children.title: Partial-Elementarity Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Intermediate regimes suppressing selected cycles without full visitation memory.

children.title: Cycle-Control Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Relaxations suppressing selected classes of repeated traversal.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Control Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxations parameterized by a selected family of forbidden directed cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a directed graph and let \(\mathcal C\) be a family of directed cycles. Define \(\mathcal W(\mathcal C)\) as the set of feasible resource-respecting walks that contain no member of \(\mathcal C\) as a contiguous closed subwalk. This is a cycle-control relaxation of elementary paths because every elementary path belongs to \(\mathcal W(\mathcal C)\), while cycles outside \(\mathcal C\) may remain admissible. If \(\mathcal C_1\subseteq\mathcal C_2\), then \(\mathcal W(\mathcal C_2)\subseteq\mathcal W(\mathcal C_1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cycle-control relaxation forbids a selected cycle family while allowing other repetitions. Enlarging the forbidden family produces a tighter feasible-walk set.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
Cycle exclusion is applied in addition to the original resource-feasibility rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C_1\subseteq\mathcal C_2\) implies \(\mathcal W(\mathcal C_2)\subseteq\mathcal W(\mathcal C_1)\).

notation.meaning: Selected family of forbidden directed cycles.
Resource-feasible walks avoiding the selected cycles.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally consistent and fits the cycle-control leaf, but it introduces specialized terminology and a particular contiguous-subwalk interpretation without cited support. A source with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Partial-Elementarity Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Relaxations preserving elementarity for only selected vertices or neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Elementarity Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementarity imposed only on a designated subset of vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a directed graph and fix \(S\subseteq V\). An \(S\)-elementary walk \(P=(v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) satisfies \[\bigl|\{i:v_i=s\}\bigr|\leq 1\qquad\text{for every }s\in S.\] Vertices in \(V\setminus S\) may repeat, subject to the remaining feasibility constraints. The family is monotone: if \(S_1\subseteq S_2\), every \(S_2\)-elementary walk is \(S_1\)-elementary. The choices \(S=\varnothing\) and \(S=V\) give unrestricted visitation and full elementarity, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial elementarity permits each protected vertex at most once and allows repetitions elsewhere. Enlarging the protected set tightens the relaxation; protecting every vertex gives full elementarity.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
\(S\subseteq V\) is the protected vertex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_1\subseteq S_2\) implies that every \(S_2\)-elementary walk is \(S_1\)-elementary.

notation.meaning: Vertices on which elementarity is enforced.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and monotonicity statement are precise and appropriate for partial elementarity, but no authoritative source is cited for this routing relaxation or its terminology.

children.title: Cycle-Suppression Regimes
children.top_down_role: Intermediate regimes distinguished by the cycles they exclude.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Suppression Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested regimes obtained by forbidding short closed subwalks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(q\geq 1\), a walk \(P=(v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) is \(q\)-cycle-suppressed when \[v_i\neq v_j\qquad\text{whenever }0\leq i<j\leq k\text{ and }j-i\leq q.\] Equivalently, \(P\) contains no closed contiguous subwalk using at most \(q\) arcs. If \(q_1\leq q_2\), the \(q_2\)-cycle-suppressed regime is contained in the \(q_1\)-cycle-suppressed regime. This hierarchy suppresses increasingly long local returns without necessarily enforcing global elementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A q-cycle-suppressed walk cannot revisit a vertex within q arcs. Larger q gives a tighter regime, though distant repetitions may remain.
assumptions_latex: \(P=(v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) is a finite directed walk.
\(q\) is a positive integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_1\leq q_2\) implies \(\mathcal W_{q_2}\subseteq\mathcal W_{q_1}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local-return definition, its closed-subwalk equivalence, and the nesting claim are mathematically consistent and fit the leaf. The named regime and parameter convention nevertheless require an inspectable source, which is absent.

children.title: Elementarity-Gap Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Boundaries where partial visitation memory permits materially weaker path sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Elementarity-Gap Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective gap induced by admitting non-elementary walks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem, let \(\mathcal P_E\) be the elementary feasible paths and let \(\mathcal P_R\supseteq\mathcal P_E\) be a relaxed feasible-walk family. With additive cost \(c(P)\), define \(z_E=\inf_{P\in\mathcal P_E}c(P)\) and \(z_R=\inf_{P\in\mathcal P_R}c(P)\). Then \(z_R\leq z_E\). Equality holds exactly when the relaxed infimum equals the elementary infimum; in particular, it holds if a relaxed optimizer is elementary. A strict gap occurs whenever every relaxed optimizer has cost below every elementary path. If repeatable negative-cost cycles are admitted, \(z_R=-\infty\) may occur while \(z_E\) remains finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing elementarity cannot raise a minimization value. The gap is strict when only non-elementary walks attain lower cost and may become infinite with repeatable negative cycles.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P_E\subseteq\mathcal P_R\).
Costs are additive and interpreted in the extended real numbers.
\(\mathcal P_E\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_R\leq z_E\), with possible boundary case \(z_R=-\infty<z_E\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the container and the relaxation inequality is coherent, but the specialized elementarity-gap framing and negative-cycle boundary have no supporting citation. A source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Labeling Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions that undermine finite settlement, strong dominance, or manageable label growth.

children.title: Exponential Label Antichains
children.top_down_role: Large collections of mutually nondominated labels.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Label Antichains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A compact layered construction producing exponentially many mutually nondominated labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(n\geq1\), construct a layered graph with \(n\) stages and two parallel choices at each stage. Choosing the first arc at stage \(i\) adds resource vector \(e_i\in\mathbb R^{2n}\); choosing the second adds \(e_{n+i}\). All arc costs are zero. At the terminal layer, the \(2^n\) labels have distinct resource vectors, each containing exactly \(n\) unit entries. Under componentwise resource dominance with equal cost, no two distinct labels dominate one another: componentwise inequality would force equality because both vectors have coordinate sum \(n\). Hence an exact dominance-based labeling method may retain exponentially many labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph with n binary stages yields 2^n resource vectors of equal coordinate sum. They are pairwise incomparable, forcing exponentially many nondominated labels.
assumptions_latex: Dominance requires no larger cost and componentwise no larger resource consumption.
All resource coordinates are minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The terminal label antichain has cardinality \(2^n\).

notation.meaning: The ith standard unit vector in the resource space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The layered construction does yield an antichain of size 2^n under the stated dominance order and fits a failure-boundary container. Because this is a nontrivial complexity construction and no source is supplied, it cannot pass source review.

children.title: Nonmonotone Resource Extensions
children.top_down_role: Resource behavior that defeats standard settlement and dominance orders.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Resource Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of componentwise dominance when resource extension is not order-preserving.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two equal-cost labels at one vertex with scalar resources \(r_1=0\) and \(r_2=1\), where smaller resource is preferred. Standard dominance deletes the second label because \(r_1\leq r_2\). Let their common outgoing arc apply the nonmonotone extension \(f(r)=1-r\), and let terminal cost equal the extended resource. The extensions produce \(f(r_1)=1\) and \(f(r_2)=0\), so the deleted label would produce the uniquely better terminal value. Therefore componentwise dominance is unsafe unless every common extension preserves the resource order relevant to feasibility and objective comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resource map r to 1-r reverses two ordered labels, so pruning the initially worse label loses the best continuation. Safe dominance requires order-preserving extensions.
assumptions_latex: Smaller scalar resource values are preferred before and after extension.
Both labels admit the same outgoing extension.
Terminal cost equals the extended resource.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_1\leq r_2\) does not imply \(f(r_1)\leq f(r_2)\); consequently the usual dominance deletion is invalid.

notation.meaning: Resources of the two competing labels.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly illustrates failure of dominance under an order-reversing extension and matches the leaf's local sense. The safety condition for extensions is a substantive labeling claim and lacks an inspectable source.

children.title: Cycle-Unboundedness Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Cycle regimes requiring elementarity, resource exhaustion, or separate unboundedness handling.

children.title: Negative-Cycle Regimes
children.top_down_role: State networks containing cost-improving repeatable cycles.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Cycle Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unboundedness caused by a reachable, repeatable negative-cost cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have finite arc costs, source \(s\), and sink \(t\). Suppose a directed cycle \(C\) is reachable from \(s\), the sink is reachable from \(C\), and \(c(C)<0\). If the walk model permits arbitrarily many traversals of \(C\) without violating resource or visitation restrictions, then for every integer \(m\geq0\) there is an admissible \(s\)-to-\(t\) walk of cost \(c_0+m c(C)\), where \(c_0\) is the fixed prefix-and-exit cost. Consequently the minimum-walk value is \(-\infty\), and a finite optimal label cannot be settled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reachable negative-cost cycle that can be repeated indefinitely drives admissible source-to-sink walk cost to negative infinity.
assumptions_latex: There are admissible connections from \(s\) to \(C\) and from \(C\) to \(t\).
No constraint bounds the number of traversals of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_m\{c_0+m c(C)\}=-\infty\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The negative-cycle unboundedness statement is mathematically standard and fits the failure-boundary leaf, but no textbook section, theorem, or page locator is cited. The supplied local inventory does not identify support for this claim.

children.title: Unbounded-Walk Regimes
children.top_down_role: Walk models permitting indefinitely improving repetition.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Walk Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource-compatible cycle repetition yielding an unbounded pricing value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider additive resource upper bounds and a minimization walk problem. Let a reachable directed cycle \(C\) have cost increment \(\Delta c(C)<0\) and resource increment vector \(\Delta r(C)\leq0\) componentwise. If a feasible prefix reaches \(C\) and a feasible suffix connects \(C\) to the sink, then inserting \(m\) copies of \(C\) never increases bounded resources and decreases cost by \(m|\Delta c(C)|\). Hence admissible walks have no finite lower cost bound. More generally, unbounded repetition occurs whenever a negative-cost cycle lies in a feasible recession direction of the resource system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-cost cycle with nonpositive bounded-resource increments can be inserted indefinitely, creating feasible walks of arbitrarily low cost.
assumptions_latex: Resources accumulate additively and satisfy componentwise upper bounds.
\(\Delta r(C)\leq0\) and \(\Delta c(C)<0\).
Compatible feasible prefix and suffix walks exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The admissible-walk objective has infimum \(-\infty\).

notation.meaning: Resource increment from one cycle traversal.
Cost increment from one cycle traversal.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sufficient condition for unbounded repetition is coherent for additive resources governed only by componentwise upper bounds and fits the leaf. The recession-direction generalization and resource-constrained interpretation require a cited source.

children.title: Resource-Exhausted Cycle Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cycle regimes bounded by finite resource exhaustion.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Exhausted Cycle Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A positive bounded-resource increment limits otherwise profitable cycle repetition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a scalar resource have upper bound \(b<\infty\). Suppose a feasible source-to-sink walk containing \(m\) traversals of cycle \(C\) uses resource \(r_0+m\delta\), where \(r_0\) includes the prefix and suffix and \(\delta>0\) is the resource consumed per traversal. Feasibility requires \[m\leq\left\lfloor\frac{b-r_0}{\delta}\right\rfloor.\] Thus even when \(c(C)<0\), resource exhaustion prevents arbitrarily many repetitions and rules out cycle-induced value \(-\infty\). This conclusion does not exclude a finite optimum containing the maximum permitted number of cycle traversals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cycle consuming a positive amount of a finitely bounded resource can repeat only finitely often, preventing negative infinity from that cycle.
assumptions_latex: The bounded resource is additive with finite upper bound \(b\).
One cycle traversal consumes \(\delta>0\).
The fixed prefix and suffix consume \(r_0\leq b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m\leq\left\lfloor(b-r_0)/\delta\right\rfloor\), so cycle repetition is bounded.

notation.meaning: Positive resource consumption per cycle traversal.
Resource used outside repeated cycle copies.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite repetition bound is correct under the stated scalar additive-resource model and the property kind is suitable. No source with a specific locator supports this resource-exhaustion boundary.

children.title: Elementarity-Based Cycle Exclusion
children.top_down_role: Path regimes where visitation restrictions exclude repeated cycles.

knowledge_statements.title: Elementarity-Based Cycle Exclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full vertex elementarity removes every positive-length directed cycle from admissible paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=(v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) be an elementary directed path, meaning that \(v_i\neq v_j\) whenever \(i\neq j\). Then \(P\) contains no positive-length closed contiguous subwalk, because such a subwalk would have equal first and last vertices at distinct positions. Consequently no directed cycle can be traversed by an elementary path. In a finite graph, every elementary path uses at most \(|V|-1\) arcs; hence the feasible elementary-path family is finite, and finite arc costs cannot produce cycle-induced objective value \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct-vertex paths contain no directed cycle and have at most |V|-1 arcs. Thus finite arc costs cannot cause negative infinity through cycle repetition.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
Every admissible path is vertex-elementary.
All arc costs are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every admissible path has at most \(|V|-1\) arcs and contains no directed cycle.

notation.meaning: Number of vertices in the graph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cycle-exclusion and finite-length properties follow coherently from vertex elementarity and fit the property container. An authoritative graph or routing source with a precise locator is still required because the record supplies no citation.

children.title: Bidirectional Join Incompatibility
children.top_down_role: Resource or memory systems that prevent efficient forward–backward joining.

assumptions_latex: A forward and a backward labeling algorithm retain only state summaries in sets \(S_F\) and \(S_B\), respectively.
A complete object is feasible exactly when its forward and backward partial objects can be joined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No exact join rule based only on \((S_F,S_B)\) exists under the displayed indistinguishability condition.

notation.meaning: Feasibility indicator for joining two partial objects

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact joining requires retained states to distinguish every feasibility-relevant continuation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic failure of exact forward-backward joining after state compression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_1,p_2\) be forward partial objects and let \(q\) be a backward partial object. Suppose \(s_F(p_1)=s_F(p_2)\), while \(s_B(q)\) is fixed, but \(J(p_1,q)\ne J(p_2,q)\). Then every join test \(\widehat J:S_F\times S_B\to\{0,1\}\) assigns the same value to \((s_F(p_1),s_B(q))\) and \((s_F(p_2),s_B(q))\). Consequently, \(\widehat J\) cannot equal \(J\) on both pairs. Thus exact bidirectional joining is impossible unless at least one retained state is refined to preserve the missing compatibility information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If two indistinguishable partial solutions have different compatibility with the same opposite label, no join test using only retained states can be exact.
knowledge_statements.title: Bidirectional Join Incompatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary statement is mathematically coherent and correctly typed, but it has no inspectable source supporting the bidirectional-labeling claim.

children.title: Dynamic-Programming Pricing Oracles
children.top_down_role: Dynamic programs used to optimize over implicit column families; master-problem theory remains in the column-generation chapters.

children.title: Pricing State Models
children.top_down_role: Translation of column feasibility and master-side information into a dynamic-programming state network.

children.title: Dual-Adjusted State Networks
children.top_down_role: Pricing networks whose transition costs incorporate master-side dual information.

assumptions_latex: Each feasible column \(p\) is represented by an origin-to-terminal path in a finite state network.
Master-row contributions and original column costs decompose additively over the path arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A shortest path under the dual-adjusted arc costs is a minimum-reduced-cost column.

notation.meaning: Original cost and master-column vector of arc e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive reduced-cost representation for a dynamic-programming pricing network.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Cutting Stock: Formulations with Many Variables p. 48

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every arc \(e\), define its adjusted cost by \(\bar c_e=c_e-\pi^{\mathsf T}a_e\). If a path \(P\) represents column \(p\), with \(c_p=\sum_{e\in P}c_e\) and \(a_p=\sum_{e\in P}a_e\), then its path cost satisfies \[\sum_{e\in P}\bar c_e=c_p-\pi^{\mathsf T}a_p=\bar c_p.\] Hence minimizing adjusted path cost over terminal paths gives the minimum reduced cost over represented feasible columns; a path of negative adjusted cost identifies an improving column under the usual minimization-master convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting dual-valued row contributions from arc costs makes every path cost equal its column's reduced cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Adjusted State Networks

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Cutting Stock: Formulations with Many Variables p. 48

children.title: Column-Feasibility States
children.top_down_role: States retaining the information required for admissible columns.

assumptions_latex: Partial constructions are extended by decisions from a finite decision alphabet.
Column feasibility is determined by the completed decision sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A state is column-feasibility sufficient exactly when equal-state partial constructions have identical feasible continuations.

notation.meaning: Set of continuations completing a partial construction feasibly

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact state-sufficiency condition for preserving admissible pricing columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A state map \(s\) is column-feasibility sufficient if and only if, for every pair of partial constructions \(u,v\), \[s(u)=s(v)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C(u)=C(v).\] Equivalently, every continuation feasible after \(u\) is feasible after \(v\), and conversely, whenever the two partial constructions share a state. Under this condition, discarding the detailed histories of \(u\) and \(v\) cannot create an inadmissible terminal column or remove an admissible one. Resource totals, temporal endpoints, and logical flags must therefore be retained whenever they affect \(C(u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state retains enough feasibility information precisely when partial constructions sharing it admit exactly the same feasible completions.
knowledge_statements.title: Column-Feasibility States

children.title: Multi-Block Pricing Architecture
children.top_down_role: Separate or shared dynamic programs for multiple commodities, blocks, or column families.

children.title: Multiple Pricing Blocks
children.top_down_role: Pricing architectures containing several distinct subproblem blocks.

assumptions_latex: The column set is a disjoint union \(\mathcal P=\biguplus_{k=1}^K\mathcal P_k\).
Each block \(k\) has an exact dynamic program for minimizing reduced cost over \(\mathcal P_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global pricing is solved by taking the least blockwise optimum \(\min_k z_k(\pi)\).

notation.meaning: Feasible columns in pricing block k
Optimal reduced cost in block k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: minimization over a finite union decomposes into blockwise minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent decomposition of a pricing oracle across column blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For dual vector \(\pi\), let \(\bar c_p(\pi)=c_p-\pi^{\mathsf T}a_p\) and define \(z_k(\pi)=\min_{p\in\mathcal P_k}\bar c_p(\pi)\). Since \(\mathcal P\) is the disjoint union of the blocks, \[\min_{p\in\mathcal P}\bar c_p(\pi)=\min_{1\le k\le K}z_k(\pi).\] Thus one may run one exact dynamic-programming oracle per block and compare their terminal values. Under the minimization-master convention, pricing terminates exactly when \(z_k(\pi)\ge 0\) for every \(k\); otherwise any block attaining a negative value supplies an improving column.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With independent column blocks, solve one pricing dynamic program per block and select the most negative blockwise reduced cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Pricing Blocks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-block decomposition is standard and the representation kind fits, but no inspectable source is supplied for the multi-block pricing architecture and termination claim.

children.title: Multiple Column Classes
children.top_down_role: Pricing architectures generating columns from several structural families.

assumptions_latex: Feasible columns are assigned to classes \(\mathcal P_1,\ldots,\mathcal P_K\).
Every feasible column belongs to at least one class, and each class has explicit feasibility and reduced-cost data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Classwise pricing is exact when the class union covers \(\mathcal P\) and each class oracle is exact.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a column-class architecture is a covering of the feasible column set by explicitly modeled subclasses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Class-indexed partition or covering of a pricing column family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multiple-column-class pricing model is a finite family \((\mathcal P_k)_{k=1}^K\) satisfying \(\mathcal P=\bigcup_{k=1}^K\mathcal P_k\), together with a class-specific reduced-cost function and exact feasibility model for every \(k\). The classes form a partition when \(\mathcal P_i\cap\mathcal P_j=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). For any dual vector \(\pi\), exact classwise pricing requires \[\min_{p\in\mathcal P}\bar c_p(\pi)=\min_{1\le k\le K}\min_{p\in\mathcal P_k}\bar c_p(\pi).\] Overlap is permitted, but duplicate generated columns must then be identified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple column classes cover the feasible columns with class-specific models; pricing takes the best reduced cost across all classes.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Column Classes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The covering/partition definition is coherent and fits the container, but the record supplies no citation for the column-class formulation or duplicate-handling assertion.

children.title: Shared-State Pricing
children.top_down_role: Multiple pricing families using a common state representation.

assumptions_latex: All column classes admit the same state set and transition relation.
Class dependence appears only in allowed terminals, initial values, terminal values, or explicitly indexed transition costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One state network can price every class without duplicating its feasibility transitions.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: common transition systems permit class-indexed value functions on one state graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Several pricing classes represented on one common feasibility-state network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(S,E)\) be a common state network with source \(s_0\). Class \(k\) is represented by paths from \(s_0\) to \(T_k\), and the reduced cost of path \(P\) is \(\gamma_k+csum_{e\in P}w_e^k\). Shared-state pricing evaluates class-indexed value functions on the same states and transitions, producing \[z_k=cmin_{t\in T_k}cmin_{P:s_0cleadsto t}cleft(cgamma_k+csum_{e\in P}w_e^kcright).\] The representation is exact when every class-feasible column corresponds to such a path and every admitted terminal path represents a class-feasible column.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared-state pricing uses one feasibility network while retaining class-specific costs, terminal conditions, or value functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared-State Pricing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intended shared-state representation is plausible, but it has no cited source and contains corrupted expressions such as csum, cmin, cleadsto, cleft, and cright. Source support is required before choosing a definitive repaired formulation.

children.title: Separate-State Pricing
children.top_down_role: Multiple pricing families using block-specific state representations.

assumptions_latex: Each pricing class \(k\) has its own exact state network \(G_k\).
Every feasible column is represented in at least one class network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The least terminal value among the separate networks equals the global minimum reduced cost.

notation.meaning: Minimum reduced cost returned by network k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: independent exact class oracles combine by taking their minimum objective value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Class-specific pricing dynamic programs with distinct state spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each class \(k\), initialize the source label of \(G_k\) to zero and all other labels to \(+\infty\). Process its states in a valid dynamic-programming order, relaxing every admissible transition with its dual-adjusted cost, and let \(z_k\) be the least permitted terminal label. After all class networks are solved, output a terminal path attaining \(\min_{1\le k\le K}z_k\). Under the minimization-master convention, stop without a column exactly when every \(z_k\ge 0\); otherwise decode an attaining path as an improving column.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate-state pricing solves a distinct dynamic program for each class, then returns the class with minimum reduced cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Separate-State Pricing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role and blockwise-minimum logic fit the leaf, but no inspectable source supports the separate-state pricing procedure and stopping condition.

children.title: Canonical DP Pricing Families
children.top_down_role: Recurring pricing subproblems with established dynamic-programming structures.

children.title: Capacity-Pattern Pricing Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Capacity-indexed pricing over selection and cutting patterns.

children.title: Knapsack Pricing
children.top_down_role: Capacity-indexed pricing for item-selection columns.

knowledge_statements.title: Knapsack Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded or unbounded integer-knapsack oracle under integral capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(F(0,q)=0\) for \(0\le q\le W\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), update \[F(i,q)=\max_{0\le x\le b_i,\;xw_i\le q}\{F(i-1,q-xw_i)+\pi_i x\}.\] Backtrack from a state attaining \(F(n,W)\) to recover \(x\). The pricing objective is \(c_0-F(n,W)\), equal to \[\min\left\{c_0-\sum_{i=1}^n\pi_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le W,\;0\le x_i\le b_i,\;x_i\in\mathbb Z\right\}.\] Output the recovered selection if this value is negative; otherwise report that this oracle has no improving column.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Knapsack pricing maximizes dual value under capacity, then subtracts that value from the column's fixed cost.
assumptions_latex: Item \(i\) has integer weight \(w_i>0\), multiplicity bound \(b_i\in\mathbb Z_+\cup\{+\infty\}\), and dual contribution \(\pi_i\).
The capacity is \(W\in\mathbb Z_+\), and a column has fixed cost \(c_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recurrence returns a feasible selection of minimum reduced cost \(c_0-\sum_i\pi_i x_i\).

notation.meaning: Maximum dual value using items 1 through i and capacity q

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Cutting Stock: Formulations with Many Variables p. 48

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Cutting Stock: Formulations with Many Variables p. 48

children.title: Cutting-Stock Pricing
children.top_down_role: Capacity-indexed pricing for cutting-pattern columns.

knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Stock Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gilmore-Gomory unit-roll pricing as an unbounded integer knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The feasible pattern set is \(\mathcal A=\{a\in\mathbb Z_+^n:\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i a_i\le L\}\). For \(a\in\mathcal A\), the reduced cost of the corresponding unit-cost roll column is \(\bar c(a)=1-\sum_{i=1}^n\pi_i a_i\). Therefore cutting-stock pricing is equivalent to the unbounded integer knapsack \[v(\pi)=\max_{a\in\mathcal A}\sum_{i=1}^n\pi_i a_i.\] An improving column exists if and only if \(v(\pi)>1\), in which case any maximizing pattern has reduced cost \(1-v(\pi)<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cutting-stock pricing finds the capacity-feasible pattern of greatest dual value; it improves the master exactly when that value exceeds one.
assumptions_latex: Stock length is \(L>0\), item lengths satisfy \(\ell_i>0\), and pattern multiplicities are nonnegative integers.
The restricted master has unit cost per stock roll and demand-row duals \(\pi_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A negative-reduced-cost cutting pattern exists exactly when the knapsack optimum exceeds \(1\).

notation.meaning: Multiplicity vector of a cutting pattern

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Cutting Stock: Formulations with Many Variables p. 48

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Cutting Stock: Formulations with Many Variables p. 48

children.title: Selection-to-Pattern Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between selection states and cutting-pattern states.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection-to-Pattern Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise equivalence between capacity-feasible selections and one-dimensional patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(X=\{x\in\mathbb Z_+^n:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le W\}\) and \(A=\{a\in\mathbb Z_+^n:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i a_i\le W\}\). The map \(\phi:X\to A\) given by \(\phi(x)_i=x_i\) is a bijection with inverse \(\phi^{-1}(a)=a\). For any value vector \(v\in\mathbb R^n\), it preserves the pricing contribution: \(v^{\mathsf T}\phi(x)=v^{\mathsf T}x\). Hence a knapsack optimizer is directly a capacity-feasible pattern, and every such pattern is represented by exactly one selection vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A knapsack selection vector and a cutting pattern are the same multiplicity vector when they share item sizes and capacity.
assumptions_latex: A selection vector \(x\in\mathbb Z_+^n\) satisfies the single capacity inequality \(\sum_i w_i x_i\le W\).
Pattern coordinates count the same item types and use the same weights and capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The identity map \(a=x\) is a bijection preserving feasibility and dual value.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Cutting Stock: Formulations with Many Variables p. 48

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Cutting Stock: Formulations with Many Variables p. 48

children.title: Resource-Constrained Shortest-Path Pricing
children.top_down_role: Pricing over routes, duties, and sequences represented by constrained paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Constrained Shortest-Path Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive resource-constrained shortest-path labeling for pricing routes or sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize vertex \(s\) with label \((0,0)\). Extending label \((d,\rho)\) along arc \(e=(u,v)\) creates \((d+\bar c_e,\rho+r_e)\) at \(v\) only when \(\rho+r_e\le R\). At a common vertex, discard \((d_2,\rho_2)\) when another label \((d_1,\rho_1)\) satisfies \(d_1\le d_2\) and \(\rho_1\le\rho_2\) componentwise. Continue until no extension can improve a terminal label. Output an \(s\)-to-\(t\) path associated with the minimum-cost surviving label at \(t\), or report infeasibility if none exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extend cost-resource labels along arcs, discard resource-infeasible and dominated labels, and return the cheapest surviving terminal path.
assumptions_latex: The directed graph is finite, has source \(s\), sink \(t\), and no reachable negative-cost cycle compatible with the resource constraints.
Each arc has additive cost and an additive resource vector, and path resources must not exceed a prescribed bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The least-cost nondominated terminal label gives an optimal resource-feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) pricing path.

notation.meaning: Dual-adjusted arc cost and nonnegative resource vector

children.title: Schedule-Duty Pricing Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Time-ordered dynamic programs generating feasible schedules or work patterns.

children.title: Schedule Pricing
children.top_down_role: Pricing for time-ordered schedule columns.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acyclic compatibility-path model for additive schedule pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign activity \(j\) the adjusted weight \(\bar c_j=c_j-\pi^{\mathsf T}a_j\), placing that weight on the activity vertex or its entering arc. If path \(P\) represents schedule \(S(P)\), additivity gives \[\sum_{j\in P}\bar c_j=\sum_{j\in P}c_j-\pi^{\mathsf T}\sum_{j\in P}a_j=\bar c_{S(P)}.\] Therefore a shortest source-to-sink path is a minimum-reduced-cost feasible schedule. Under the minimization-master convention, a negative path value yields an improving schedule column, while a nonnegative shortest-path value certifies that this schedule class contains no improving column.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent compatible activities as a path and weight them by reduced cost; the shortest path is the best schedule column.
assumptions_latex: Activities form a finite acyclic compatibility graph with source and sink.
Every feasible schedule corresponds to exactly one source-to-sink path, and every such path is a feasible schedule.
Activity costs and master-row contributions are additive along paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Schedule pricing equals a shortest-path problem with dual-adjusted activity or arc weights.

notation.meaning: Original cost and master contribution of activity j

children.title: Duty Pricing
children.top_down_role: Pricing for feasible work-duty or crew-duty columns.

knowledge_statements.title: Duty Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduced-cost pricing for temporally feasible duties in a set-partitioning master problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given tasks, feasible duty-transition rules, duty costs \(c_d\), task dual prices \(\pi_i\), and convexity dual price \(\sigma\), initialize a label at the duty source with value \(-\sigma\). Extend a label by an admissible task or transition while updating its temporal-feasibility state and adding the corresponding cost minus covered-task dual prices. Retain the least-valued label for each state whenever dominance is valid. At every admissible duty sink, the label value equals \(\bar c_d=c_d-\sum_i\pi_i a_{id}-\sigma\). Output a feasible duty attaining the minimum sink label; it is an improving column exactly when \(\bar c_d<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A temporal dynamic program minimizes duty reduced cost; a feasible sink label below zero identifies an improving duty column.
assumptions_latex: \(a_{id}\in\{0,1\}\) indicates whether duty \(d\) covers task \(i\).
Every feasible duty has a finite state-path representation with additive transition cost.
Label dominance preserves at least one minimum-cost completion for every state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[d^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{d\in D}\left(c_d-\sum_i\pi_i a_{id}-\sigma\right),\qquad \bar c_{d^*}<0\iff d^*\text{ is improving}.\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the Duty Pricing leaf and its reduced-cost formula is plausible, but no citation supports the duty model, temporal dynamic program, or exactness and dominance claims. Source support is required before the mathematical specification can be assessed reliably.

children.title: Temporal-Feasibility States
children.top_down_role: State structures carrying time-related feasibility across priced patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Temporal-Feasibility States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State sufficiency for dynamic programs that construct schedules or duties chronologically.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a partial chronological sequence \(p\), a temporal-feasibility state is a summary \(s(p)\) containing exactly the retained information needed to test future extensions, such as current time, location, elapsed duty time, and accumulated resource counters. It is sufficient when any two partial sequences \(p\) and \(q\) with \(s(p)=s(q)\) admit the same feasible continuation set and each common continuation changes their objective values by the same amount. Consequently, among labels with the same state, retaining one of minimum accumulated cost cannot remove an optimal complete sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A temporal state is sufficient when equal states have identical feasible continuations and identical continuation costs, permitting safe label dominance.
assumptions_latex: Partial sequences are extended only forward in time.
Feasibility and incremental cost depend on history solely through the retained state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[s(p)=s(q)\Longrightarrow \mathcal C(p)=\mathcal C(q)\text{ and }\Delta(p,r)=\Delta(q,r)\quad\text{for every }r\in\mathcal C(p).\]

notation.meaning: Incremental objective value of continuation r.

children.title: Schedule–Duty Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural overlap between generic schedule pricing and duty-specific pricing.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule–Duty Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive correspondence between a schedule and its ordered maximal duties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a feasible schedule \(S\) have uniquely identified duty boundaries and decompose as \(S=d_1\circ\cdots\circ d_k\), where each \(d_j\) is a feasible duty and concatenation respects inter-duty compatibility. Conversely, every compatible ordered tuple \((d_1,\ldots,d_k)\) defines a feasible schedule. If schedule cost and task incidence are additive across duties, then \(c(S)=\sum_{j=1}^k c_{d_j}\) and \(a_i(S)=\sum_{j=1}^k a_{id_j}\). Hence, for task dual prices \(\pi_i\) and no nonadditive cross-duty dual term, schedule reduced cost is the sum of the corresponding duty reduced-cost contributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unique duty boundaries give a bijection between feasible schedules and compatible duty sequences, with additive cost, incidence, and reduced cost.
assumptions_latex: Duty boundaries are uniquely determined.
Feasibility across duties is completely characterized by the stated compatibility relation.
Costs and task incidences contain no nonadditive cross-duty term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S\longleftrightarrow(d_1,\ldots,d_k),\qquad \bar c(S)=\sum_{j=1}^k\left(c_{d_j}-\sum_i\pi_i a_{id_j}\right).\]

notation.meaning: Incidence of task i in schedule S.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the Schedule–Duty Correspondence leaf, but its asserted bijection, unique maximal-duty decomposition, compatibility characterization, and reduced-cost additivity depend on a particular scheduling model for which no source is supplied.

children.title: Recursive-Substructure Pricing Family
children.top_down_role: Pricing for columns with recursive tree or bounded-interface structure.

children.title: Recursive-Tree Pricing
children.top_down_role: Pricing for columns represented by recursively composed trees.

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive-Tree Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact additive pricing over a rooted tree of recursively composable substructures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a rooted tree \(T\), a finite state set \(S_v\) at each node, local reduced-cost terms, and compatibility relations between parent and child states, process nodes in postorder. For every node \(v\) and state \(s\in S_v\), set \(F_v(s)\) to the local reduced cost plus, for each child \(u\), the minimum \(F_u(t)\) over states \(t\in S_u\) compatible with \(s\). Store minimizing child states. At the root \(r\), choose a feasible state minimizing \(F_r\), reconstruct the associated column by backtracking, and report it as improving exactly when its reduced cost is negative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Postorder dynamic programming combines compatible child states, then backtracks from the cheapest root state to obtain an exact priced column.
assumptions_latex: The decomposition graph \(T\) is a finite rooted tree.
The objective is additive over local substructures.
Parent-child states encode every cross-substructure feasibility condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_v(s)=\ell_v(s)+\sum_{u\in\operatorname{ch}(v)}\min_{t\sim_{uv}s}F_u(t),\qquad \min_{s\in S_r^{\mathrm{feas}}}F_r(s)=\min_{x\in X}\bar c(x).\]

notation.meaning: Minimum subtree reduced cost conditional on state s at v.
Compatibility of child and parent states.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and postorder recurrence fit Recursive-Tree Pricing, but the cited general dynamic-programming chapter does not specifically support the tree-decomposition pricing recurrence, its separability assumptions, or the exact reduced-cost conclusion. A tree-DP or decomposition-specific locator is required.

children.title: Bounded-Interface Substructure Pricing
children.top_down_role: Pricing for recursively composed substructures with limited interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Interface Substructure Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact separator-state pricing when recursive substructures have uniformly bounded interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a tree decomposition with \(n\) bags, maximum interface size \(w\), and at most \(q\) values per interface variable. Suppose local feasibility and reduced-cost contributions can be evaluated in polynomial time and every interaction between a processed subtree and its remainder is represented by the assignment on their interface. An exact bottom-up pricing dynamic program stores at most \(q^w\) states per directed interface. If combining a bag requires enumerating at most one additional interface assignment, its running time is \(O(nq^{w+1}\operatorname{poly}(L))\) and its state memory is \(O(nq^w)\), where \(L\) is the input encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With interface width w and q-valued variables, separator-state pricing uses exponentially many states in w but is polynomial for fixed w and q.
assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) bags and every interface contains at most \(w\) variables.
Each interface variable has at most \(q\) values.
Local evaluation and table-entry combination take \(\operatorname{poly}(L)\) time apart from state enumeration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{time}=O\!\left(nq^{w+1}\operatorname{poly}(L)\right),\qquad \text{memory}=O(nq^w).\]

notation.meaning: Maximum domain size of an interface variable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A complexity bound is appropriate for this leaf, but the stated time bound depends on an unsubstantiated combination model. Interface size alone does not establish that only one additional interface assignment must be enumerated, and no source fixes the computational model or supports the exponent and memory bound.

children.title: Substructure Composition States
children.top_down_role: State representations supporting composition of priced substructures.

assumptions_latex: All constraints coupling \(H\) to its exterior interact through \(B(H)\).
Reduced cost decomposes into an internal contribution and an exterior-completion contribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\equiv_H y\iff \left(\forall z,\;x\text{ is compatible with }z\iff y\text{ is compatible with }z\right)\text{ and }\left(\forall z\text{ compatible with both},\;\Delta(x,z)=\Delta(y,z)\right),\qquad V_H(s)=\min_{x\in s}\bar c_H(x).\]

notation.meaning: Incremental reduced cost contributed by exterior completion z to partial solution x.
Minimum internal reduced cost represented by state s.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary summaries enabling exact composition of recursively decomposed pricing subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a substructure \(H\) with interface \(B(H)\) to the unprocessed exterior, a composition state \(s_H\) is an equivalence class of feasible partial solutions in \(H\). Two partial solutions \(x\) and \(y\) are equivalent when every exterior partial solution \(z\) is compatible with \(x\) exactly when it is compatible with \(y\), and every exterior completion compatible with both contributes the same incremental reduced cost to each. A state is exact when this equivalence is preserved by every permitted composition operation. The dynamic-programming table records the minimum internal reduced cost among partial solutions in each exact state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composition state groups partial solutions having identical exterior compatibility and continuation costs, so only the cheapest representative must be retained.
knowledge_statements.title: Substructure Composition States

children.title: Interface-Width Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Pricing boundaries governed by the size of substructure interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Interface-Width Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-space explosion for exact separator-based pricing as interface width grows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an interface of \(w\) binary variables. There exist decomposed pricing instances in which every assignment \(belongsinary^w\) has a distinct set or cost of feasible exterior completions. Under these instances, no two assignments are continuation-equivalent, so any exact dynamic program whose state identifies partial solutions solely by their future behavior must retain at least \(2^w\) interface states. Thus bounded interface width yields fixed-parameter tractability for this state-enumeration scheme, whereas unbounded width destroys a polynomial bound based only on input size unless additional symmetry, dominance, or compression is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every binary boundary assignment has different completions, exact separator-state pricing needs at least 2^w states; unbounded width causes exponential growth.
assumptions_latex: The interface contains \(w\) binary variables.
States may merge partial solutions only when their feasible continuation sets and continuation costs agree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[|	ext{exact interface states}|
ge 2^w	ext{ in the worst case}.\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A failure boundary is the correct role, but the record contains corrupted notation and advances a worst-case state lower bound under a specialized future-behavior state model without a supporting source. The computational model and the claimed fixed-parameter consequence require authoritative support.

children.title: Pricing Search Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complete and incomplete uses of a pricing dynamic program.

children.title: Certifying Pricing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complete pricing searches capable of certifying the relevant oracle outcome.

children.title: Exact Pricing Search
children.top_down_role: Complete pricing exploration over the represented state space.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Pricing Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive dynamic-programming search for a globally minimum reduced-cost column.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite column set \(X\), dual vector \(inarydual\), column cost \(c(x)\), and master coefficient vector \(a(x)\), initialize the exact pricing dynamic program at its source state. Process all reachable states and every admissible transition without heuristic pruning, applying only dominance rules proved to preserve an optimal completion. Compute \(ar c(x)=c(x)-inarydual^	op a(x)\) for represented complete columns and return \(x^*\) attaining the smallest terminal value. If \(ar c(x^*)<0\), return \(x^*\) as an improving column; otherwise return the lower-bound certificate \(ar c(x)
ge0\) for every \(xelongs X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact pricing search explores all relevant states and returns either a globally cheapest improving column or a proof that none exists.
assumptions_latex: The feasible column set \(X\) is finite or has a finite exact state representation.
Every feasible column corresponds to a processed terminal path.
All pruning rules preserve at least one globally minimum reduced-cost column.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[ar c(x^*)=
min_{xelongs X}ar c(x);
quad ar c(x^*)
ge0
implies ar c(x)
ge0	ext{ for all }xelongs X.\]

notation.meaning: Feasible columns of the pricing problem.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits Exact Pricing Search, but numerous reduced-cost, membership, minimum, and inequality commands are corrupted. More importantly, no source supports the exact exploration and global certification specification, so source uncertainty must be resolved before a replacement is reviewed.

children.title: Pricing Certification
children.top_down_role: Oracle outcomes supporting a conclusive pricing determination.

knowledge_statements.title: Pricing Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable certificate that no negative-reduced-cost column remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the minimization pricing problem \(z^*=
min_{xelongs X}ar c(x)\), an exact dynamic-programming table together with its terminal optimum \(L\) is a pricing certificate when each table entry satisfies the stated recurrence, boundary values are correct, all feasible terminal states are included, and every discarded label is covered by a valid dominance relation. These checks establish \(L=z^*\). Therefore \(L
ge0\) certifies that no improving column exists, while a reconstructed feasible column \(xelongs X\) with \(ar c(x)<0\) certifies the existence of an improving column.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A validated exact DP table certifies the pricing optimum; a nonnegative optimum proves no improving column exists, while a negative feasible column proves one exists.
assumptions_latex: The pricing recurrence is exact for \(X\).
Every table entry and dominance deletion is independently checkable.
Reduced costs use the current master dual vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[L=z^*;
quad L
ge0
gives orall xelongs X,ar c(x)
ge0,
quad ar c(x)<0
gives 
exists	ext{ an improving column}.\]

notation.meaning: Certified terminal value of the exact dynamic program.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A certificate is appropriate for Pricing Certification, but the mathematical notation is corrupted and no source establishes that the proposed table, recurrence checks, coverage checks, and dominance witnesses form an independently verifiable certificate. Its encoding and verification conditions require a supporting reference.

children.title: Complete-Exploration Regimes
children.top_down_role: Search regimes retaining completeness despite pruning or decomposition.

assumptions_latex: The state-transition model represents every feasible column in \(X\).
Every retained terminal path represents a feasible column in \(X\).
The search terminates after finitely many state and transition evaluations.
Every dominance comparison is exact and preserves an optimal completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\left(\forall x\in X,\;\exists p\in P_{\mathrm{retained}}\text{ such that }\bar c(p)\leq\bar c(x)\right)\Longrightarrow \min_{p\in P_{\mathrm{retained}}}\bar c(p)=\min_{x\in X}\bar c(x).\]

notation.meaning: Retained terminal paths representing feasible columns.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which dynamic-programming pricing search is globally certifying.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the feasible pricing-column set. A pricing search is in a complete-exploration regime when it terminates after processing every reachable state that can represent a feasible column, evaluates every admissible outgoing transition from each processed state, includes every feasible terminal state, and deletes a label only by exact equivalence or by a dominance rule preserving an optimal completion. Equivalently, every column \(x\in X\) has a generated state path or is represented by a retained terminal path \(p\in P_{\mathrm{retained}}\) satisfying \(\bar c(p)\leq\bar c(x)\). If every retained terminal path also represents a feasible column in \(X\), then the minimum retained terminal value equals the global minimum reduced cost over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exploration is complete when every feasible column is generated or safely dominated by a retained feasible terminal path, making the least retained terminal value the global pricing optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Complete-Exploration Regimes

children.title: Certification Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions separating improving-column discovery from conclusive oracle outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Certification Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why incomplete search cannot certify absence of improving columns without a valid global bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incomplete search may miss a negative column; failure to find one certifies nothing unless a valid bound covers every unexplored column.
assumptions_latex: The search evaluates \(x_0\) but not \(x_1\).
No valid dominance argument or lower bound covers \(x_1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[\min_{x	ext{ inspected}}ar c(x)=0
ot
gimplies 
min_{xelongs X}ar c(x)
ge0,
quad	ext{since }
min_{xelongs X}ar c(x)=-1.\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly targets a certification failure boundary in principle, but its set, reduced-cost, minimum, membership, inequality, and implication commands are corrupted. No source is supplied for the general certification-boundary claim, so source review should precede a corrected replacement.

children.title: Incomplete Pricing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Incomplete state exploration used to locate improving columns without certification.

children.title: Heuristic Pricing
children.top_down_role: Incomplete pricing guided by problem-specific estimates or priorities.

knowledge_statements.title: Heuristic Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incomplete reduced-cost search intended to discover improving columns without proving their absence.
