knowledge_statements.title: DP-Based Separation Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state optimization oracle for a structured inequality family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\) be a finite family of valid inequalities \(a^	op x\leq b\), and suppose each pair \((a,b)\in\mathcal A\) is encoded by a terminal path of a finite-state dynamic program. Given \(\bar x\), define the path reward as \(a^	op\bar x-b\) and solve the DP maximizing this reward. If the optimal value \(v^*>0\), output the associated inequality; if \(v^*\leq0\), report that \(\bar x\) satisfies every inequality in \(\mathcal A\). The report is exact only when the DP represents all and only members of \(\mathcal A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize violation over a DP-encoded inequality family; a positive optimum gives a cut, while a nonpositive optimum certifies family-wide satisfaction.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is represented exactly by terminal DP paths.
The path reward equals the represented inequality's violation at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^*=\max_{(a,b)\in\mathcal A}(a^\top\bar x-b)\).

notation.meaning: Maximum violation computed by the dynamic program.

children.title: State Representation Omissions

knowledge_statements.title: State Representation Omissions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by omitting history needed for feasible continuation or cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two partial histories \(h\) and \(h'\) be mapped to the same state \(s\). The state representation is invalid if either their feasible continuation sets differ, \(C(h)\neq C(h')\), or some common continuation \(y\) has history-dependent incremental value that is not retained in \(s\). In that case a Bellman value indexed only by \(s\) cannot distinguish all feasible or objective-relevant futures: merging \(h\) and \(h'\) may admit an infeasible solution, remove a feasible solution, or assign an incorrect objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state is insufficient when merged histories have different feasible futures or future costs, invalidating Bellman recursion and generated solver artifacts.
assumptions_latex: The DP maps partial histories to states.
Future feasibility or incremental objective is evaluated from the stored state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(h)\neq C(h')\), or unequal continuation values, makes the merge of \(h\) and \(h'\) semantically unsound.

notation.meaning: Feasible continuations of partial history h.

review_flags: A source formalizing sufficient-state semantics and omission failures is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure phenomenon fits the leaf, but the asserted sufficient-state criterion and consequences of merging histories require an authoritative DP source.

children.title: Solver-Side Semantic Assumptions
children.top_down_role: Solver interpretations that rely on information not encoded by the supplied state model.

knowledge_statements.title: Solver-Side Semantic Assumptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility conditions required when exposing a DP representation to a solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A solver interface is semantically compatible with a dynamic-programming model only if it preserves four predicates: every exposed path decodes according to the DP decision order; every accepted path has the feasibility status asserted by the interface; its reported objective equals the decoded solution's objective; and any bound has the declared direction for every represented completion. Formally, for decoder \(\delta\) and path score \(w(P)\), an exact interface requires \(P\in\mathcal P(D)\iff\delta(P)\in F\) and \(w(P)=f(\delta(P))\). Relaxed or restricted interfaces must replace the equivalence by the appropriate containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver may consume a DP artifact only under explicit agreements on decoding, feasibility, objective values, and bound direction.
assumptions_latex: Every solver-visible path has a defined decoder \(\delta\).
The interface declares whether its diagram is exact, relaxed, or restricted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact semantic compatibility requires \(P\in\mathcal P(D)\iff\delta(P)\in F\) and \(w(P)=f(\delta(P))\).

notation.meaning: Original-model solution decoded from path P.
Objective score reported for path P.

review_flags: The exact interface contract is a formal synthesis and lacks a supplied solver-integration source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatibility conditions fit the leaf, but the biconditional is not by itself a complete exactness condition unless the path universe and decoder coverage of every feasible solution are specified. The synthesized interface contract is also unsourced.

children.title: Cross-Model Identity Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Failures in correspondence between dynamic-programming states, solver variables, columns, or network objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Model Identity Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure when DP and solver identifiers do not denote the same objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_{DP}\) and \(I_S\) be identifiers used by a DP artifact and a solver model, and let \(\phi:I_{DP}\to I_S\) translate between them. Correct transfer of coefficients, decisions, or cuts requires \(\phi\) to be injective on simultaneously distinct DP objects and to preserve their semantic attributes. If distinct identifiers \(i\neq j\) satisfy \(\phi(i)=\phi(j)\), or if an identifier is mapped to an object with different domain, coefficient, stage, or constraint meaning, then transferred paths or inequalities need not represent the DP object intended by the solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identifier translation fails when distinct objects collide or mapped objects differ in domain, coefficient, stage, or constraint meaning.
assumptions_latex: DP artifacts and the solver use potentially different identifier sets.
Transferred objects are interpreted through a map \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Noninjective or attribute-inconsistent \(\phi\) invalidates semantic preservation across the models.

notation.meaning: Identifier set of the dynamic-programming artifact.
Identifier set of the solver model.

review_flags: No supplied source formalizes identity preservation across DP and solver models.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate, but the necessity of injectivity and the listed semantic attributes depend on the artifact-transfer model. No source or formal model establishes the stated conditions.

children.title: Generated-Artifact Inconsistency
children.top_down_role: Invalid columns, bounds, or formulations arising from incomplete cross-model information.

knowledge_statements.title: Generated-Artifact Inconsistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of equivalence between a DP network and its generated solver artifact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a layered dynamic-programming network whose source-to-sink paths \(P_G\) encode feasible decisions with cost \(c_G(P)\), and let \(H\) be the generated solver model with feasible set \(F_H\) and objective \(c_H\). Exact generation requires a bijection \(\phi:P_G\to F_H\) satisfying \(c_H(\phi(P))=c_G(P)\) for every \(P\in P_G\). If this condition fails, equality of optimal values is not guaranteed. In particular, omission of a valid path makes \(H\) a restriction, while inclusion of a solver-feasible point not represented by a valid DP path makes it a relaxation or a semantically different model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generated solver model is equivalent to its DP only when feasible solutions correspond bijectively and preserve costs; omitted or spurious solutions destroy that guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite layered network with well-defined path costs.
\(H\) is intended to represent the same optimization problem as \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\text{ not cost-preserving and bijective}\;\Longrightarrow\;\min_{x\in F_H}c_H(x)=\min_{P\in P_G}c_G(P)\text{ is not guaranteed}.\)

notation.meaning: Set of source-to-sink paths in the DP network.
Feasible set of the generated solver model.
Intended correspondence between DP paths and solver solutions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited chapter-level locators do not specifically support this formulation-interface claim. A cost-preserving bijection is sufficient for exact representation but is not necessary merely for equality of optimal values, and classifying a spurious solver point as a relaxation requires both models to be embedded in a common decision space or connected by a specified mapping. The intended mathematical version therefore depends on source-supported semantics.

children.title: State-Modification Bound-Direction Failures
children.top_down_role: Incorrect state modification that reverses an intended primal or dual bounding role.

children.title: Restriction-Induced Bound Reversal
children.top_down_role: Bound-direction failures caused by state modifications intended to restrict the represented feasible region.

assumptions_latex: \(F'\subseteq F\) and \(F'\neq\varnothing\).
The same function \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}\) is used on both sets, and the displayed infima and suprema are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v'_{\min}\geq v_{\min}\) and \(v'_{\max}\leq v_{\max}\).

notation.meaning: Minimization infima and maximization suprema over the indicated feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correct optimal-value direction after restricting a DP state or transition set.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Methods for Solving Integer Programs p. 5

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F'\subseteq F\) be nonempty feasible sets obtained before and after deleting DP states, transitions, or admissible decisions, and let \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}\). Define \(v_{\min}=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\), \(v'_{\min}=\inf_{x\in F'}f(x)\), \(v_{\max}=\sup_{x\in F}f(x)\), and \(v'_{\max}=\sup_{x\in F'}f(x)\), and suppose these values are finite. Then \[v'_{\min}\geq v_{\min}\qquad\text{and}\qquad v'_{\max}\leq v_{\max}.\] Thus the restricted value is an upper bound for minimization and a lower bound for maximization. Reporting either bound in the opposite direction is a restriction-induced bound reversal. Equality in the corresponding case is guaranteed if an original optimizer for that case belongs to \(F'\), but it does not follow from set inclusion alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting feasibility cannot lower the minimization infimum or raise the maximization supremum. Treating the restricted value as the opposite type of bound reverses the valid direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Restriction-Induced Bound Reversal

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Methods for Solving Integer Programs p. 5

children.title: Relaxation-Induced Bound Reversal
children.top_down_role: Bound-direction failures caused by state modifications intended to relax the represented feasible region.

assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq R\) and \(F\neq\varnothing\).
The same function \(f:R\to\mathbb{R}\) is used on both sets, and the displayed infima and suprema are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^{R}_{\min}\leq v^{F}_{\min}\) and \(v^{R}_{\max}\geq v^{F}_{\max}\).

notation.meaning: Minimization infima and maximization suprema over the indicated feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correct optimal-value direction after relaxing a DP state or transition model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq R\) be nonempty feasible sets, where \(R\) results from adding DP states or transitions, weakening constraints, or dropping integrality, and let \(f:R\to\mathbb{R}\). Define \(v^{F}_{\min}=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\), \(v^{R}_{\min}=\inf_{x\in R}f(x)\), \(v^{F}_{\max}=\sup_{x\in F}f(x)\), and \(v^{R}_{\max}=\sup_{x\in R}f(x)\), and suppose these values are finite. Then \[v^{R}_{\min}\leq v^{F}_{\min}\qquad\text{and}\qquad v^{R}_{\max}\geq v^{F}_{\max}.\] Thus the relaxed value is a lower bound for minimization and an upper bound for maximization. Assigning either value the opposite bound direction is a relaxation-induced bound reversal. Equality in the corresponding case is guaranteed if the relaxation has an optimizer belonging to \(F\), but it does not follow from set inclusion alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing feasibility cannot raise the minimization infimum or lower the maximization supremum. Assigning the relaxed value the opposite type of bound reverses the valid direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Induced Bound Reversal

children.title: Primal Bound-Direction Errors
children.top_down_role: Incorrect primal bounding roles produced by misclassified state modifications.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Bound-Direction Errors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound orientation supplied by feasible primal DP solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\neq\varnothing\), let \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(\bar x\in F\) be any feasible solution reconstructed from a DP path. If \(v_{\min}=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\), then \(v_{\min}\leq f(\bar x)\), so \(f(\bar x)\) is an upper bound. If \(v_{\max}=\sup_{x\in F}f(x)\), then \(f(\bar x)\leq v_{\max}\), so \(f(\bar x)\) is a lower bound. Calling a feasible primal value a lower bound for minimization or an upper bound for maximization is a bound-direction error, unless separate information establishes such a bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible primal solution gives an upper bound in minimization and a lower bound in maximization; the converse labels are generally unjustified.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\in F\neq\varnothing\).
The objective \(f\) is real-valued at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{\min}\leq f(\bar x)\) and \(f(\bar x)\leq v_{\max}\).

notation.meaning: Feasible primal solution reconstructed from a DP path.
Minimization infimum and maximization supremum over the original feasible set.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Methods for Solving Integer Programs p. 5

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Methods for Solving Integer Programs p. 5

children.title: Dual Bound-Direction Errors
children.top_down_role: Incorrect dual bounding roles produced by misclassified state modifications.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(D\) are nonempty.
For the minimization case, \(g(y)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\) and \(y\in D\); for the maximization case, \(g(y)\geq f(x)\) for every such pair.
The corresponding primal infimum or supremum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In the minimization case, \(g(y)\leq v_{\min}\) for every \(y\in D\); in the maximization case, \(g(y)\geq v_{\max}\) for every \(y\in D\).

notation.meaning: Primal minimization infimum and maximization supremum, respectively.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality orientation for bounds attached to DP-derived formulations.

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Lagrangian Relaxation and Dual Formulation p. 45
3.4 Optimal Generating Multiplier and Optimal Primal-Dual Pair p. 77

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) and \(D\) be nonempty primal and dual feasible sets, with objective functions \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(g:D\to\mathbb{R}\). For a minimization primal, define \(v_{\min}=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\). If weak duality gives \(g(y)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\) and \(y\in D\), then \(g(y)\leq v_{\min}\) for every \(y\in D\), so each dual-feasible value is a lower bound. For a maximization primal, define \(v_{\max}=\sup_{x\in F}f(x)\). If weak duality instead gives \(g(y)\geq f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\) and \(y\in D\), then \(g(y)\geq v_{\max}\) for every \(y\in D\), so each dual-feasible value is an upper bound. Reversing either label is a dual bound-direction error. Dual feasibility and weak duality alone do not imply equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under weak duality, a dual-feasible value is a lower bound for a minimization primal and an upper bound for a maximization primal. Reversing either label is erroneous, and dual feasibility alone does not establish equality.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Bound-Direction Errors

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1 Lagrangian Relaxation and Dual Formulation p. 45
3.4 Optimal Generating Multiplier and Optimal Primal-Dual Pair p. 77

children.top_down_role: Cases where a state change lacks a stable restriction or relaxation interpretation for the relevant formulation.

assumptions_latex:

Any comparison uses the same real-valued objective on \(F\cup M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither \(v_M\leq v_F\) nor \(v_M\geq v_F\) follows universally from the stated set relations.

notation.meaning: Optimal values of the original and modified models for the same specified optimization sense.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: No generic bound when modified and original DP feasible sets are incomparable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) and \(M\) be nonempty feasible sets for an original model and a state-modified model, respectively. Suppose neither \(M\subseteq F\) nor \(F\subseteq M\). For a common real-valued objective on \(F\cup M\), set inclusion alone then supplies no universal ordering between the original optimal value \(v_F\) and the modified optimal value \(v_M\), whether both models are minimized or both are maximized. Consequently, a modification that removes some original feasible states and introduces other states cannot be classified as a restriction or relaxation without an additional mapping or dominance condition, and its value is not automatically a primal or dual bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the original and modified feasible sets are incomparable, set inclusion alone determines no optimal-value ordering. A modification that both removes and adds solutions therefore needs an additional mapping or dominance argument before its value can be treated as a bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Ambiguous State Modification Regimes

children.title: Explicit-Network Size Explosion
children.top_down_role: DP-derived formulations becoming too large to materialize or solve directly.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-Network Size Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential materialization cost for a DP-derived layered network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a \(T\)-stage DP represented by a layered directed acyclic graph with reachable state set \(S_t\) at layer \(t\) and transition set \(A_t\subseteq S_t\times S_{t+1}\). Its explicit representation contains \(N=\sum_{t=0}^{T}|S_t|\) nodes and \(M=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}|A_t|\) arcs, requiring \(\Omega(N+M)\) time and storage merely to materialize. If, at some layer, all subsets of \(b\) independent binary resource components are reachable and must remain distinct, then \(|S_t|\geq 2^b\). Hence explicit construction has worst-case storage and generation time \(\Omega(2^b)\), even before applying a network optimization algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit DP network costs at least its node-plus-arc count to build, and independent binary resource states can force exponentially many nodes.
assumptions_latex: The DP network is stored explicitly by enumerating every reachable state and transition.
At one layer, \(2^b\) binary resource configurations are reachable and pairwise state-distinct.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\geq 2^b\) and explicit materialization requires \(\Omega(2^b)\) time and storage.

notation.meaning: Reachable DP states at layer t.
Transitions from layer t to layer t+1.
Total explicit node and arc counts.

children.title: Numerical State-Identity Failures
children.top_down_role: Loss of reliable state equivalence when discretized resources do not align with the original model.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical State-Identity Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unsafe merging of numerically keyed DP states with different feasible continuations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r\in\mathbb{R}^k\) be an exact DP resource vector and let \(q:\mathbb{R}^k\to K\) be the numerical key used to identify stored states. Exact state merging requires that whenever \(q(r_1)=q(r_2)\), the states \(r_1,r_2\) have identical feasible continuation sets and identical continuation costs, up to any explicitly tracked offset. If there exist \(r_1\neq r_2\) with \(q(r_1)=q(r_2)\) but an action feasible after only one state, or with unequal continuation values, then replacing both by one stored state can delete a valid path, introduce an invalid path, or change the optimum. Thus a non-injective discretization is safe only when it respects continuation equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rounded states may be merged only when they have the same feasible continuations and continuation costs; otherwise the DP can lose, invent, or misvalue paths.
assumptions_latex: DP feasibility or future cost may depend on the exact accumulated resource vector \(r\).
Stored-state identity is determined by the key \(q(r)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(r_1)=q(r_2)\not\Rightarrow r_1\sim r_2\) implies that quotient-state optimization need not preserve feasibility or optimal value.

notation.meaning: Equality of feasible continuations and continuation costs, modulo a tracked offset.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind and local topic match, but the chapter-level citation does not specifically support numerical key collisions or the asserted continuation-equivalence criterion. Identical continuation sets and costs characterize a strong exact quotient, while preservation of only the optimal value can require weaker conditions. A source specifying which equivalence notion is intended is needed before choosing a reliable mathematical version.
